15 
 
 
 
 CHAPTER 1 
 
 
Introduction 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
16 
 
Memory consolidation: introducing sleep and emotion  
Memory is critical to our survival. This innate property of cognition, often taken 
for granted, allows us to react and behave appropriately in all manner of 
situations. Without memory, we would not have a language; the words you are 
reading would be meaningless. We would have no history, concepts or values, 
and forming relationships with one another would present an impossible task. 
Virtually every aspect of our lives is heavily dependent on an active and flexible 
memory system.  
 
When memories are formed, they are not instantaneously stabilised within our 
long-term memory networks. Instead, newly acquired information must undergo 
a period of consolidation, whereby it is gradually adjusted from a weak and 
fragile trace to a strong an enduring representation. The consolidation of newly 
formed memories can be modulated by several factors, such as emotion. A 
number of studies have demonstrated that memories associated with the 
evocation of emotion, as defined by valence (pleasant/unpleasant) or arousal 
(high/low), are encoded and persist more strongly than their more neutral or 
mundane counterparts (Kensinger, 2004; McGaugh, 2004). Importantly, the 
mnemonic influence of emotion increases as the delay between learning and 
testing increases (Anderson, et al., 2006; Dolcos, et al., 2005; Kleinsmith & 
Kaplan, 1963; Sharot & Phelps, 2004) indicating that emotion mediates slow, 
time-dependent consolidation processes (Hu, et al., 2006). Moreover, when 
compared to neutral memories, emotional memories are commonly associated 
with increased responses in the amygdala and medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) 
(Buchanan, 2007), suggesting that affective representations undergo a distinct 
form of processing at retrieval. 
 
Nearly a century of research has demonstrated that memory consolidation 
processes can also be modulated by post-learning sleep (Fowler, et al., 1973; 
Gais, et al., 2006; Jenkins & Dallenbach, 1924; Newman, 1939; Van Ormer, 
1933; Wilhelm, et al., 2011; Yaroush, et al., 1971). These studies and others 
17 
 
utilising modern physiological research techniques (Gais, et al., 2007; 
Sterpenich, et al., 2007; Sterpenich, et al., 2009; Takashima, et al., 2006) have 
contributed to the concept of sleep-dependent consolidation and theories 
regarding the mechanisms underpinning this effect (Born & Wilhelm, 2011; 
Diekelmann & Born, 2010; Tononi & Cirelli, 2003, 2006).   
 
Several studies have indicated that sleep preferentially consolidates emotionally 
affective memory representations, and that this process is principally supported 
by rapid eye movement sleep (REM) (Hu, et al., 2006; Nishida, et al., 2008; 
Payne, et al., 2008; Wagner, et al., 2001; Wagner, et al., 2006), although a 
recent study failed to reveal such effects (Baran, et al., 2012). As such, a 
modern theory of sleep and emotional memory processing proposes a REM-
dependent mechanism, which maintains the relative strength of a newly formed 
representation whilst alleviating its associative emotional propensity 
(Van der Helm, et al., 2011; Walker, 2009; Walker & van der Helm, 2009). While 
compelling, this line of research is still in its relative infancy and a number of 
questions regarding the processes underpinning sleep-dependent emotional 
memory consolidation remain unanswered.  
 
The aim of this thesis is to examine some of these key research questions and 
expand our understanding of how emotional and neutral memories are 
influenced by post-learning time and sleep. Broadly, these questions can be 
segregated into two main themes: 1) Mechanisms – what are the neural 
mechanisms underpinning time- and sleep-dependent emotional memory 
processing? 2) Specificity – are focal and contextual elements of emotional and 
neutral memory influenced in different manners by post-learning sleep? 
 
An overview of research examining the contribution of time and sleep to 
emotional memory processing, along with a detailed description of the 
questions that will be addressed in this thesis, is provided at a later stage of this 
chapter. However, for now it is important to offer the reader a broader review of 
18 
 
the literature and theory that is relevant to all of the work carried out in this 
thesis. Thus, a detailed introduction to memory systems, consolidation and 
sleep-dependent memory processing will be provided at this point.  
 
Memory systems and consolidation 
Despite an extensive wealth of literature, memory remains at the forefront of 
cognitive neuroscience research, with investigators relentlessly contributing to 
our knowledge and understanding of this complex phenomenon. Due to its 
considerable diversity, a number of memory classification systems have been 
proposed, the most accepted of which involving the distinction between 
declarative and non-declarative memory (Squire & Zola, 1996). Declarative 
memory relates to representations for facts (semantic memory) and events 
(episodic memory) that are subject to conscious retrieval (Eichenbaum, 1997). 
Neural models of episodic declarative memory highlight the importance of the 
medial temporal lobe (MTL) for encoding and short-term retrieval, with particular 
emphasis placed on the hippocampal region (Squire, 1992). Over time however, 
declarative retrieval is thought to become less dependent on the hippocampus 
and related structures, presumably due to some transfer of retrieval 
dependency to the neocortical networks (Frankland & Bontempi, 2005; 
Sutherland & McNaughton, 2000). Non-declarative memory on the other hand, 
is expressed through behavioural changes and includes procedural motor skill 
and action learning, as well as conditioning and priming (Walker, 2008). The 
hippocampal formation is not thought to be of any particular importance for the 
non-declarative memory system, which is instead principally reliant upon the 
striatocortical network (Doyon & Benali, 2005). 
 
Psychological investigations of human memory processing have traditionally 
focused on one of, or a combination of, its three fundamental components: 
encoding, consolidation and retrieval. Encoding refers to the process by which 
new information is learned and formed into a memory trace or representation, 
whereas retrieval refers to the subsequent recall of memories. Consolidation 
19 
 
however, which is the fundamental focus of this thesis, refers to a process of 
stabilisation or enhancement, where recently formed, weak and labile memory 
traces are transformed into strong and enduring representations over time. 
 
Memory consolidation is a broad term in its own right and can be used to 
describe two processes, which are separated on the basis of distinct 
neurophysiological properties (Dudai, 1996, 2004). The first, known as synaptic 
consolidation, is accomplished within minutes or hours after learning and 
involves the stabilisation of synaptic changes in the neural circuits that encoded 
the representation (Born, et al., 2006). Thus, within a short time after training, 
memories that have undergone synaptic consolidation may become resistant to 
interference or agents, which would normally inhibit the formation of long-term 
memory (Davis & Squire, 1984; Freeman, et al., 1995). The second, referred to 
as systems consolidation, can take days, months or even years to complete and 
is thought to involve a form of neural reorganisation, whereby the brain regions 
supporting retrieval are modified over time (Dudai, 2004). As a theoretical 
construct, systems consolidation is principally associated with declarative 
memory (Born, et al., 2006). While this should not be taken to imply that a 
process of neural reorganisation does not occur in the non-declarative domain, 
an exclusive focus upon the systems consolidation of declarative memories will 
be taken from this point forward.  
 
Models of memory consolidation 
Although it is agreed that declarative memory consolidation involves a form of 
neural reorganisation, the specific nature of this process has been a matter of 
intense debate. Accordingly, the standard model of  consolidation (Marr, 1971a, 
McClelland et al., 1995, Frankland and Bontempi, 2005b) and the multiple trace 
theory (Moscovitch & Nadel, 1998; Nadel & Moscovitch, 1997) offer two 
relatively diverse accounts of mnemonic processing in the declarative domain. 
A description of both of these models, and the evidence supporting them, is 
offered below. 
20 
 
The standard model of consolidation 
When encoding new information, we are faced with the problem of doing so 
without overwriting pre-existing knowledge. In order to cope with this issue, the 
standard model (Frankland & Bontempi, 2005; Marr, 1971; McClelland, et al., 
1995) proposes that memory consolidation processes are dependent upon two 
distinct memory stores (see figure 1). During learning, information is thought to 
be encoded within both the short-term hippocampal circuitry and the long-term 
neocortical networks. Due to the nature of neocortical encoding however, 
various multi-modal components of an experience are believed to exist in a 
highly distributed form. As such, when retrieving recently formed memories, the 
hippocampus is proposed to integrate or ‘bind’ patterns of activation within 
these disparate neocortical traces in order to bring a coherent memory 
representation to consciousness (Eichenbaum, 2004).  Over time, experience-
dependent patterns of neural activity are thought to be covertly reactivated in 
this hippocampal-neocortical network, leading to a progressive strengthening or 
establishment of cortico-cortical connections and concurrent weakening of 
hippocampal-cortical connections. As a result, declarative representations 
become independent of the limited hippocampal store and gradually integrated 
within the long-term neocortical memory network, which also forms the locus of 
their retrieval. Importantly, this process also allows the hippocampus to maintain 
a refreshed encoding capacity, enabling new information to be learned 
throughout life.  
 
A central line of evidence for this model is derived from the amnesic population. 
Many amnesia patients display a temporally graded form of retrograde amnesia 
(RA), whereby episodic memories formed prior to the brain damage are 
impaired, but the extent of the impairment depends on the age of the memory at 
the time that the atrophy occurred, with more recently formed memories 
suffering the most (Wixted, 2004).  Temporally graded RA is commonly 
associated with damage to the MTL, including the hippocampal circuitry, 
whereas flat non-graded RA is associated with neocortical trauma (Squire, et al., 
2001). Such findings imply that the role of the hippocampus in declarative 
21 
 
memory is temporally limited, and that the storage of memories is ultimately 
dependent on the neocortex (Dudai, 2004). Similarly, animal studies have 
shown that retrieval performance is unaffected by hippocampal lesions that 
occur several weeks after learning (Tse, et al., 2007; Zola-Morgan & Squire, 
1990), whereas manipulations of the cortex preferentially disrupt the retrieval of 
old, but not recently formed, memories (Frankland, et al., 2004; Maviel, et al., 
2004). 
 
Neuroimaging research with animals and humans has provided further support 
for the standard consolidation model. By mapping changes in brain metabolic 
activity at the regional level in mice, Bontempi and colleagues (1999) 
demonstrated that new spatial memories were associated with increased 
responses in the hippocampal formation. Contrastingly, recall of older spatial 
representations was predominantly associated with activation in several cortical 
areas, including the prefrontal, anterior cingulate and temporal cortices. 
 
Figure 1: The standard model of consolidation (Fran kland & Bontempi, 2005) 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
The retrieval of recently formed memories is highly dependent on the hippocampus, which integrates widely distributed neocortical memory modules into a coherent memory trace. Successive reactivation of this hippocampal-neocortical network leads to a strengthening of cortico-cortical connections, eventually allowing memories to become independent of the hippocampus. 
22 
 
Using functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) techniques, Takashima 
and colleagues (2009; 2006) reported that, over time, the retrieval of declarative 
memories became less reliant on the hippocampus and more reliant on several 
neocortical regions. In addition, recent work has shown that hippocampal 
responses associated with image recollection after 3 days were absent 6 
months later, where increased responses were found in several cortical regions 
instead (Sterpenich, et al., 2007; Sterpenich, et al., 2009). However, while these 
studies provide considerable support for a time-dependent redistribution of 
declarative memories away from the hippocampus, neuroimaging research 
comparing the neural correlates of memory at different delays should be 
approached with some caution. Specifically, it is possible that a reduction in 
hippocampal activity following a delay of several months, relative to as many 
hours, may reflect a weaker memory trace, rather than an active consolidation 
mechanism. Issues such as this cannot be ignored in fMRI studies of neural 
reorganisation, and should always be considered when interpreting the resulting 
data, especially when the delay between encoding and retrieval is extensive.  
 
The multiple trace theory 
In contrast to the standard consolidation model, multiple trace theory proposes 
that the temporal gradient of amnesia is dependent upon the extent of 
hippocampal damage and the type of declarative memory being probed.  
Accordingly, consolidation processes are thought to evoke the generation of 
multiple memory traces in the hippocampus, which are linked to corresponding 
modules in distributed neocortical networks. Since hippocampal traces are 
presumed to be associated with spatial and temporal context, the retrieval of 
contextually rich episodic memories is believed to be dependent upon a 
hippocampal-neocortical memory network. However, as neocortical 
representations are believed to be context free or semantic in nature, the 
retrieval of remote semantic memories is thought to be possible even in the 
absence of a functioning hippocampus. Therefore, in terms of the amnesic 
population, incomplete hippocampal atrophy should selectively disrupt the 
retrieval of recent rather than remote episodic or semantic memories as trace 
23 
 
proliferation should protect older episodic memories from partial hippocampal 
trauma. Comprehensive hippocampal damage however, should abolish all 
episodic memories, irrespective of age, but spare remote semantic memories, 
which are predominantly dependent upon the neocortex (Frankland & Bontempi, 
2005). 
 
In support of this view, several patient studies have reported that major bilateral 
lesions of the hippocampal formation result in a flat, non-graded form of RA for 
autobiographical and detailed spatial memories (Cipolotti, et al., 2001; Damasio, 
et al., 1985; Rempel-Clower, et al., 1996; Rosenbaum, et al., 2000; Tulving, et 
al., 1988), whilst general semantic knowledge remains largely intact (Barr, et al., 
1990; McCarthy & Warrington, 1992). In a fascinating study, Warrington and 
McCarthy (1988) specifically tested a patient’s general semantic knowledge for 
words that had come into circulation during the period for which he had dense 
RA for autobiographic episodes and public events. Importantly, he knew the 
meaning of several words, including AIDS, telecom and shuttle and could also 
provide detailed descriptions for them. Similar results were reported by 
Verfaellie and colleagues (1995), who found that a group of amnesic patients 
displayed only a slight, but not significant, loss of memory for words that had 
entered the vocabulary in the preceding 25 years. 
 
Functional imaging techniques have provided an additional avenue of research 
to support the multiple trace theory. Bosshardt and colleagues (2005) for 
example, reported that, relative to an interval of 1 day, episodic memory 
information was associated with stronger responses in the hippocampus and 
neocortex 1 month after learning.  In a similar study, the retrieval of episodic 
memories was associated with increased activity in the left hippocampus 
following a delay of 24 hours, relative to 10 minutes (Bosshardt, Schmidt, et al., 
2005). Moreover, Janzen and colleagues (2008) reported that object memories 
encoded 12 hours before retrieval were associated with stronger responses in 
the bilateral hippocampus than those encoded immediately before retrieval.  
24 
 
The multiple trace theory therefore offers a framework to account for instances 
when MTL damage results in extensive, non-graded RA. However, this model is 
not without its share of difficulty. Teng and Squire (1999) for example, reported 
on a patient who had excellent episodic memory from his youth despite 
extensive bilateral lesions of the MTL, indicating that episodic representations 
may eventually become entirely independent of the hippocampus.  
 
Both the standard model and multiple trace theory are based on the principle 
that mnemonic representations are reorganised as consolidation processes 
unfold over time. However, while systems consolidation is thought to require 
several months or even years to complete (Dudai, 2004), animal and human 
research into this process has produced highly inconsistent findings. Studies 
within the amnesic population for example, have reported temporally graded 
memory loss over many years (Corkin, 1984; Scoville & Milner, 1957; Squire & 
Alvarez, 1995; Squire, et al., 2001), whereas animal studies using surgical 
(Anagnostaras, et al., 1999; Clark, et al., 2002) and pharmacological (Maviel, et 
al., 2004; Riedel, et al., 1999) lesions of the hippocampus have shown a 
gradient which varies from only a few days to several weeks. Human 
neuroimaging research on the other hand, suggests that a substantial degree of 
mnemonic reorganisation occurs over just one day (Janzen, et al., 2008; 
Takashima, et al., 2009). Inconsistencies such as these may suggest that an 
initial ‘short term’ form of systems consolidation occurs across the course of 
hours or days, whilst a more refined ‘long term’ consolidation process unfolds 
over the coming weeks, months and years. Future research should focus on 
these issues and endeavour to gain further insight into the time scale of 
memory consolidation in the declarative domain.  
 
Of the two memory consolidation models described in this section, the standard 
model is generally more established. Importantly, the standard model also 
forms an integral component of a core theory surrounding the principal focus of 
this thesis: sleep-dependent memory consolidation. This theory will be 
25 
 
discussed in detail at a later stage of this chapter. For now however, an 
introduction to sleep and its role in memory processing will be provided.  
 
Sleep and memory consolidation 
The cycle of sleep 
Like memory, sleep is not a unitary phenomenon, but is broadly divided into two 
main stages: rapid eye movement sleep (REM) and non-rapid eye movement 
sleep (NREM). In addition to the global muscle atonia and rapid eye movements 
which characterise REM, these principal stages of sleep are highly dissociable 
on the basis of several features including, distinct electrophysiology and 
neurochemistry (Pace-Schott & Hobson, 2002), temporal regulation (Borbely & 
Achermann, 1999) and regional brain activity (Maquet, et al., 1996). In primates 
and felines, NREM can be subdivided into stages one to four (see figure 2) 
which, in the same ascending order, correspond to deeper forms of sleep.  
 
Figure 2: The cyclic occurrence of sleep stages (Wa lker, 2008) 
 
 
 
 
 
 
The early portion of nocturnal sleep is dominated by slow-wave sleep (SWS), whereas rapid eye movement sleep (REM) prevails in the latter half of the night. 
 
In the electroencephalogram (EEG) stage one sleep is characterised by an 
oscillation at the frequency of approximately 9 to 12 Hz known as alpha activity 
and sharp waves called vertex spikes (Rosenzweig, et al., 2005). Stage two 
26 
 
sleep is recognisable through the presence of sleep spindles, which are 
observed as short synchronous bursts of activity in the EEG with a frequency 
between 12 and 15Hz, and K complexes (Born, et al., 2006). NREM stages 
three and four are collectively known as slow-wave sleep (SWS), which is 
characterised by slow oscillations (~0.75 Hz), delta activity (1 - 4 Hz) and sleep 
spindles (Steriade, 2003). Throughout the night, NREM and REM periods occur 
in ultradian cycles, each of which last approximately ninety minutes (Peigneux, 
et al., 2001). Due to an underlying circadian rhythm and a homeostatic 
regulation of SWS, the early portion of nocturnal sleep in humans is dominated 
by SWS and contains very little REM. This relationship is reversed in the late 
part of the night however, where SWS subsides and REM prevails (Born, et al., 
2006). 
 
Sleep-dependent memory consolidation  
In their pioneering study, Jenkins & Dallenbach (1924) reported that the 
retention of nonsense syllables was better after sleep relative to wakefulness. 
Since then, a substantial body of evidence has accumulated to support the 
hypothesis that sleep plays an active role in declarative memory processing, an 
effect known as sleep-dependent memory consolidation (Gais, et al., 2006; 
Lovatt & Warr, 1968; Newman, 1939; Takashima, et al., 2006; Van Ormer, 1933; 
Wilhelm, et al., 2011).   
 
In addition to examining sleep in its entirety, a number of earlier investigations 
also sought to assess the specific components of sleep which contribute to the 
formation of declarative memory. Due to its links with vivid dreams and 
cognitive processing, research was initially focused on REM (Born, et al., 2006). 
A popular method was to deprive participants of post-learning REM and 
compare their memory performance against those who had slept normally. 
However, in addition to producing inconsistent findings (Empson & Clarke, 1970; 
Greenberg, et al., 1983; Tilley & Empson, 1978), these studies were 
confounded on the basis of the stress associated with REM deprivation.  Other 
27 
 
studies addressed post-learning changes in REM, but these too produced 
conflicting results (Castaldo, et al., 1974; De Koninck, et al., 1989). Using an 
innovative design, Ekstrand and colleagues (Fowler, et al., 1973; Yaroush, et al., 
1971) began to compare the relative contributions of SWS and REM to 
declarative memory consolidation. After learning a list of paired associates, 
participants would either sleep in the early half of the night (11pm-3am), which 
is dominated by SWS, or in the late half of the night (3am-7am) where REM 
prevails (see figure 2), and then have their memory tested. Interestingly, the 
authors reported that declarative memory performance was better following a 
four-hour retention period of early SWS-rich nocturnal sleep relative to an 
equivalent period of late REM-rich nocturnal sleep. These findings and those of 
more recent studies (Plihal & Born, 1997, 1999a) have contributed to the dual 
process hypothesis, which proposes that declarative memory consolidation is 
augmented by SWS, whereas REM supports the formation of non-declarative 
memories. This hypothesis is important as it forms a fundamental component of 
a model central to sleep and declarative memory processing, known as active 
systems consolidation. This model is discussed in detail at a later stage of this 
chapter.  
 
The dual process hypothesis has however, been criticised on the basis of 
inconsistent research findings. Rauchs and colleagues (2004) for example, 
reported that REM-rich late sleep had a beneficial impact upon the retention of 
declarative memories, whereas Gais and colleagues (2000) observed 
improvements in procedural learning over a period of SWS-rich early sleep. An 
alternative sequential hypothesis (Ambrosini & Giuditta, 2001; Giuditta, et al., 
1995) suggests that memory consolidation may be equally reliant upon SWS 
and REM. Specifically, an initial processing operation is thought to weaken non-
adaptive memory traces during SWS, whilst the remaining representations are 
believed to be stored again in a more efficient configuration during the ensuing 
REM episode (Giuditta, et al., 1995).  In support of this view, Stickgold and 
colleagues (2000b) reported that performance improvements in a visual search 
task were correlated with the amount of SWS and REM obtained in the first and 
last quarter of the night respectively. However, this study and others like it 
28 
 
(Stickgold, et al., 2000a) have focused on procedural learning alone, thus the 
applicability of the sequential hypothesis to declarative memory consolidation is 
unknown.  
 
Models of sleep-dependent consolidation  
Decades of committed research has led to the formulation and development of 
two central models of sleep-dependent memory processing, known as the 
active systems consolidation model (Born, et al., 2006; Born & Wilhelm, 2011; 
Diekelmann & Born, 2010) and the synaptic homeostasis hypothesis (Tononi & 
Cirelli, 2003, 2006). While these models both highlight the importance of SWS 
for mnemonic processing, their mechanistic perspectives are entirely different. 
A comprehensive account of each model, including supporting evidence, is 
provided below.  
 
Active systems consolidation 
As a modern adaptation of the standard consolidation model (Marr, 1971; 
McClelland, et al., 1995), the active systems model proposes that the sleep 
slow oscillation plays a resounding role in the reactivation, and subsequent 
reorganisation of hippocampal-dependent declarative memory representations 
(see figure 3). Generated in the neocortex, slow oscillations reflect widespread 
synchronised down-states of neuronal hyperpolarisation and neural silence, 
followed by depolarising up-states of excitation where neural firing is similar to 
that of waking levels (Steriade, 2006; Steriade & Timofeev, 2003). Via efferent 
pathways, slow oscillations also synchronise activity in memory relevant brain 
regions outside of the neocortex. These include the thalamus, where sleep 
spindles are generated (De Gennaro & Ferrara, 2003), and the hippocampus 
where memory reactivations occur conjointly with bursts of activity in the 
hippocampal EEG known as sharp-wave ripples (Kudrimoti, et al., 1999). 
Accordingly, previous work has demonstrated that hippocampal sharp-wave 
ripple events, thalamocortical sleep spindles and replay-related activity in the 
neocortex can be temporally driven by slow oscillations (Mölle, et al., 2009; 
29 
 
Mölle, et al., 2002; Mölle, et al., 2004; Mölle, et al., 2006). This synchronising 
influence of the slow oscillation allows for the formation of spindle-ripple events, 
whereby hippocampal ripple activity and associated memory information 
become integrated within the oscillatory troughs of thalamocortical sleep 
spindles (Mölle, et al., 2009; Siapas & Wilson, 1998; Sirota & Buzsaki, 2005). 
Thus, synchronous inputs fed back to the neocortex in parallel from the 
thalamus and hippocampus are thought to be critical for the permanent 
redistribution of declarative retrieval dependency (Born, 2010).  
 
Figure 3: The active systems consolidation model (W alker, 2009) 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Hippocampal-neocortical replay, as described in the standard model of consolidation, is thought to be augmented by SWS-dependent processes, allowing a rapid and more efficient reorganisation of memory 
 
Evidence 
The development of the active systems model can be largely attributed to Born 
and colleagues (Born, et al., 2006; Born & Wilhelm, 2011; Diekelmann & Born, 
2010), who have provided a substantial body of evidence to support their 
perspective (Marshall, et al., 2006; Marshall, et al., 2004; Plihal & Born, 1999a, 
1999b; Rasch, et al., 2007). An overview of this evidence, and that of others, is 
provided below.  
30 
 
Electrophysiology: slow oscillations 
Since the slow oscillation forms a major constituent of the active systems model, 
it is not surprising that a number of studies have examined the role of these 
electrophysiological phenomena in offline mnemonic processing. Using 
transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS), which involves the application of 
weak electrical stimulation to the scalp in order to acutely modify the membrane 
potential of neurons in the brain, Marshall and colleagues (2006; 2004) provided 
direct evidence for a causal role of slow oscillations in declarative memory 
consolidation. In these studies, healthy participants received tDCS over the 
bilateral pre-frontal cortex during post-learning SWS-rich early sleep at a 
frequency of 0.75Hz, which corresponds to the dominant frequency of naturally 
occurring slow oscillations. As compared to sham stimulation, tDCS had a 
positive impact upon memory for verbal and non-verbal paired associates, but 
not finger tapping or mirror tracing, indicating that slow oscillation stimulation 
had enhanced the consolidation of hippocampal-dependent declarative 
representations exclusively. In addition, 0.75Hz tDCS induced an immediate 
increase in SWS, endogenous slow oscillations and spindle activity in the frontal 
cortex. Stimulation with a faster frequency of 5Hz however, had no effect upon 
declarative memory performance and actually tended to suppress endogenous 
slow oscillations. Similarly, Kirov and colleagues (2009) reported that 
declarative memory retention was unaffected when slow oscillation stimulation 
was applied during post-learning wakefulness. Taken together, these findings 
suggest that slow oscillation stimulation during SWS amplifies the normal 
pattern of activity in the thalamocortical networks, thus providing strong support 
for a role of slow-oscillations in declarative memory consolidation (Born, 2010).  
 
Electrophysiology: sleep spindles 
A considerable amount of research has also focused on the spindle oscillation, 
another important electrophysiological component of the active systems model. 
Numerous studies have indicated that spindles are critical to the formation of 
stabilised declarative memory representations. Gais and colleagues (2002) for 
example, reported an increase in sleep-spindle density after an intense 
31 
 
declarative learning period, the extent of which was positively correlated with 
subsequent memory performance. Importantly, no such relationship, or change 
in spindle architecture, was observed for a non-learning control task which was 
matched in terms of visual stimulation and cognitive demands. These findings 
are consistent with those of Schabus and colleagues (2004), who found that 
overnight benefits for verbal memory retention were correlated with sleep 
spindle activity, and Clemens and colleagues (2006; 2005), who identified 
region-specific relationships between spindles and different forms of declarative 
memory. Specifically, verbal memory retention was predicted by spindles in left 
frontocentral areas, whilst spindles detected in parietal regions were associated 
with visuo-spatial memory performance. Nonetheless, since other studies have 
suggested that sleep spindles also play an important role in procedural motor 
learning (Fogel & Smith, 2006; Nishida & Walker, 2007), spindle activity may 
support consolidation processes in numerous systems of memory.  
 
Sleep spindles can also be separated into fast frequency (12-13.5Hz) and slow 
frequency (13.5-15Hz) subtypes (Knoblauch, et al., 2003). Since fast spindles 
are associated with activity in the hippocampal circuitry, lateral and medial 
prefrontal cortices and posterior parietal regions (Schabus, et al., 2007), they 
are thought to be more amenable to the consolidation of declarative information. 
Accordingly, a number of recent studies have shown that fast sleep spindles, 
but not slow, can predict both memory performance and learning ability in the 
declarative domain (Mander, et al., 2011; Saletin, et al., 2011; van der Helm, et 
al., 2011). 
 
Mnemonic reactivation 
In order for a sleep-dependent reorganisation of memories to occur, it is thought 
that the neural networks implicated in encoding must be subsequently 
reactivated during SWS. Thus, a key component of sleep and memory research 
is focused on neural replay in animals and humans. Initial research with rodents 
demonstrated that temporal patterns of encoding activity, observed during a 
32 
 
hippocampal-dependent spatial task, were replayed during post-learning SWS 
(Kudrimoti, et al., 1999; Sutherland & McNaughton, 2000; Wilson & 
McNaughton, 1994), and also during REM (Louie & Wilson, 2001). Moreover, Ji 
and Wilson (2007) reported that during SWS, hippocampal replay tended to 
precede that of the visual cortex in a temporally coordinated manner. Similar 
effects have been observed in humans. Using positron emission tomography 
(PET), Peigneux and colleagues (2004) reported that patterns of regional brain 
activity observed during a declarative spatial learning task were also active 
during post-learning SWS, and that the extent of this activity was positively 
correlated with spatial memory performance after sleep. While compelling, 
reactivation studies with humans and animals were criticised for failing to 
demonstrate a causal role of neural replay in memory consolidation. Indeed, it 
has been acknowledged that neural replay may reflect a mere epiphenomenon 
of previous waking activity, rather than a genuine mechanism of memory 
consolidation (Gais & Born, 2004). 
 
In view of this issue, recent investigations have indicated that SWS-dependent 
neural replay can be manipulated in humans with associative mnemonic cues, 
providing strong evidence for a causal role of this phenomenon in offline 
memory processing. Rasch and colleagues (2007) for example, reported that 
memory performance on a hippocampal-dependent visuo-spatial task was 
significantly better when participants were re-presented with a learning 
associated odour during SWS, relative to an odourless control vehicle. 
Importantly, control experiments showed that this effect was specific to 
declarative and not non-declarative memory, and that it did not occur when the 
odour was re-presented during REM or a waking retention interval. Moreover, 
functional imaging data revealed an increase in hippocampal activity when 
odour cues were re-presented during SWS, suggesting that odour re-exposure 
stimulated neural replay in memory relevant brain regions, potentially enhancing 
an active reorganisation of declarative information. In support of these findings, 
Diekelmann and colleagues (2011) reported that re-presenting learning-
associated odours during SWS, as compared to wakefulness, increased the 
resistance of visuo-spatial memories to retroactive interference, providing 
33 
 
further evidence that neural replay underpins sleep-dependent consolidation 
processes in the declarative domain. Research examining a causal role of 
SWS-dependent neural replay has also been extended to auditory modalities. In 
a study by Rudoy and colleagues (2009), participants undertook a visuo-spatial 
learning task in which study pictures were paired with semantically related 
sounds (e.g. a picture of a kettle and a sound of whistling). Participants then 
took a diurnal nap and were re-presented with half of the sounds during SWS.  
Interestingly, picture-location memory accuracy was better for items whose 
associative sounds were re-presented, suggesting that auditory cues may have 
augmented the neural replay, and thus consolidation, of individual memory 
representations.  
 
Neural reorganisation 
Neuroimaging techniques have provided a powerful tool for demonstrating the 
temporal reorganisation of declarative memories, and how this process is 
influenced by post-learning sleep. Using fMRI, Takashima and colleagues (2006) 
showed that, over 90 days of consolidation, the successful retrieval of image 
memories elicited a gradual but continuous decrease of activation in the 
bilateral hippocampus and a concomitant increase of activation in the bilateral 
ventromedial prefrontal cortex (vmPFC). Crucially, the original learning phase 
was followed by a diurnal nap, during which participants’ sleep was monitored 
with polysomnography (PSG). In addition to predicting superior memory 
performance in the subsequent retrieval test, the duration of post-learning SWS 
was associated with reduced retrieval-related responses in the left anterior 
hippocampus, providing evidence that this sleep stage supports an active 
redistribution of declarative memories. In a later study, Takashima and 
colleagues (2009) showed that the retrieval of face-location memories was 
associated with a decrease of activity in the posterior hippocampus, and an 
increase of activity in the neocortical circuitry, following 24 hours of sleep-
inclusive consolidation. Moreover, while functional connectivity between the 
hippocampus and neocortex decreased with consolidation, cortico-cortical 
connectivity between representational regions increased. In a similar fMRI study, 
34 
 
Gais and colleagues (2007) reported that post-learning sleep, as compared to 
an equivalent period of sleep deprivation, enhanced hippocampal activity, and 
connectivity between the hippocampus and mPFC, during the recall of word 
pairs 48 hours after learning. Importantly, 6 months later, retrieval was 
associated with stronger responses in the mPFC when learning took place 
before a night of sleep, whereas retrieval in the sleep deprivation group was 
associated with increased activation in the left hippocampus. These findings 
suggest that sleep deprivation on the first post-encoding night may disrupt both 
short- and long-term consolidation processes in declarative memory (Gais, et al., 
2007).   
 
Memory selectivity 
While vast amounts of information are encoded by the brain throughout the day, 
natural cognitive limitations allow for only a small proportion of this information 
to be stored within long-term memory. Therefore, the active systems model also 
predicts that memory consolidation is a selective process, such that the most 
important or salient aspects of memory are strengthened ahead of neutral or 
mundane information over sleep. Recent research has demonstrated that 
increasing the salience of a memory after learning can modulate its affinity for 
sleep-dependent memory processes. In a study by Wilhelm and colleagues 
(2011), participants encoded both verbal and non-verbal declarative memories 
before overnight sleep or an equivalent period of wakefulness. Critically, after 
learning, participants were either informed that their memory would 
subsequently tested, thus increasing the salience of the newly acquired 
information, or were left ignorant to the experimental procedures. Importantly, 
sleep-related memory benefits only occurred when participants had been 
informed of the upcoming test, suggesting that retrieval expectancy induced a 
targeted form of consolidation over sleep. Strikingly, knowledge of the upcoming 
test was also associated with increased slow oscillation activity, and the extent 
of this change was correlated with subsequent memory performance.  
Increases in SWS-dependent sleep spindles were also correlated with 
declarative memory performance for those that expected the test, but only in the 
35 
 
non-verbal domain. Similarly, using a verbal directed forgetting paradigm 
(Nowicka, et al., 2011; Wylie, et al., 2008), a study by Saletin and colleagues 
(2011) indicated that stimuli cued to be remembered, relative to those cued to 
be forgotten, were selectively strengthened over a post-learning nap, and that 
the extent of this effect was predicted by fast sleep spindles. Collectively, these 
findings support the notion of a targeted consolidation process, whereby the 
most important, and thus salient, components of memory are preferentially 
strengthened during post-learning sleep.   
 
Additional evidence 
Importantly, the active systems model predicts that the hippocampus has a 
limited encoding capacity. Therefore, if a transfer of declarative retrieval 
dependency from the hippocampus to the neocortex is modulated by sleep, 
then blocking sleep should reduce the ability of the hippocampus to encode new 
information. Using fMRI, Yoo and colleagues (2007) reported that a single night 
of sleep deprivation led to a substantial reduction in hippocampal encoding 
activity, and a subsequent memory impairment at retrieval. Thus, sleep appears 
to be critical for both strengthening recently formed memories and preparing the 
brain for the acquisition of new information the following day.  
 
The synaptic homeostasis hypothesis 
In more recent years an alternative model for the role of SWS in memory 
consolidation has emerged, namely the synaptic homeostasis hypothesis 
(Tononi & Cirelli, 2003, 2006). During SWS, neocortical neurons predominantly 
fire in waves of activity with frequencies of ~0.75Hz. This slow wave activity 
(SWA) 1  increases linearly with previous time spent awake and gradually 
                                                          
 
1 Slow wave activity (SWA) and slow oscillation activity are terms used to describe the same electrophysiological phenomena. SWA will be used when describing the synaptic homeostasis hypothesis in order to maintain clarity with the terms adopted by its authors (Tononi and Cirelli, 2003, 2006). 
 
36 
 
decreases during the course of sleep (Borbely & Achermann, 1999). Such a 
homeostatic regulation of SWA forms a critical component of the synaptic 
homeostasis hypothesis, as it is thought to be linked to some restorative 
function of sleep for memory. 
 
Figure 4: The synaptic homeostasis hypothesis (Tono ni & Cirelli, 2006)  
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Levels of sleep slow-wave activity (SWA) are thought to be homeostatically regulated by the amount of synaptic potentiation that occurs during wakefulness. The role of SWA is to proportionally downscale synaptic strength to baseline levels, a process which is proposed to remove weak and inefficient synapses, leaving behind a more efficient memory trace. 
 
This hypothesis makes three core predictions, each of which will be described 
in their mechanistic order. Firstly, in accordance with long-term potentiation 
(LTP), learning is thought to potentiate a large and distributed proportion of 
cortical synapses, resulting in an overall increase in synaptic weight. Secondly, 
the homeostatic regulation of SWA is believed to be predicted by the degree of 
synaptic potentiation that has occurred during previous wakefulness. Thirdly, 
rather than being mere epiphenomenon of waking synaptic potentiation, SWA is 
proposed to hold a critical mnemonic function. Specifically, through repeated 
sequences of depolarisation and hyperpolarisation, a process known as 
synaptic downscaling is believed to promote a generalised reduction in synaptic 
37 
 
strength, which continues until the total synaptic weight converging on each 
neuron returns to baseline levels. 
 
Since downscaling is thought to occur proportionally, the relative strengths of 
cortical synapses, and thus memory traces, can be maintained. However, weak 
and inefficient synapses, which may represent labile or irrelevant components 
of memory, are proposed to be downscaled beyond a preservation threshold 
and eradicated (see figure 4).  Accordingly, after sleep, only the strongest 
memory traces are maintained in cortical circuitry, but in a more efficient form, 
which also affords superior recall. Importantly, downscaling not only offers a 
potential mechanism of consolidation, but also prevents synaptic 
overpotentiation during wakefulness, allowing new learning to continue 
throughout life.   
 
Evidence  
Research supporting the synaptic homeostasis hypothesis has accumulated in 
relation to each of its three core predictions. The evidence for each of these 
points will be addressed in the same order that they were described above.  
 
Learning and synaptic potentiation  
Animal research has demonstrated that a global increase in synaptic density 
can be induced by exposing subjects to an enriched waking environment 
(Klintsova & Greenough, 1999). Similarly, Knott and colleagues (2002) found 
that stimulating a mouse whisker for 24 hours produced a selective net increase 
of synaptic density on corresponding cortical neurons. Molecular studies have 
shown that LTP-related genes are upregulated during wakefulness (Ying, et al., 
2002), an effect which can be accentuated when animals engage in increased 
explorative behaviour within their environment, or are kept awake through 
gentle handling (Cirelli & Tononi, 2000b; Tononi & Cirelli, 2006). During sleep 
38 
 
however, the expression of LTP-related genes is dramatically reduced or 
completely absent (Cirelli, et al., 2004; Cirelli & Tononi, 2000a). 
 
Synaptic potentiation and slow-wave homeostasis 
Since learning is thought to potentiate cortical synapses, sleep SWA should not 
depend on the amount of previous wakefulness alone, but also the quality or 
eminence of the waking period (Tononi & Cirelli, 2003). Accordingly, research 
has shown that when animals spend more time exploring their environment, and 
thus enriching their experience, markers of synaptic potentiation are 
upregulated and the amount of SWA in subsequent sleep is increased (Tononi 
& Cirelli, 2006). Indeed, if these findings are to be taken as evidence for this 
component of the synaptic homeostasis hypothesis, then the opposite effect 
should be observed when wakefulness is not accompanied by changes in 
synaptic density, namely the homeostatic increase in SWA should not occur 
(Tononi & Cirelli, 2006). Animal lesion studies have provided evidence to this 
effect. The commencement of LTP is highly reliant upon the induction of 
noradrenalin (Walling & Harley, 2004), and lesions to noradrenergic system 
reduce waking levels of LTP-related genes to those observed during sleep 
(Cirelli & Tononi, 2000a). As such, Cirelli and colleagues (2005) showed that, 
despite the length and timing of sleep remaining normal, noradrenergic lesions 
led to a substantial reduction in the SWA peak normally observed following 
enriched waking activity, and a decrease in the normal SWA response to sleep 
deprivation.  
 
Synaptic downscaling and mnemonic processing 
Using high definition EEG, Huber and colleagues (2004) examined the sleep of 
healthy human participants following the learning of a visuomotor task in which 
participants unconsciously adapted to rotation learning whilst reaching for visual 
targets. One week earlier or later, participants learned a control task which was 
kinematically identical to the visuomotor task, but did not involve implicit rotation 
learning. On the basis of previous PET research, the experimenters reasoned 
39 
 
that the right parietal cortex would be implicated in rotation learning, meaning 
that an increase in synaptic potentiation would occur in this area. Indeed, 
relative to the control task, rotation adaption learning was associated with a 27 
per cent increase of SWA over a small cluster of electrodes at the right parietal 
cortex. Strikingly, post-sleep performance enhancements were exclusively 
correlated with SWA increases in this right parietal area, providing strong 
evidence for a mnemonic impact of localised changes in synaptic weight. More 
recently, Huber and colleagues (2006) examined whether the opposite effect 
could be observed by negating the amount of experience-dependent 
potentiation obtained throughout the day. As expected, a period of arm 
immobilisation, which was assumed to reduce plastic changes occurring during 
wakefulness, reduced the levels of SWA observed in associated cortical areas 
during subsequent sleep.  
 
Summary and conclusions 
While the slow oscillation forms an essential component of both the active 
systems model and the synaptic homeostasis hypothesis, these frameworks 
offer entirely different perspectives of sleep-dependent memory processing. The 
active systems model suggests that memories are actively strengthened and 
reorganised during sleep, whereas the synaptic homeostasis hypothesis 
proposes that sleep enhances learning and memory through a proportional 
downscaling of synapses impinging on each neuron. 
 
Although its core features have been supported by a diverse wealth of 
behavioural, molecular and electrophysiological evidence, the synaptic 
homeostasis hypothesis faces a rather challenging issue in that the mnemonic 
influences of several subcortical structures, including the hippocampus, are not 
accounted for. This does not mean to say however, that the active systems 
model is flawless. While it explains how declarative information is reorganised 
and integrated within a long-term neocortical memory network, active systems 
theory does not explain how post-learning sleep strengthens the synaptic 
40 
 
connections underpinning newly formed memory traces (Diekelmann & Born, 
2010). Owing to an upregulation of plasticity-related immediate early gene 
activity during REM (Ribeiro, et al., 2002; Ulloor & Datta, 2005), recent work has 
suggested that this sleep stage may mediate a process of synaptic 
consolidation upon the memory representations that are reorganised during the 
preceding SWS period (Diekelmann & Born, 2010). While compelling, evidence 
supporting such a view is relatively scarce (Ficca & Salzarulo, 2004; Stickgold, 
et al., 2000b) and other work has suggested that SWS and REM may hold an 
alternative complimentary role in memory consolidation. Specifically, the 
‘overnight alchemy’ hypothesis (Walker & Stickgold, 2010) proposes that SWS 
facilitates the preservation of new memories, whilst REM supports an 
assimilation of novel and older information into rich associative networks. This 
model is supported by a large body of work suggesting that sleep, and REM in 
particular, may support an integrative stage of mnemonic processing (Cai, et al., 
2009; Ellenbogen, et al., 2007; Stickgold, et al., 1999; Walker, et al., 2002), and 
explains how sleep both protects memories and allows them to develop into 
more generalised representations of the world around us (Walker & Stickgold, 
2010). Nevertheless, further research is undoubtedly required to reconcile the 
relative contributions of SWS and REM to declarative memory consolidation.  
 
Emotional memory  
Emotional memories can be defined as declarative representations which, upon 
being retrieved, are associated with the evocation of emotion, pertaining to their 
valence (pleasant/unpleasant) or arousal (boring/exciting). Accordingly, 
functional imaging research has demonstrated that, when compared to neutral 
memories, affective representations are associated with increased responses in 
emotional processing centres of the brain, such as the amygdala (Buchanan, 
2007). An fMRI study by Maratos and colleagues (2001) for example, reported 
that recognition memory for previously presented (old) relative to novel words 
activated brain areas commonly associated with declarative retrieval including 
the precuneus, cingulate cortex and parahippocampal gyrus. However, old 
words retrieved in an emotional context, relative to a neutral context, elicited 
41 
 
stronger responses in brain regions that are not typically active in recognition 
tasks, such as the amygdala. While activity in the amygdala did not differentiate 
between positive and negative old words, positive old words were associated 
with stronger responses in the mPFC than negative and neutral old words, 
suggesting a potential role of this structure in reward processing (O'Doherty, et 
al., 2001). Importantly, these findings suggest that the retrieval of emotional 
memory representations utilises brain areas that are also involved in the 
retrieval of neutral memories, in addition to a subset of supplementary areas 
that are commonly implicated in emotional processing, such as the amygdala 
and mPFC (Buchanan, 2007). 
 
It is well established that the emotional strength of newly acquired information 
can modulate the formation of declarative memory (McGaugh, 2002, 2004). 
Several studies have shown that emotional memories are better remembered 
than those with a more neutral or mundane tone (Bradley, et al., 1992; 
Kensinger & Corkin, 2004). The effects of emotion on memory retention 
increase over hours (LaBar & Phelps, 1998; Sharot & Phelps, 2004), days 
(Kleinsmith & Kaplan, 1963), weeks (Anderson, et al., 2006) and even years 
(Dolcos, et al., 2005), indicating that emotion promotes slow, time-dependent 
consolidation processes (Hu, et al., 2006). Findings such as these may be 
interpreted as evidence to support the memory modulation hypothesis (LaBar & 
Cabeza, 2006; McGaugh, 2004; McGaugh, et al., 1996). Accordingly, through 
the engagement of stress hormones, the amygdala is thought to exert a 
neuromodulatory influence upon MTL memory areas in response to emotionally 
arousing experiences, augmenting consolidation processes and the persistence 
of memories over time (Ritchey, et al., 2008). 
 
While a substantial proportion of the evidence supporting this framework has 
arisen from animal studies (Hatfield & McGaugh, 1999; Liang, et al., 1990; 
McGaugh, 2002; Roozendaal & McGaugh, 1996), it is most appropriate in the 
context of this thesis to focus on studies of human emotional memory. A 
popular paradigm used in event-related fMRI research examines encoding-
42 
 
related brain activity for learned items that are subsequently remembered or 
forgotten (LaBar & Cabeza, 2006; Paller & Wagner, 2002). Using this method, 
researchers can identify the difference to memory (Dm) effect, which describes 
a pattern of brain activity thought to represent successful encoding operations 
(Paller & Wagner, 2002). Dolcos and colleagues (2004b) found that the Dm 
effect in the amygdala and MTL memory structures was greater and more 
strongly correlated for emotional relative to neutral pictures.  Similarly, Ritchey 
and colleagues (2008) reported that encoding activity in the amygdala was a 
better predictor of subsequent memory for emotional pictures. While this 
difference did not vary with the delay between encoding and retrieval, the extent 
to which amygdala-MTL encoding connectivity predicted subsequent memory 
for emotional pictures increased with time. Taken together, these studies 
provide considerable evidence that the amygdala plays a critical role in the 
long-term consolidation of emotionally affective memories. 
 
Sleep and emotional memory processing  
Emotional memory representations are often found to be selectively 
strengthened across post-learning sleep (Holland & Lewis, 2007; Walker, 2009; 
Walker & van der Helm, 2009), an effect demonstrated with texts (Wagner, et 
al., 2001; Wagner, et al., 2006) and pictures (Hu, et al., 2006; Nishida, et al., 
2008; Payne, et al., 2008), although a recent study indicated that this is not 
always true for the latter (Baran, et al., 2012). As mentioned earlier, sleep 
dependent consolidation processes appear to act in a highly selective manner, 
such that the most salient components of memory are strengthened ahead of 
their more neutral or mundane counterparts (Born & Wilhelm, 2011; Wilhelm, et 
al., 2011). In keeping with this proposal, it is possible that the systems 
consolidation of highly salient emotional memories, which is modulated by the 
amygdala-dependent processes during wakefulness, may also be augmented 
during overnight retention intervals. Accordingly, emotionally salient memories 
may undergo an active and targeted consolidation process during post-learning 
sleep, such that a reduction in hippocampal retrieval dependency occurs in a 
more rapid and efficient manner.  
43 
 
Nevertheless, a large number of questions regarding the mechanisms and 
specificity of both time- and sleep-dependent consolidation processes in 
emotional and neutral memory remain unanswered. The aim of this thesis is to 
examine these questions and refine current knowledge regarding the role of 
time and sleep in emotional and neutral memory processing. 
 
At this point, an overview of the research that is undertaken in this thesis will be 
provided. In order to maintain clarity with the two core research themes, the 
work relating to mechanisms and specificity, and their sub-topics, will be 
considered separately 
 
Mechanisms 
Neural reorganisation of emotional memory 
As described earlier, a number of neuroimaging studies have demonstrated that 
time-dependent consolidation processes are accompanied by changes in the 
brain regions supporting retrieval, indicating that declarative memory 
representations are actively reorganised as they are integrated within long-term 
memory (Sterpenich, et al., 2007; Sterpenich, et al., 2009; Takashima, et al., 
2009; Takashima, et al., 2006). More recently, researchers have also utilised 
fMRI techniques to examine the temporal reorganisation of emotionally affective 
memory representations. Two studies (Lewis, et al., 2011; Payne & Kensinger, 
2011) reported that the retrieval of emotional memories was associated with 
increased responses in several memory-relevant brain regions after 12 hours of 
overnight consolidation, including the parahippocampal gyrus, precuneus, 
amygdala, posterior cingulate and vmPFC. Similarly, Sterpenich and colleagues 
(2007) showed that the successful recollection of emotional pictures elicited 
increased responses in the hippocampus and various cortical areas after 3 days 
of consolidation. 
  
 
44 
 
While compelling, the aforementioned studies and others like them have 
addressed the reorganisation of emotional memories over relatively short 
consolidation periods of 12 hours to 3 days (Lewis, et al., 2011; Payne & 
Kensinger, 2011; Sterpenich, et al., 2007), or longer periods of 6 months to 1 
year (Dolcos, et al., 2005; Sterpenich, et al., 2009). Therefore, how memories 
are redistributed across a more intermediate period of consolidation forms an 
unexplored area of research. In addition, how the extent to which a memory is 
consolidated over time impacts upon the brain regions supporting its retrieval is 
unknown. Accordingly, in chapter 2 we used event-related fMRI to examine the 
neural correlates of emotionally positive, negative and neutral image memories 
that had been consolidated across 1 week (remote memory) relative to 30 
minutes (recent memory).  Furthermore, a combined analysis of our behavioural 
and functional imaging data enabled us to examine how the relative strength of 
remote memories influenced the brain regions associated with their retrieval. 
 
The role of SWS and REM in emotional memory processing 
Although previous research has established a relationship between mnemonic 
reorganisation and post-learning SWS (Takashima, et al., 2006), it is unclear 
whether SWS or another parameter of sleep augments a functional 
redistribution of emotional memory representations. Recent work has suggested 
that slow oscillation activity supports the consolidation of highly salient memory 
traces (Wilhelm, et al., 2011). Therefore, emotional memories, which also carry 
a high degree of salience, may be selectively strengthened during states of 
vigilance when slow oscillations prevail, namely SWS. However, due in part to 
its unique biology, REM is thought to play a particularly important role in the 
consolidation of emotional memory representations (Walker, 2009; Walker & 
van der Helm, 2009). During REM, levels of hippocampal acetylcholine (ACh) 
are four times higher than those of SWS, and two times higher than those of 
wakefulness (Marrosu, et al., 1995). Since experimental enhancements of ACh 
have a beneficial impact upon emotional memory retention (Power, 2004), such 
a procholinergic REM state, in addition to increased amygdala activity (Maquet, 
et al., 2000), may offer an optimum environment for the consolidation of 
45 
 
affective information (Hu, et al., 2006). In line with this view, previous studies 
have revealed predictive relationships between REM and subsequent emotional 
memory performance (Nishida, et al., 2008; Wagner, et al., 2001), although 
others have failed to show such an effect (Baran, et al., 2012). In chapter 3 we 
used PSG and event-related fMRI to examine the role of SWS, REM and other 
sleep stages in the reorganisation of emotionally positive, negative and neutral 
image memories over 24 hours (remote memory), as compared to 30 minutes 
(recent memory). 
 
Collectively, the research reported in chapters 2 and 3 also allowed us to 
investigate the reorganisation of emotional and neutral image memories over 
periods between 24 hours and 1 week, and how post-learning sleep may impact 
upon this process. Since systems consolidation is a long-term process, 
occurring across may days, weeks, months or even years (Dudai, 2004), it is 
certainly possible that a consolidation-related change in brain activity 
associated with the recollection of emotional image memories after 24 hours 
may be accentuated after 1 week.  
 
Mnemonic replay of emotional representations 
While recent work has indicated that SWS-dependent neural replay can be 
manipulated with auditory cues, leading to better memory retention (Rudoy, et 
al., 2009), the particular nature of these effects is unclear. Specifically, 
stimulating neural reactivation could either strengthen a memory directly, or 
indirectly ‘prime’ a memory for a targeted consolidation process which unfolds 
throughout the ensuing SWS period. Moreover, since previous studies have 
focused on the reactivation of neutral memories alone, it is unclear how 
manipulating replay with auditory cues would influence the processing of 
affective memory information. Using a napping paradigm with PSG, we 
attempted to address these issues in chapter 4 by investigating how SWS-
dependent auditory cued replay impacted upon the consolidation of emotionally 
negative and neutral picture-location memories.   
46 
 
Specificity 
The consolidation of emotional context memory over sleep 
Declarative representations contain both central and contextual memory 
components. Central memory information relates to the focal point of a memory, 
such as an object or a person. Contextual information however, may relate to a 
number of factors, such as the emotion associated with the central memory 
component itself. Therefore, if you were to make a cup of coffee, and the 
experience was problem-free, it would be encoded within an emotionally neutral 
context. However, if you were unfortunate enough to accidentally spill boiling 
water out of the kettle and scald your hand, the same coffee making experience 
would be tainted with a rather unpleasant contextual association. While a 
number of studies have shown that central components of emotional memory 
can be preferentially consolidated over sleep (Hu, et al., 2006; Payne, et al., 
2008; Wagner, et al., 2001), research addressing how sleep influences the 
processing of emotional context memories is somewhat limited (Lewis, et al., 
2011). In chapter 5, we investigated how a daytime nap, relative to an 
equivalent period of wakefulness, influenced the consolidation of emotionally 
negative and neutral context memories. PSG sleep monitoring and sleep 
spindle analyses also enabled us to explore the parameters of sleep which play 
a more resounding role in contextual memory processing.  
 
Sleep and environmental context-dependent memory 
Chapter 5 is focused on the sleep-dependent consolidation of emotional 
contexts, which are explicitly associated with the to-be-learned materials. 
However, as mentioned above, contextual components of memory can relate to 
several elements of an experience, including those which exist in a more implicit 
form. An example of such an implicit contextual association is the specific 
environment of the learning episode, otherwise known as the environmental 
context. Numerous studies have contributed to what is known as the 
environmental context reinstatement effect (Smith, 1979; Smith, et al., 1978), 
whereby memory performance is typically better in a context which is 
47 
 
environmentally congruent to that of the learning phase (Godden & Baddeley, 
1975; Parker, et al., 2007; Schab, 1990; Smith, 1985). However, as with 
emotional memory, studies addressing the consolidation of environmental 
associations over sleep are limited (van der Helm, et al., 2011). Therefore, in 
chapter 6 we moved to a broader domain of contextual memory processing and 
investigated how environmental context-dependent memory effects were 
influenced by a night of post-learning sleep, as compared to an equivalent 
period of daytime wakefulness.
