48 
 
 
 
CHAPTER 2 
 
 
      The neural correlates of emotional memory retrieval 
after thirty minutes or one week of consolidation 
 
 
Scott A. CAIRNEY, University of Manchester, UK 
Simon J. DURRANT, University of Lincoln, UK 
Penelope A. LEWIS, University of Manchester, UK 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
This chapter is based on a manuscript that is being prepared for submission for peer 
review. 
49 
 
Abstract 
Recent neuroimaging research has indicated that the brain regions supporting 
emotional memory are reorganised over relatively short (hours to days) or long 
(months to years) periods of consolidation. How affective representations are 
redistributed across a more intermediate retention interval however, forms an 
unexplored area of research. Here, we used event-related functional magnetic 
resonance imaging (fMRI) to compare the neural correlates of recognition 
memory for emotionally positive, negative and neutral images that had 
undergone 1 week (remote memory), relative to 30 minutes (recent memory), of 
consolidation. In addition, by combining behavioural and functional imaging data, 
we examined how the extent to which image memories were consolidated over 
1 week related to the brain regions exclusively associated with their retrieval. 
Overall remote memory (i.e. combined across valences), as compared to recent, 
was associated with increased responses in superior and middle temporal gyri. 
Although positive remote (vs. recent) memory was associated with stronger 
activity in the right superior frontal gyrus, negative and neutral remote memories 
were not associated with any greater brain response than their recent 
counterparts. Interestingly, the extent of memory consolidation occurring over 1 
week predicted the strength of the neural response in several brain regions 
supporting remote retrieval. Specifically, more strongly consolidated remote 
memories were associated with increased responses in the right precuneus, 
whereas more weakly consolidated remote memories were associated with 
increased activity in several occipital areas, including the calcarine sulcus. 
These findings suggest that the retrieval of strong and enduring remote image 
memories is more dependent upon general memory-relevant brain areas, such 
as the precuneus. The retrieval of weaker, more labile remote image memories 
however, appears to be more reliant upon sensory-specific memory regions, 
such as the primary visual or ‘calcarine’ cortex.  
 
Keywords : Emotional Memory, Memory Consolidation, Precuneus, Occipital 
Lobe, Neocortex.  
50 
 
Introduction 
When we learn new information, it is not automatically integrated within our 
long-term memory networks. Instead, newly formed and fragile memories must 
undergo a period of consolidation, during which they are stabilised and become 
resistant to interference from distracting stimuli, injuries or toxins (Dudai, 2004). 
A number of factors can impact upon memory consolidation processes, 
including the emotional strength of newly acquired information (Kensinger & 
Corkin, 2004). As such, emotionally affective memories are often better 
remembered than their neutral counterparts (Bradley, et al., 1992; McGaugh, 
2004; McGaugh, et al., 1996), an effect which increases over time (Anderson, et 
al., 2006; Dolcos, et al., 2005; Sharot & Phelps, 2004), indicating that emotion 
induces an enhanced but gradual consolidation process (Hu, et al., 2006). 
 
According to the standard model of consolidation (Frankland & Bontempi, 2005; 
Marr, 1971; McClelland, et al., 1995), the long-term storage of declarative 
memories is underpinned by a process of neural reorganisation, whereby 
retrieval dependency is gradual shifted away from the short-term hippocampus 
to the long-term neocortical memory networks. In support of this view, retrieval 
performance in animals is unaffected by hippocampal lesions when they occur 
several weeks after learning (Tse, et al., 2007; Zola-Morgan & Squire, 1990), 
whereas lesions of the cortex preferentially disrupt the retrieval of old, but not 
recently formed, memories  (Frankland, et al., 2004; Maviel, et al., 2004). 
Similarly, in humans, damage to the medial temporal lobe, including the 
hippocampal formation, can produce extensive deficits in new learning, whilst 
memory for information acquired well before the lesion is often left intact (Squire 
& Zola-Morgan, 1991). On the other hand, extensive and flat retrograde 
amnesia is usually associated with neocortical atrophy in both the lateral and 
anterior temporal lobe (Squire, et al., 2001).  
 
Neuroimaging techniques have provided an invaluable resource for examining 
the temporal reorganisation of declarative memory in animals and humans. 
Using the (14C)2-deoxyglucose autoradiographic method (Sokoloff, et al., 1977) 
51 
 
with mice, a technique that is similar to position emission tomography (PET) in 
humans, Bontempi and colleagues (1999) reported that new and old spatial 
memories were predominantly associated with activity in respective 
hippocampal and cortical brain regions. Making use of functional magnetic 
resonance imaging (fMRI) techniques, Takashima and colleagues (2009; 2006) 
demonstrated that time-dependent consolidation processes in humans were 
accompanied by a gradual decrease of activity in the hippocampus and 
concomitant increase of activity in several neocortical areas. In addition, 
Sterpenich and colleagues (2007; 2009) reported that hippocampal retrieval 
responses observed after 3 days of consolidation were absent 6 months later, 
where instead, recollection was associated with increased activity in frontal and 
parietal cortices. However, also see Bosshardt and colleagues (2005; 2005), 
who reported a time-dependent increase in hippocampal retrieval dependency. 
 
Building on these findings, recent research has addressed the temporal 
reorganisation of emotionally affective memory representations. Using fMRI, 
two studies showed that, following 12 hours of overnight consolidation, the 
retrieval of emotional memories was associated with stronger responses in a 
number of memory relevant brain regions, including the ventromedial prefrontal 
cortex (vmPFC), parahippocampal gyrus, amygdala and precuneus (Lewis, et 
al., 2011; Payne & Kensinger, 2011). In addition, Sterpenich and colleagues 
(2009) demonstrated that the recollection of emotionally negative images was 
associated with increased activity in the vmPFC, amygdala and precuneus 
following several months of consolidation, highlighting the significance of these 
regions for long-term emotional memory processing. 
 
While the aforementioned studies provide insight to the neural mechanisms 
underpinning the consolidation of emotional memories, a number of questions 
remain unanswered. Firstly, previous research has focused on the 
reorganisation of affective representations across relatively short intervals of 12 
hours to 3 days (Lewis, et al., 2011; Payne & Kensinger, 2011; Sterpenich, et 
al., 2007), or longer intervals of 6 months to 1 year (Dolcos, et al., 2005; 
52 
 
Sterpenich, et al., 2009). How memories are redistributed across a more 
intermediate retention interval however, forms an unexplored area of research. 
Secondly, how the extent to which an emotional memory is consolidated over 
time relates to the brain regions supporting its retrieval has, to our knowledge, 
not been previously investigated.  
 
Accordingly, in the present study, we used event-related fMRI to examine the 
neural regions associated with the successful retrieval of emotionally positive, 
negative and neutral image memories that had undergone 1 week (remote 
memory), as compared to 30 minutes (recent memory), of consolidation. We 
predicted that remote memories would be associated with greater activity than 
recent memories in several neocortical brain areas, and that these effects would 
be amplified for emotionally affective representations. Moreover, by 
incorporating a measure of behavioural consolidation (remote hits – recent hits) 
into our functional imaging analyses, we were able to explore how the extent of 
consolidation occurring over 1 week relates to the brain regions exclusively 
associated with remote image retrieval.  
 
Materials and Methods 
Participants 
Twenty-one (9 male) healthy participants aged 19-36 years (mean age = 24.00, 
S.D. ± 5.24) were recruited on a voluntary basis. However, 5 participants were 
excluded due to data corruption (3) and incorrect or poor task performance (2). 
Thus, the data presented in this study is based upon the remaining 16 
participants (8 male) aged 19-35 years (mean age = 23.63, S.D. ± 4.91). As 
evaluated with pre-study screening questionnaires and telephone interviews, 
participants had no history of neurological, depressive or sleep disorders and 
reported a regular sleep pattern over the month preceding the study. Aside from 
females using the contraceptive pill, participants were also free from any form of 
medication. All participants were native English speakers and were right-
handed, as indicated by a score of 80% or higher on the Edinburgh handedness 
53 
 
inventory (Oldfield, 1971).  Written informed consent was acquired from all 
participants in accordance with the research ethics committees of The 
University of Manchester and The University of Liverpool. Participants were 
required to refrain from alcohol, caffeine and daytime napping from 24 hours 
prior to the study start and throughout the study period.  Before any scanning 
took place, participants were assessed by a qualified radiographer to ensure 
their safety within an MRI environment. The Stanford Sleepiness Scale was 
also used to check for differences in alertness between the experimental 
sessions. Participants were compensated with a standard payment of £50.  
 
Stimuli  
Two  hundred and seventy images were taken from the international affective 
picture system (IAPS) (Lang, et al., 2005) for use in this study. IAPS pictures 
range from everyday scenes, to images of injury, violence, decay and 
contaminated foods, and are rated on 9-point scales for valence (1 = negative; 
5 = neutral; 9 = positive) and arousal (1 = calm; 9 = exciting). Images were 
initially selected on the basis of their emotional valence rating and split into 
three sets: 90 positive, 90 negative and 90 neutral. Thus, the mean valence 
rating of each picture set was significantly different (positive: 7.55 [S.D. ± 0.36], 
negative: 2.40 [S.D. ± 0.34], neutral: 5.03 [S.D. ± 0.19], F(2,178) = 40101.16; p 
<0.0001). Although the mean arousal rating of the neutral picture set was 
significantly different to that of the emotional picture sets (positive: 5.35 [S.D. ± 
0.80], negative: 5.39 [S.D. ± 0.48], neutral: 3.10 [S.D. ± 0.52], F(2,178) = 420.15; 
p <0.0001), the difference in arousal rating between positive and negative 
picture sets alone was not significant t(89) = 0.34; p = 0.73. 
 
One hundred and eighty images (60 positive, 60 negative, 60 neutral) were 
used for the encoding and retrieval phase, while the remaining 90 images (30 
positive, 30 negative, 30 neutral) were used as foils in the retrieval phase alone. 
Of those images used for encoding, half were presented 1 week prior to 
retrieval and referred to as ‘remote’ images whilst the other half, known as 
54 
 
‘recent’ images, were presented 30 minutes prior to retrieval. The order in which 
these subsets were used (i.e. as remote images or recent images) was 
counterbalanced across participants.   
 
Experimental protocol 
All participants undertook two experimental sessions, separated by a period of 1 
week (± 1.5) hours. Both sessions took place at the Magnetic Resonance and 
Image Analysis Research Centre (MARIARC), University of Liverpool. Before 
arriving for the first study session, participants were explicitly informed of all the 
experimental procedures, including the memory tests. The experimental design 
is illustrated in figure 5A. 
 
Session one 
The first experimental session began at 2pm (± 30 minutes) and lasted 
approximately 25 minutes. Here, participants were presented with 90 
photographic images on a computer screen (30 positive, 30 negative and 30 
neutral) in random order twice, with a short interval (< 1 min) between both 
encoding runs. At the beginning of the encoding task, participants saw a black 
screen with a white crosshair in the centre for 2000ms. They were then 
presented with the first image for 3000ms, which was followed by the black 
screen and white crosshair for another 2000ms until the next image was 
presented. This pattern continued for each remaining image until the end of the 
task. In one encoding run, using the corresponding keys on the keyboard, 
participants were asked to rate the images in terms of their emotional valence 
on a scale of 1-7 (1 = highly negative, 4 = neutral and 7 = highly positive), whilst 
in the other, participants were asked to rate the same images for emotional 
arousal, again on a scale of 1-7 (1 = non-arousing or boring and 7 = highly 
arousing or exciting). Participants were asked to respond as quickly as possible, 
and were advised that they could make their responses during either the 
presentation of the picture or the subsequent crosshair. The order of rating type 
(i.e. valence or arousal rating in the first or second encoding run) was 
55 
 
counterbalanced across participants. Upon completion participants were free to 
leave. 
 
Session two 
One week later (2pm ± 1 hour), participants repeated the procedures of session 
one but with a new batch of 90 images. Approximately 30 minutes after 
completing encoding (3pm ± 1 hour), participants began the retrieval phase, 
which took place inside the MRI scanner. The retrieval test was in the form of a 
recognition task, which encompassed all previously encoded remote and recent 
images and an additional 90 previously unseen foils (30 positive, 30 negative 
and 30 neutral), making a total of 270 images. The retrieval phase was divided 
into two scanning sessions, with a short (< 1 min) break between each. Thus, 
both sessions consisted of 90 encoded images and 45 foils presented in a 
randomised order. At the beginning of the retrieval task, participants saw a 
black screen with a white crosshair in the centre for 2000ms. They were then 
presented with the first image for 1000ms, which was followed by the black 
screen and white crosshair for another 2000ms until the next image was 
presented. This pattern continued for each remaining image until the end of the 
task. For each presented image, participants were required to make a 
remember/know/new judgement (Tulving, 1985) using a three-button keypad 
which they held in their right hand. A “remember” (R) response was provided 
when participants could consciously recollect seeing the image in one of the 
previous encoding sessions. A “know” (K) response indicated that participants 
knew that they had seen the image at encoding, but could not retrieve any 
contextual details about its occurrence. Finally, a “new” (N) response was 
provided when participants believed that they had not seen the image in either 
encoding session. Participants were asked to make their responses as quickly 
and accurately as possible, and were advised that they could make their 
responses during either the presentation of the picture or the subsequent 
crosshair. The encoding and retrieval tasks are illustrated in figure 5B. 
 
56 
 
Figure 5 : (A) Study procedures for all participants and (B)  encoding and retrieval tasks  
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
A: In the first session, participants encoded 90 (30 positive, 30 negative and 30 neutral) images. One week later, participants encoded another 90 images before completing a recognition task for all previously learned images in the MRI scanner. B: At encoding, participants were required to rate each image in terms of its emotional valence (unpleasant-pleasant) and emotional arousal (boring-exciting). At retrieval, participants were required to indicate if they recognised the image with recollection (R response) or familiarity (K response), or if they thought that the image was new (N response). 
57 
 
Equipment 
Experimental task 
The experimental tasks were created using Cogent 2000 developed at the 
functional imaging laboratory (FIL), University College London. The tasks were 
written and implemented using MatLab© version 6.5 on a Toshiba Satellite Pro 
laptop with a 13” screen. During the encoding sessions, participant responses 
were recorded using the laptop keyboard, whilst retrieval session responses 
were recorded with a serial multi-button box attached to a Domino 2 
microcontroller from Micromint© with a time resolution of approximately 1ms. 
The order of buttons used in the retrieval task was counterbalanced across 
participants.  
 
fMRI data acquisition 
Event-related fMRI data were attained using a Siemens MAGNETOM Trio 3T 
Allegra MR scanner with an 8-channel head coil. Stimuli were projected onto a 
screen at the rear of the magnet bore and comfortably viewed with an angled 
mirror attached to the head coil. Blood Oxygen Level Dependent (BOLD) signal 
was recorded using T2*-weighted fMRI images obtained with a gradient echo-
planar sequence (EPI). Fifty oblique transaxial slices tilted at 15° were acquired 
in an ascending sequence with a voxel size of 3 x 3 x 2.8 mm3 including an 
interslice gap of 40%, matrix size of 64*64, TR of 2960ms, TE of 30ms and flip 
angle of 80°.  A T1-weighted structural image was also  acquired in the same 
session for each participant using a 3D IR/GR sequence with a matrix size of 
224 x 256 x176, cubic isovoxels of 1mm3, TR of 2040ms, TE of 5.57ms and a 
flip angle of 8°. 
 
 
 
 
58 
 
Data analysis 
Behaviour  
Our experimental task was designed to allow for separate analyses of the two 
components of recognition memory: recollection (R responses) and familiarity 
(K responses) (Tulving, 1985). However, since the vast majority of previously 
encoded images received an R response, there was insufficient statistical 
power to analyse K responses effectively.  One sample t-tests showed that 
familiarity performance (K hits - K false alarms) was not significantly greater 
than chance for remote or recent images (p > 0.2). Therefore, our behavioural 
analyses were focused entirely upon recollection performance, which was 
significantly above chance for both remote and recent images (R hits – R false 
alarms), irrespective of emotional valence (one sample t-tests, all p < 0.0001). 
 
The sensitivity index (d’) [Normalised (hits / (hits + misses)) – Normalised (false 
alarms / (false alarms + correct rejections))] was calculated for remote and 
recent images and used as a measure of memory performance. Our 
behavioural analyses were also focused on response times (RT’s) for correctly 
recollected remote and recent images.  
 
A combination of two retention types and three emotional valences produced a 
2x3 repeated measures ANOVA design with factors ‘Retention Type’ 
(remote/recent) and ‘Valence’ (positive/negative/neutral). All behavioural data 
was analysed with SPSS statistical software version 16.0 with a two-tailed p < 
0.05 considered as significant. 
 
fMRI  
Functional imaging data was processed using the Statistical Parametric 
Mapping 8 software (SPM8; Wellcome Department of Cognitive Neurology, 
London, UK, http://www.fil.ion.ucl.ac.uk/spm).  To allow for T1 equilibration 
59 
 
effects, the first three volumes of each retrieval session were discarded from 
our analysis. Single subject EPI volumes were realigned to correct for minor 
motion artefacts before slice-timing correction, referenced to the middle slice, 
was carried out. Images were then transformed into standard stereotaxic space, 
corresponding to the Montreal Neurological Institute (MNI). This was 
accomplished by registering the mean EPI volume (acquired during realignment) 
to SPM8’s EPI template and applying the subsequent transform to all image 
volumes. A spherical Gaussian smoothing kernel with a full-width half-maximum 
of 8mm was then applied to the normalised data to attenuate variations in inter-
subject localisation.  
 
Data analysis was conducted with a two level, random effects general linear 
model (GLM) (Friston, et al., 1995). To minimise the impact of guessing, our 
functional imaging analyses were focused on successful recollection (correct R 
responses) alone. At the first level, our design matrix contained eighteen 
regressors. These were: remote hits (remote-positive-R, remote-negative-R, 
remote-neutral-R), recent hits (recent-positive-R, recent-negative-R, recent-
neutral-R), correct rejections (new-positive-N, new-negative-N, new-neutral-N), 
misses (remote-positive-N, remote-negative-N, remote-neutral-N, recent-
positive-N, recent-negative-N, recent-neutral-N) and false alarms (new-positive-
R, new-negative-R, new-neutral-R). Each regressor was convolved with a 
canonical haemodynamic response function. In addition, the movement 
parameters estimated during the realignment phase were included as six non-
convolved regressors of no interest. In order to ensure that our fMRI analyses 
contained sufficient statistical power, participants with fewer than 10 successful 
recollection trials for each image combination of retention type (remote/recent) 
and emotional valence (positive/negative/neutral) were excluded from the study. 
Two participants were excluded on these grounds. The mean number of 
successful remote and recent recollection trials for each emotional valence are 
shown here: remote positive: 22.63 [S.D. ± 5.24], remote negative: 22.63 [S.D. 
± 4.67], remote neutral: 25.00 [S.D. ± 4.65], recent positive: 25.13 [S.D. ± 4.06], 
recent negative: 25.81 [S.D. ± 3.02], recent neutral: 25.56 [S.D. ± 4.05]. 
60 
 
Eight linear t-contrasts were calculated at the first level.  These included t-tests 
for the effect of remote recollection [all remote hits > all recent hits], the effect of 
recent recollection [all recent hits > all remote hits] and valence-specific 
analyses to examine the effect of remote or recent recollection for memories 
that were emotionally positive [positive remote hits > positive recent hits; 
positive recent hits > positive remote hits], negative [negative remote hits > 
negative recent hits; negative recent hits > negative remote hits] or neutral 
[neutral remote hits > neutral recent hits; neutral recent hits > neutral remote 
hits]. In order to assess group effects, the resulting contrast images were then 
taken forward to 8 second-level, one sample t-tests. The results of these 
analyses indicated changes in neural activity associated with overall (all images 
combined across valences) and emotion-specific (positive, negative and neutral) 
memory as a result of one week of consolidation. 
 
Four additional linear t-contrasts were calculated at the first level in order to 
examine differences in the brain regions associated with emotional and neutral 
remote recollection. These included t-tests for the difference between positive 
and neutral remote recollection [positive remote hits > neutral remote hits; 
neutral remote hits > positive remote hits] and the difference between negative 
and neutral remote recollection [negative remote hits > neutral remote hits; 
neutral remote hits > negative remote hits]. In order to assess group effects, the 
resulting contrast images were then taken forward to 4 second-level, one 
sample t-tests. 
 
We also sought to assess how the extent to which overall and emotion-specific 
image memories were consolidated over 1 week related to the brain regions 
exclusively associated with their recollection. To do this, we first carried out the 
following calculations on the behavioural data for each participant: all remote 
hits – all recent hits, positive remote hits – positive recent hits, negative remote 
hits – negative recent hits, neutral remote hits – neutral recent hits. The 
difference between these scores provided a measure of behavioural 
consolidation, which indexed the degree of remote memory consolidation that 
61 
 
had occurred over 1 week. Thus, a positive outcome represented superior 
remote (vs. recent) memory and a negative outcome represented weaker 
remote (vs. recent) memory. The contrast images acquired from the 8 
aforementioned first-level analyses [all remote hits > all recent hits; all recent 
hits > all remote hits, positive remote hits > positive recent hits; positive recent 
hits > positive remote hits, negative remote hits > negative recent hits; negative 
recent hits > negative remote hits, neutral remote hits > neutral recent hits; 
neutral recent hits > neutral remote hits] were then carried forward to 8 
additional second-level, one sample t-tests where the appropriate behavioural 
consolidation measure was included as a covariate (i.e. for the contrasts 
pertaining to positive memory [positive remote hits > positive recent hits; 
positive recent hits > positive remote hits], the behavioural consolidation 
measure for positive remote memory was included as a covariate). Thus, 
activation changes were suggestive of brain areas whose association with 
remote image recollection was predicted by the extent of consolidation 
occurring over 1 week. Specifically, positive responses represented brain 
activity that was associated with more strongly consolidated remote image 
memories. Negative responses however, represented activity that was 
associated with more weakly consolidated remote image memories.  
 
Functional imaging analyses were conducted at the whole brain level with a 
threshold of p < 0.001 (uncorrected) and a minimum cluster extent threshold of 
k = 10 voxels. 
 
Results   
Pre-study sleep data 
The mean number of hours slept on the night preceding the first experimental 
session was 7.53 [S.D. ± 0.90], and the mean hours slept in an average night 
was 7.31 [S.D. ± 0.79]. The difference between these two measures was not 
significant (t(15) = 1.20; p = 0.25), confirming that participants’ pre-study sleep 
did not deviate from their usual practices.  
62 
 
Alertness 
Scores on the Stanford Sleepiness Scale were not significantly different 
between session one (1.81 [S.D. ± 0.75]) or session two (2.13 [S.D. ± 0.72]) 
(t(15) = 1.16; p = 0.26), indicating that the results of this study were not affected 
by differences in participant alertness.  
 
Behaviour 
As mentioned earlier, our experimental task was designed to allow for separate 
analyses of recollection (R responses) and familiarity (K responses) in 
recognition memory (Tulving, 1985). However, one sample t-tests showed that, 
while recollection performance (R hits - R false alarms) was above chance for 
remote and recent images, irrespective of valence (all p < 0.0001), familiarity 
performance (K hits - K false alarms) was not (p > 0.2). Thus, our behavioural 
analyses were focused exclusively upon recollection performance (d’) and RT’s 
for correctly recollected remote and recent images. All relevant behavioural data 
is available in tables 1A and 1B.

An initial 2x3 repeated measures ANOVA with factors ‘Retention Type’ 
(remote/recent) and ‘Valence’ (positive/negative/neutral) was conducted for 
both memory performance (d’) and RT’s. Although recent images were 
generally better remembered than their remote counterparts, no main effect of 
Retention Type was found for memory performance (d’) (F(1,15) = 2.58; p = 
0.13) or RT’s (F(1,15) = 0.23; p = 0.64). No main effect of valence was found for 
memory performance (d’) (F(2,30) = 2.36; p = 0.11), but RT’s for negative 
images were significantly slower than those for positive or neutral images 
(F(2,30) = 10.18; p < 0.0001). Finally, while no significant interaction was found 
between factors for RT’s (F(2,30) = 2.01; p = 0.15), such an effect was revealed 
for memory performance (d’) F(2,30) = 3.60; p = 0.04). Subsequent analyses 
revealed that neutral remote images were significantly better remembered than 
negative remote (t(15) = 3.46; p = 0.003) and positive remote images (t(15) = 
2.46; p = 0.03). Furthermore, negative recent images were significantly better 
remembered than negative remote images (t(15) = 2.80; p = 0.01). Equivalent 
remote vs. recent comparisons for positive and neutral images were not 
significant (positive: t(15) = 1.17; p = 0.26, neutral: t(15) = 0.52; p = 0.61). 
These results are illustrated in figure 6.

Functional imaging  
In order to avoid performance confounds, our fMRI analyses were focused on 
successful recollection (correct R responses) alone. We first examined 
differences between brain responses associated with the recollection of 
emotional and neutral remote image memories [positive remote hits <> neutral 
remote hits; negative remote hits <> neutral remote hits]. While no difference 
was found between the neural correlates of positive and neutral remote memory, 
negative remote memories were associated with greater activity in the right 
fusiform gyrus than neutral remote memories. Interestingly however, the 
retrieval of neutral remote memories elicited greater responses in the right 
angular gyrus than the retrieval of negative remote memories. The results of 
these whole brain analyses are provided in table 2 (p <0.001 uncorrected, 
minimum cluster extent threshold: k = 10 voxels).

positive remote memory than for positive recent memory, while negative and

By including a behavioural consolidation measure (remote hits - recent hits) as 
a covariate regressor in our functional imaging analyses, we were also able to 
explore how the extent to which overall and emotion-specific memories had 
been consolidated over 1 week related to the brain regions exclusively 
associated with their retrieval. These analyses suggested that more strongly 
consolidated remote memories (combined across valences), were associated 
with increased responses in the right precuneus and a cluster of activation 
encompassing the right supramarginal and angular gyrus (see figure 8). More 
weakly consolidated remote memories however, were associated with 
increased activity across several occipital areas, including the calcarine sulcus. 
These findings suggest that strong and enduring remote image memories may 
be more dependent upon general memory-relevant brain regions, such as the 
precuneus. In contrast, the retrieval of weaker, more labile remote image 
memories may be more reliant upon visual processing resources housed in the 
occipital lobe.  
 
Emotion-specific analyses suggested that more weakly consolidated remote 
image memories with a positive or negative tone were associated with 
increased responses in several brain regions, including the fusiform gyrus and 
insula. However, no significant activation was associated with positive or 
negative remote image memories which existed in a stronger or more stabilised 
form. The extent to which neutral remote image memories had been 
consolidated over 1 week had no impact upon the brain regions supporting their 
retrieval. A full account of these results can be found in table 4 (p <0.001 
uncorrected, minimum cluster extent threshold: k = 10 voxels).
