Summary 
Behaviourally, neutral remote images were better remembered than positive or 
negative remote images, and negative recent images were better remembered 
than negative remote images. Moreover, RT’s for correctly recollected negative 
images were slower than those for correctly recollected positive or neutral 
images, irrespective of retention type (remote or recent). Functionally, overall 
remote memory was associated with stronger responses in the superior and 
middle temporal gyri than overall recent memory. Although positive remote (vs. 
positive recent) memory was associated with increased responses in the right 
superior frontal gyrus, negative and neutral remote memories were not 
associated with any greater brain response than their recent counterparts. 
Interestingly, our fMRI analyses also suggested that strongly consolidated 
remote memories were associated with increased responses in the right 
precuneus, whereas poorly consolidated remote memories were associated 
with greater activity in several occipital areas. 
 
Discussion 
Although a wealth of research has demonstrated that the brain regions 
supporting emotional memory retrieval are reorganised over time, these studies 
have typically addressed relatively short consolidation periods of 12 hours to 3 
days (Lewis, et al., 2011; Payne & Kensinger, 2011; Sterpenich, et al., 2007), or 
longer periods of 6 months to 1 year (Dolcos, et al., 2005; Sterpenich, et al., 
2009). Using event-related fMRI, we examined the time-dependent 
reorganisation of emotionally positive, negative and neutral image memories 
across an intermediate retention period of 1 week (remote memory), relative to 
30 minutes (recent memory). In addition, by incorporating a measure of 
behavioural consolidation within our functional imaging analyses, we also 
investigated how the extent to which image memories are consolidated over 1 
week relates to the brain regions supporting their retrieval.  
 
70 
 
The recollection of overall remote image memory, as compared to recent, was 
associated with stronger responses in the superior and middle temporal gyri. 
While positive remote memories were associated with stronger responses in the 
right superior frontal gyrus than positive recent memories, negative and neutral 
remote memories elicited no greater response than their recent counterparts. 
Thus, image memories that had undergone 1 week of consolidation appeared to 
be more dependent upon cortical brain regions than those that were encoded 
30 minutes prior to retrieval, with emotion-specific effects occurring for positive 
images alone. Interestingly, our findings also suggested that the extent to which 
a remote memory is consolidated across 1 week has important implications for 
the brain regions exclusively associated with its retrieval. Specifically, the 
recollection of strongly consolidated remote memories was associated with 
increased responses in several parietal areas, including the right precuneus. 
Conversely, the recollection of more weakly consolidated remote memories was 
associated with greater activity across several occipital gyri.  A full discussion of 
these findings is provided below. 
 
Reorganisation of memory with consolidation 
The principle tenet of the standard model of consolidation (Frankland & 
Bontempi, 2005; Marr, 1971; McClelland, et al., 1995) is that as declarative 
representations become integrated within long-term memory, their retrieval 
dependency shifts from the hippocampus to the neocortical circuitry, which 
eventually forms their self-sufficient locus of control. This transfer of retrieval 
dependency is also thought to be accompanied by a process of semanticisation, 
whereby the resultant cortical representations code stable decontextualised 
memories, forming the basis of semantic knowledge (McClelland, et al., 1995).  
In line with this model, our findings suggest that the recollection of remote 
image memories was more dependent upon superior and middle temporal gyri 
than the recollection of recent image memories. Under the standard 
consolidation framework however, we may have also expected to observe 
greater hippocampal dependency during the retrieval of recent relative to 
remote images, but this was not so.  Several functional imaging studies have 
71 
 
indicated that the retrieval of newly formed  declarative memories is largely 
reliant upon the hippocampus, and that this hippocampal retrieval dependency 
undergoes a time-dependent decline (Sterpenich, et al., 2007; Sterpenich, et al., 
2009; Takashima, et al., 2009; Takashima, et al., 2006), although other work 
has suggested that hippocampal retrieval dependency actually increases with 
consolidation (Bosshardt, Degonda, et al., 2005; Bosshardt, Schmidt, et al., 
2005). Nonetheless, it is possible that modifications in the hippocampal retrieval 
response may not have been observable under the protocol adopted in the 
current study. For example, the aforementioned studies used an entirely 
different task (Takashima, et al., 2009) or a substantially longer retention 
interval (Sterpenich, et al., 2009; Takashima, et al., 2006) than that used here. 
 
Although positive remote image memories appeared to be more dependent 
upon superior frontal regions than their recent counterparts, we found no 
significant difference between the brain regions associated with the recollection 
of negative remote and negative recent images. In contrast to this result, 
Sterpenich and colleagues (2009) reported that the retrieval of negative remote 
image memories was associated with increased responses in the amygdala and 
vmPFC after consolidation, two areas that, amongst others, are regularly 
implicated in emotional memory processing (Dolcos, et al., 2004a; Dolcos, et al., 
2004b; Pelletier, et al., 2005). Because Sterpenich and colleagues (2009) 
adopted a paradigm in which remote memories were consolidated across 6 
months, one possible explanation for our disparate results is that our retention 
interval of 1 week, as compared to one of 30 minutes, was not long enough to 
reveal significant changes in the neural regions associated with the recollection 
of emotionally affective memories. However, it is also important to consider that, 
when compared with neutral remote memories, the recollection of negative or 
positive remote memories was not associated with an increase of activity in the 
amygdala, medial prefrontal cortex or any other brain region commonly 
associated with emotional memory retrieval (Buchanan, 2007; Dolcos, et al., 
2004a; Dolcos, et al., 2004b). It is therefore possible that memories categorised 
as emotional may not have been processed any differently from their neutral 
counterparts at encoding or retrieval, suggesting a common impact of the 1 
72 
 
week consolidation delay upon newly formed image memories, irrespective of 
their emotional properties.  
 
The extent of consolidation 
Interestingly, the right precuneus played a greater role in the effect of remote 
recollection when remote memories were more strongly consolidated, whereas 
the retrieval of more weakly consolidated remote memories was associated with 
greater activity in several occipital areas.   
 
Due to its hidden location and virtual absence of focal lesion studies, the 
precuneus was a region that received very little attention until the application of 
functional neuroimaging methods in psychological research (Cavanna & Trimble, 
2006). Today, the precuneus is thought to play a central role in a wide range of 
highly integrated tasks, including episodic memory retrieval (Cavanna & Trimble, 
2006; Shallice, et al., 1994; Tulving, et al., 1994). The occipital lobe has also, to 
a lesser extent, been previously implicated in recognition memory (Heun, et al., 
2004). However, as this region forms a great proportion of the brains visual 
response network (McKeefry, et al., 2009), which includes the primary visual or 
‘calcarine’ cortex, it is more commonly associated with visual processing. 
Accordingly, a number of studies have shown that damage or interference 
within different components of the occipital lobe causes impairments to different 
aspects of visual function (Meadows, 1974; Thielscher, et al., 2010; Zeki, 1990; 
Zihl, et al., 1983).  
 
Neuroscience research has demonstrated that remembering an episodic 
memory may involve the reactivation of sensory-specific brain regions that were 
engaged during the initial encoding process (Hofstetter, et al., 2012). For 
example, it has been shown that retrieving a visual memory elicits activation in 
visual cortices, whilst the retrieval of auditory information activates auditory 
areas (Nyberg, et al., 2000; Wheeler, et al., 2000). When considered alongside 
73 
 
those of previous investigations, our findings suggest that the relative strength 
of remote memories is reflected in the brain responses, and thus neural 
processes, associated with their retrieval. While speculative, it is possible that 
the retrieval of poorly consolidated remote image memories may be more 
dependent upon visual processing areas housed in the occipital lobe, such as 
the calcarine sulcus, perhaps reflecting a greater reliance upon sensory-specific 
memory processes than a stabilised and robust memory trace. Conversely, the 
retrieval of stronger and more enduring remote image memories may be largely 
dependent upon brain regions that play a crucial role in the retrieval of 
contextually rich episodic representations, such as the precuneus (Addis, et al., 
2004; Gilboa, et al., 2004). Therefore, well-stabilised remote image memories 
may be retrieved in the relative absence of visual processing resources, 
reflecting a more general and sensory-independent episodic memory system. 
Such a greater degree of mnemonic stabilisation may result from a potentially 
enhanced consolidation process occurring throughout the 1 week retention 
interval. Specifically, previous research has demonstrated that increasing the 
perceived relevance, and thus salience, of recently formed memory 
representations can increase their affinity for sleep-dependent consolidation 
(Fischer & Born, 2009; Wilhelm, et al., 2011). Thus, certain participants may 
have attributed a greater degree of importance to the learned images, 
increasing their access to offline consolidation processes occurring across 
consecutive nights of sleep, ultimately strengthening the remote memory trace.  
 
Nevertheless, it is important to consider a note of caution regarding the 
interpretation of these activation changes. Using PET imaging, Fletcher and 
colleagues (1995) showed that memory-related imagery was associated with 
significant bilateral activation of the anterior precuneus, providing evidence that 
this region forms an important component of the neural substrate of visual 
imagery in episodic retrieval (Buckner, et al., 1995). However, subsequent PET 
research has indicated that the posterior precuneus may support the retrieval of 
both imageable and non-imageable memories (Krause, et al., 1999; Schmidt, et 
al., 2002), resulting in a functional segregation between the anterior and 
posterior portions of this structure (Cavanna & Trimble, 2006). Since our fMRI 
74 
 
data show that peak activation occurred in a relatively medial portion of the 
precuneus, we are unable to place our findings on either side of this line of 
evidence.  
 
Emotional memory processing  
Emotional experiences are usually better remembered than those with a more 
neutral or mundane tone (Bradley, et al., 1992; McGaugh, 2004). This effect 
occurs as a result of increased cognitive resources at encoding (Dolcos, et al., 
2004a; Kensinger & Corkin, 2004) and arousal-driven enhancements of both 
encoding and consolidation processes, which augment the persistence of 
memories over time (LaBar & Cabeza, 2006; McGaugh, 2004; McGaugh, et al., 
1996). Decades of research have demonstrated that the mnemonic superiority 
of emotional relative to neutral information increases over hours (Sharot & 
Phelps, 2004), days (Kleinsmith & Kaplan, 1963), weeks (Anderson, et al., 2006) 
and even 1 year (Dolcos, et al., 2005). Therefore, our finding that neutral 
remote memories were better remembered than positive or negative remote 
memories forms a rather surprising outcome. However, as mentioned earlier, 
since our functional imaging data suggested that emotional and neutral remote 
image memories were processed in a comparable manner at retrieval, these 
representations may have also undergone a similar form of consolidation across 
1 week, providing a potential explanation for such disparity between our 
behavioural data and that of previous investigations.  
 
In line with recent findings (Rea, et al., 2011), RT’s were significantly slower for 
correctly retrieved negative images, as compared to positive and neutral images. 
Since previous research has demonstrated that it is harder to disengage 
attention from aversive relative to neutral stimuli (Ohman & Mineka, 2001), 
negative images may have increased attentional load at retrieval, which was 
manifested within slower RT’s for these items (Clark-Foos, et al., 2009).  
 
75 
 
Forgetting 
While recent memories were better remembered than remote memories, the 
fact that this result was not statistically significant may be considered as rather 
surprising. A substantial body of literature has suggested that forgetting occurs 
as a result of mental exertion, whereby the formation of new memories 
interferes with ongoing consolidation processes in the hippocampus 
retroactively (Fillmore, et al., 2001; Lamberty, et al., 1990; Müller & Pilzecker, 
1900; Skaggs, 1933; Wixted, 2004). As such, memory is often improved when 
new hippocampal input is blocked with pharmacological interventions (Bruce & 
Pihl, 1997; Hinrichs, et al., 1984; Mann, et al., 1984; Parker, et al., 1980; Parker, 
et al., 1981), indicating that the consolidation of previously formed memories 
can continue without disruption (Wixted, 2004). As such, a considerable degree 
of retroactive interference should have disrupted the formation of image 
memories over 1 week, but our behavioural data suggest that this was not the 
case. Further work is undoubtedly required to explore both the causes and 
reliability of this result. 
 
Conclusions 
Here, we examined the neural correlates of emotionally positive, negative and 
neutral image memories that had undergone either 30 minutes (recent memory) 
or 1 week (remote memory) of consolidation. In line with standard consolidation 
theory (Frankland & Bontempi, 2005; Marr, 1971; McClelland, et al., 1995), our 
findings indicate that remote memories are more reliant upon neocortical 
structures than their recent counterparts. Our data also suggest that, unlike 
weakly consolidated remote image memories, which are reliant upon sensory-
specific memory resources, strongly consolidated remote image memories are 
largely dependent upon general memory-relevant brain regions, perhaps 
reflecting a sensory-independent retrieval process.  
 
 
76 
 
Acknowledgments 
This research was funded by the Engineering and Physical Sciences Research 
Council (EPSRC) and Unilever. PAL and SJD were supported by a 
Biotechnology and Biological Sciences Research Council (BBSRC) New 
Investigator Award to PAL.   
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
77 
 
 
 
CHAPTER 3 
 
 
  Complimentary roles of slow-wave sleep and rapid eye 
movement sleep in emotional memory consolidation:             
an fMRI study 
 
 
Scott A. CAIRNEY, University of Manchester, UK 
Simon J. DURRANT, University of Lincoln, UK 
Penelope A. LEWIS, University of Manchester, UK 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
This chapter is based on a manuscript that is being prepared for submission for peer 
review. 
78 
 
Abstract 
While neuroimaging research has demonstrated that sleep mediates an active 
reorganisation of emotional memories, the specific components of sleep that 
support this process are not well understood. Here, we used event-related 
functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) and polysomnography (PSG) to 
investigate this issue. Healthy participants encoded emotionally positive, 
negative and neutral images before a night of PSG monitored sleep (remote 
memories), and immediately before a recognition test in an MRI scanner 24 
hours later (recent memories). Behaviourally, the consolidation of negative 
remote memories appeared to be facilitated by slow-wave sleep (SWS), 
whereas rapid eye movement sleep (REM) appeared to exert an inhibitory 
influence upon the formation of positive remote memories.  Functionally, we 
observed a SWS-related reduction in right hippocampal activity for negative 
remote memory, and a similar albeit weaker relationship for overall remote 
memory (i.e. combined across valences). Interestingly, while a SWS-related 
reduction in hippocampal-cortical connectivity was found for overall and positive 
remote memory, REM was associated with an increase in hippocampal-cortical 
connectivity for overall and negative remote memory. These findings provide 
the first evidence for a targeted reorganisation of emotionally negative 
memories during SWS, a result which is in keeping with previous research 
linking the consolidation of highly salient memories with slow-oscillation activity.  
Recent work has suggested that REM may support the assimilation of newly 
acquired information, which is stabilised during the preceding SWS period, into 
rich associative memory networks. While speculative, such an effect may 
manifest within REM-related increases in hippocampal-cortical connectivity, 
which were exclusive to negative and overall remote memory.  
 
Keywords : Emotional Memory, Memory Consolidation, Slow-Wave Sleep, 
Rapid Eye Movement Sleep, Hippocampus.  
 
 
79 
 
Introduction  
Consolidation refers to the progressive stabilisation of fragile, newly formed 
memory representations. According to the standard model of consolidation 
(Frankland & Bontempi, 2005; Marr, 1971; McClelland, et al., 1995), the 
retrieval of recently acquired declarative memories is highly reliant on the 
hippocampus, which integrates distributed neocortical memory modules, each 
coding for different components of an experience, into a coherent 
representation. However over days, weeks or months, a gradual reorganisation 
of declarative information is thought to take place, such that retrieval eventually 
becomes an entirely neocortical process, independent of the hippocampus 
(Frankland & Bontempi, 2005). In recent years, functional magnetic resonance 
imaging (fMRI) research has provided compelling support for the standard 
consolidation model, demonstrating that image retrieval is associated with a 
time-dependent decrease of activity in the hippocampus and a concomitant 
increase of activity in numerous neocortical regions (Sterpenich, et al., 2007; 
Sterpenich, et al., 2009; Takashima, et al., 2009; Takashima, et al., 2006). 
However, also see Bosshardt and colleagues (2005; 2005), who reported a 
time-dependent increase in hippocampal retrieval dependency.  
 
A wealth of evidence now exists to support the contention that sleep, 
particularly slow-wave sleep (SWS), exerts a beneficial impact upon 
subsequent declarative memory performance (Marshall, et al., 2006; Plihal & 
Born, 1997, 1999a; Rasch, et al., 2007; Rudoy, et al., 2009; Wilhelm, et al., 
2011). As such, an adapted version of standard consolidation theory, known as 
the active systems model, has incorporated SWS as a dynamic feature, 
suggesting that the electroencephalographic (EEG) slow oscillations (<0.75Hz) 
which characterise this sleep stage play a pivotal role in stabilising declarative 
memory traces (Born, 2010; Born, et al., 2006; Born & Wilhelm, 2011; 
Diekelmann & Born, 2010). These slow oscillations are thought to drive a covert 
reactivation of experience-dependent patterns of neural activity within the 
hippocampal-neocortical memory network, supporting the reorganisation, and 
thus consolidation, of newly formed memory representations.   
80 
 
Previous work has suggested that emotionally affective memories undergo a 
targeted consolidation process during post-learning sleep (Holland & Lewis, 
2007; Walker, 2009; Walker & van der Helm, 2009). This effect has been shown 
with  emotional texts (Wagner, et al., 2001; Wagner, et al., 2006) and pictures 
(Hu, et al., 2006; Nishida, et al., 2008; Payne, et al., 2008), although a recent 
study by Baran and colleagues (2012) indicated that this is not always the case 
for the latter. Building upon these findings, recent research has utilised fMRI to 
examine the neural reorganisation of emotional memories over sleep. Two 
studies (Lewis, et al., 2011; Payne & Kensinger, 2011) have shown that, relative 
to an equivalent period of wakefulness, the retrieval of emotional memories is 
associated with increased responses in a number of memory relevant brain 
regions after sleep, including the amygdala, ventromedial prefrontal cortex 
(vmPFC), cingulate gyrus, precuneus and parahippocampal gyrus. Moreover, 
Payne and Kensinger (2011) reported that functional connectivity between the 
amygdala and other regions of the emotional memory network, such as the 
hippocampus and vmPFC, was stronger after sleep than wake. Importantly, 
these effects were specific to the retrieval of emotionally affective memories and 
were similar to those found in a functional connectivity analysis conducted by 
Lewis and colleagues (2011). 
 
In addition, Sterpenich and colleagues (2007) demonstrated that a night of post-
learning sleep, as compared to a corresponding period of sleep deprivation, 
was associated with stronger responses in the hippocampus and various 
cortical regions during the retrieval of emotional image memories 3 days later. 
In a follow up study 6 months later, participants in the sleep group showed 
greater retrieval-related responses in the vmPFC, precuneus and amygdala 
than those in the sleep deprivation group, suggesting that sleep on the first 
post-encoding night profoundly influences long-term consolidation processes in 
emotional memory (Sterpenich, et al., 2009). 
 
While an association between neural reorganisation and SWS has been 
demonstrated in neutral declarative memory (Takashima, et al., 2006), it is 
81 
 
currently unclear whether SWS, or another parameter of sleep, may modulate 
the functional modifications underpinning the consolidation of emotional 
memory representations. Indeed, a number of studies have implicated rapid eye 
movement sleep (REM) in the consolidation of affective memories (Hu, et al., 
2006; Wagner, et al., 2001; Walker, 2009), but a specific role for this sleep 
stage in neural reorganisation has yet to be established. Moreover, recent 
research has demonstrated that slow oscillation activity, which characterises 
SWS, selectively supports the consolidation of memories that are relevant to 
future plans (Wilhelm, et al., 2011). Accordingly, memories with a high degree 
of salience, such as emotional experiences, may undergo a refined form of 
consolidation during SWS, which is reflected by a greater extent of neural 
reorganisation at post-sleep retrieval. 
 
In the present study, we used event-related fMRI to examine the neural 
correlates of successful recollection for emotional memories that had been 
consolidated across 30 minutes (recent memories) or 24 hours (remote 
memories). In addition, we used overnight polysomnography (PSG) to examine 
the parameters of sleep which play a more direct role in the neural 
reorganisation of emotional representations. Participants encoded a number of 
positive, negative and neutral images in the afternoon before returning to the 
laboratory to sleep overnight. The next afternoon, participants encoded another 
set of images and then completed a recognition task for all previously learned 
images in the MRI scanner. In line with the active systems model of 
consolidation (Born, 2010; Born & Wilhelm, 2011; Diekelmann & Born, 2010), 
we predicted that SWS would be associated with a reduction in both 
hippocampal activity and hippocampal-cortical connectivity during the retrieval 
of remote as compared to recent memories. Moreover, due to their high degree 
of salience, we expected that a weakening of retrieval-related responses in the 
hippocampal region over SWS would be progressively more developed for 
emotionally affective memories, reflecting a greater degree of SWS-related 
consolidation at the neural level. 
 
82 
 
Materials and Methods 
Participants 
Twenty-two (12 male) healthy participants aged 19-28 years (mean age = 22.47, 
S.D. ± 2.37) were recruited on a voluntary basis. However, 6 participants were 
excluded for a number of reasons including: incorrect or poor task performance 
(3), insufficient overnight sleep (2) and failing the pre-scan medical (1). 
Therefore, the data presented in this study is based upon the remaining 16 
participants (10 male) aged 19-28 years (mean age = 22.67, S.D. ± 2.47). As 
evaluated with pre-study screening questionnaires and telephone interviews, 
participants had no history of neurological, depressive or sleep disorders and 
reported a regular sleep pattern over the month preceding the study. Aside from 
females using the contraceptive pill, participants were also free from any form of 
medication. All participants were native English speakers and were right-
handed, as indicated by a score of 80% or higher on the Edinburgh handedness 
inventory (Oldfield, 1971). Written informed consent was acquired from all 
participants in accordance with the research ethics committees of The 
University of Manchester and The University of Liverpool. Participants were 
paid £50 and were required to remain alcohol and caffeine free from 24 hours 
prior to the study start and throughout the study period. Before any scanning 
took place, participants were assessed by a qualified radiographer to ensure 
their safety within an MRI environment. Participants were asked not to nap on 
experiment days and the Stanford Sleepiness Scale was also used to check for 
differences in alertness between the experimental sessions. In order to ensure 
that there was no deficit in alertness related to homeostatic sleep pressure, we 
also examined correlations between the amount of SWS obtained overnight and 
all retrieval response times (see results). 
 
Stimuli  
Two  hundred and seventy images were taken from the international affective 
picture system (IAPS) (Lang, et al., 2005) for use in this study. IAPS pictures 
range from everyday scenes, to images of injury, violence, decay and 
83 
 
contaminated foods, and are rated on 9-point scales for valence (1 = negative; 
5 = neutral; 9 = positive) and arousal (1 = calm; 9 = exciting). Images were 
initially selected on the basis of their emotional valence rating and split into 
three sets: 90 positive, 90 negative and 90 neutral. Thus, the mean valence 
rating of each picture set was significantly different (positive: 7.55 [S.D. ± 0.36], 
negative: 2.40 [S.D. ± 0.34], neutral: 5.03 [S.D. ± 0.19], F(2,178) = 40101.16; p 
<0.0001). Although the mean arousal rating of the neutral picture set was 
significantly different to that of the emotional picture sets (positive: 5.35 [S.D. ± 
0.80], negative: 5.39 [S.D. ± 0.48], neutral: 3.10 [S.D. ± 0.52], F(2,178) = 420.15; 
p <0.0001), the difference in arousal rating between positive and negative 
picture sets alone was not significant t(89) = 0.34; p = 0.73. 
 
One hundred and eighty images (60 positive, 60 negative, 60 neutral) were 
used for the encoding and retrieval phase, while the remaining 90 images (30 
positive, 30 negative, 30 neutral) were used as foils in the retrieval phase alone. 
Of those images used for encoding, half were presented 24 hours prior to 
retrieval and referred to as ‘remote’ images whilst the other half, known 
as ’recent’ images, were presented 30 minutes prior to retrieval. The order in 
which these subsets were used (i.e. as remote images or recent images) was 
counterbalanced across participants.   
 
Experimental protocol 
All participants undertook two experimental sessions, separated by a period of 
24 (± 1.5) hours. The first took place at the Manchester Sleep Laboratory, 
University of Manchester, whilst the second took place at the Magnetic 
Resonance and Image Analysis Research Centre (MARIARC), University of 
Liverpool. Before arriving for the first study session, participants were explicitly 
informed of all the experimental procedures, including the memory tests. The 
experimental design is summarised in figure 9A. 
 
84 
 
Figure 9 : (A) Study procedures for all participants and (B)  encoding and retrieval tasks                
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
A: In the first session, participants encoded 90 (30 positive, 30 negative and 30 neutral) images and then returned in the evening for overnight sleep with PSG monitoring. The next day, participants encoded another 90 images before completing a recognition task for all previously learned images in the MRI scanner. B: At encoding, participants were required to rate each image in terms of its emotional valence (unpleasant-pleasant) and emotional arousal (boringexciting). At retrieval, participants were required to indicate if they recognised the image with recollection (R response) or familiarity (K response), or if they thought that the image was new (N response). 
85 
 
Session one 
The first experimental session began at 2pm (± 30 minutes) and lasted 
approximately 25 minutes. Here, participants were presented with 90 
photographic images on a computer screen (30 positive, 30 negative and 30 
neutral) in random order twice, with a short interval (< 1 min) between both 
encoding runs. At the beginning of the encoding task, participants saw a black 
screen with a white crosshair in the centre for 2000ms. They were then 
presented with the first image for 3000ms, which was followed by the black 
screen and white crosshair for another 2000ms until the next image was 
presented. This pattern continued for each remaining image until the end of the 
task. In one encoding run, using the corresponding keys on the keyboard, 
participants were asked to rate the images in terms of their emotional valence 
on a scale of 1-7 (1 = highly negative, 4 = neutral and 7 = highly positive), whilst 
in the other, participants were asked to rate the same images for emotional 
arousal, again on a scale of 1-7 (1 = non-arousing or boring and 7 = highly 
arousing or exciting). Participants were asked to respond as quickly as possible, 
and were advised that they could make their responses during either the 
presentation of the picture or the subsequent crosshair. The order of rating type 
(i.e. valence or arousal rating in the first or second encoding run) was 
counterbalanced across participants. Upon completing session one, participants 
were free to go about their usual daily activities before returning at 10pm to 
spend a night sleeping in the Manchester Sleep Laboratory until 8am the next 
morning. During their overnight stay, participants’ sleep was monitored with 
PSG (see below for further details). After waking, participants were 
disconnected from the PSG unit and given a two hour break before being 
transported, via car or train, to Liverpool for the second experimental session.  
 
Session two 
At 2pm (± 1 hour) the next day, participants repeated the procedures of session 
one but with a new batch of 90 images. Approximately 30 minutes after 
completing encoding (3pm ± 1 hour), participants began the retrieval phase, 
which took place inside the MRI scanner. The retrieval test was in the form of a 
86 
 
recognition task, which encompassed all previously encoded remote and recent 
images and an additional 90 previously unseen foils (30 positive, 30 negative 
and 30 neutral), making a total of 270 images. The retrieval phase was divided 
into two scanning sessions, with a short (< 1 min) break between each. Thus, 
both sessions consisted of 90 encoded images and 45 foils presented in a 
randomised order. At the beginning of the retrieval task, participants saw a 
black screen with a white crosshair in the centre for 2000ms. They were then 
presented with the first image for 1000ms, which was followed by the black 
screen and white crosshair for another 2000ms until the next image was 
presented. This pattern continued for each remaining image until the end of the 
task. For each presented image, participants were required to make a 
remember/know/new judgement (Tulving, 1985) using a three-button keypad 
which they held in their right hand. A “remember” (R) response was provided 
when participants could consciously recollect seeing the image in one of the 
previous encoding sessions. A “know” (K) response indicated that participants 
knew that they had seen the image at encoding, but could not retrieve any 
contextual details about its occurrence. Finally, a “new” (N) response was 
provided when participants believed that they had not seen the image in either 
encoding session. Participants were asked to make their responses as quickly 
and accurately as possible, and were advised that they could make their 
responses during either the presentation of the picture or the subsequent 
crosshair. The encoding and retrieval tasks are illustrated in figure 9B. 
 
Equipment 
Experimental task 
The experimental tasks were created using Cogent 2000 developed at the 
functional imaging laboratory (FIL), University College London. The tasks were 
written and implemented using MatLab© version 6.5 on a Toshiba Satellite Pro 
laptop with a 13” screen. During the encoding sessions, participant responses 
were recorded using the laptop keyboard, whilst retrieval session responses 
were recorded with a serial multi-button box attached to a Domino 2 
microcontroller from Micromint© with a time resolution of approximately 1ms. 
87 
 
The order of buttons used in the retrieval task was counterbalanced across 
participants.  
 
PSG recording 
PSG monitoring was carried out using an Embla© N7000 sleep monitoring 
system, with silver-silver chloride (Ag-AgCl) electrodes attached using EC2© 
electrogel after the scalp was cleaned using NuPrep© exfoliating agent.  Scalp 
electrodes were attached according to the international 10-20 system at six 
standardised locations: central (C3 & C4), frontal (F3 & F4) and occipital (O1 & 
O2), and each was referenced to the contralateral mastoid (A1 or A2). Left and 
right electrooculagram, left, right and upper electromyogram, and a ground 
electrode were also attached. All electrodes were verified to have a connection 
impedance of less than 5kOhms. All signals were digitally sampled at a rate of 
200Hz.  
 
fMRI data acquisition 
Event-related fMRI data were attained using a Siemens MAGNETOM Trio 3T 
Allegra MR scanner with an 8-channel head coil. Stimuli were projected onto a 
screen at the rear of the magnet bore and comfortably viewed with an angled 
mirror attached to the head coil. Blood Oxygen Level Dependent (BOLD) signal 
was recorded using T2*-weighted fMRI images obtained with a gradient echo-
planar sequence (EPI).  Fifty oblique transaxial slices tilted at 15° were acquired 
in an ascending sequence with a voxel size of 3 x 3 x 2.8 mm3 including an 
interslice gap of 40%, matrix size of 64*64, TR of 2960ms, TE of 30ms and flip 
angle of 80°.  A T1-weighted structural image was also  acquired in the same 
session for each participant using a 3D IR/GR sequence with a matrix size of 
224 x 256 x176, cubic isovoxels of 1mm3, TR of 2040ms, TE of 5.57ms and a 
flip angle of 8°. 
 
 
88 
 
Data analysis 
Behaviour  
Our experimental task was designed to allow for separate analyses of the two 
components of recognition memory: recollection (R responses) and familiarity 
(K responses) (Tulving, 1985). However, since the vast majority of previously 
encoded images received an R response, there was insufficient statistical 
power to analyse K responses effectively.  One sample t-tests showed that 
familiarity performance (K hits - K false alarms) was not significantly greater 
than chance for remote or recent images (all p > 0.2). Therefore, our 
behavioural analyses were focused entirely upon recollection performance, 
which was significantly above chance for both remote and recent images (R hits 
– R false alarms), irrespective of emotional valence (one sample t-tests, all p < 
0.0001). 
 
The sensitivity index (d’) [Normalised (hits / (hits + misses)) – Normalised (false 
alarms / (false alarms + correct rejections))] was calculated for remote and 
recent images and used as a measure of memory performance. Our 
behavioural analyses were also focused on response times (RT’s) for correctly 
recollected remote and recent images.  
 
A combination of two retention types and three emotional valences produced a 
2x3 repeated measures ANOVA design with factors ‘Retention Type’ 
(remote/recent) and ‘Valence’ (positive/negative/neutral). All behavioural data 
was analysed with SPSS statistical software version 16.0 with a two-tailed p < 
0.05 considered as significant. 
 
Sleep scoring 
PSG sleep recordings were visually scored independently by two experienced 
sleep researchers using RemLogic© 1.1 software.  Sleep data were categorised 
89 
 
into 30s epochs and scored on the referenced central electrodes (C3-A2 and 
C4-A1) according to the standardised sleep scoring criteria of Rechtschaffen 
and Kales (1968), with sleep stages three and four grouped together as SWS. 
Scored data were then partitioned in terms of the percentage of total sleep time 
spent in each stage of sleep: stage one sleep (S1), stage two sleep (S2), SWS 
and REM.  
 
We sought to examine how SWS and REM, which have been previously 
implicated in the respective consolidation of declarative and emotional memory 
(Born & Wilhelm, 2011; Hu, et al., 2006; Wagner, et al., 2001), and other sleep 
stages, influenced remote memory performance (d’). To do this, we first created 
a difference measure for emotionally positive, negative and neutral images by 
subtracting recent from remote memory performance (d’) (remote – recent). The 
difference between these scores provided a measure of behavioural 
consolidation, which indexed the extent to which remote memories had been 
consolidated across 24 hours. Thus, a positive outcome represented superior 
remote (vs. recent) memory and a negative outcome represented weaker 
remote (vs. recent) memory. These behavioural consolidation measures were 
then correlated with SWS, REM and the other sleep stages defined above, 
enabling us to assess potential relationship between these sleep parameters 
and the consolidation of positive, negative and neutral remote memories. 
 
In a similar fashion, RT difference measures were calculated for correctly 
retrieved positive, negative and neutral images by subtracting remote RT’s from 
recent RT’s (recent – remote). Thus, a positive outcome corresponded to faster 
remote (vs. recent) RT’s, whereas a negative outcome represented slower 
remote (vs. recent) RT’s.   
 
 
 
90 
 
fMRI  
Functional imaging data was processed using the Statistical Parametric 
Mapping 8 software (SPM8; Wellcome Department of Cognitive Neurology, 
London, UK, http://www.fil.ion.ucl.ac.uk/spm).  To allow for T1 equilibration 
effects, the first three volumes of each retrieval session were discarded from 
our analysis. Single subject EPI volumes were realigned to correct for minor 
motion artefacts before slice-timing correction, referenced to the middle slice, 
was carried out. Images were then transformed into standard stereotaxic space, 
corresponding to the Montreal Neurological Institute (MNI). This was 
accomplished by registering the mean EPI volume (acquired during realignment) 
to SPM8’s EPI template and applying the subsequent transform to all image 
volumes. A spherical Gaussian smoothing kernel with a full-width half-maximum 
of 8mm was then applied to the normalised data to attenuate variations in inter-
subject localisation.  
 
Data analysis was conducted with a two level, random effects general linear 
model (GLM) (Friston, et al., 1995). To minimise the impact of guessing, our 
functional imaging analyses were focused on successful recollection (correct R 
responses) alone. At the first level, our design matrix contained eighteen 
regressors. These were: remote hits (remote-positive-R, remote-negative-R, 
remote-neutral-R), recent hits (recent-positive-R, recent-negative-R, recent-
neutral-R), correct rejections (new-positive-N, new-negative-N, new-neutral-N), 
misses (remote-positive-N, remote-negative-N, remote-neutral-N, recent-
positive-N, recent-negative-N, recent-neutral-N) and false alarms (new-positive-
R, new-negative-R, new-neutral-R). Each regressor was convolved with a 
canonical haemodynamic response function. In addition, the movement 
parameters estimated during the realignment phase were included as six non-
convolved regressors of no interest. In order to ensure that our fMRI analyses 
contained sufficient statistical power, participants with fewer than 10 successful 
recollection trials for each image combination of retention type (remote/recent) 
and emotional valence (positive/negative/neutral) were excluded from the study. 
Three participants were excluded on these grounds. The mean number of 
91 
 
successful remote and recent recollection trials for each emotional valence are 
shown here: remote positive: 26.06 [S.D. ± 2.86], remote negative: 26.13 [S.D. 
± 3.01], remote neutral: 25.63 [S.D. ± 3.77], recent positive: 25.31 [S.D. ± 4.38], 
recent negative: 26.50 [S.D. ± 3.14], recent neutral: 25.31 [S.D. ± 3.59]. 
 
Eight linear t-contrasts were calculated at the first level for the effect of remote 
recollection [all remote hits > all recent hits], the effect of recent recollection [all 
recent hits > all remote hits] and valence-specific analyses to examine the effect 
of remote or recent recollection for memories that were emotionally positive 
[positive remote hits > positive recent hits; positive recent hits > positive remote 
hits], negative [negative remote hits > negative recent hits; negative recent 
hits > negative remote hits] or neutral [neutral remote hits > neutral recent hits; 
neutral recent hits > neutral remote hits]. In order to assess group effects, the 
resulting contrast images were then taken forward to 8 second-level, one 
sample t-tests. The results of these analyses indicated changes in neural 
activity associated with overall (all images combined across valences) and 
emotion-specific (positive, negative and neutral) image memory as a result of 
24 hours of consolidation. 
 
Four additional linear t-contrasts were calculated at the first level in order to 
examine differences in the brain regions associated with emotional and neutral 
remote recollection. These included t-tests for the difference between positive 
and neutral remote recollection [positive remote hits > neutral remote hits; 
neutral remote hits > positive remote hits] and the difference between negative 
and neutral remote recollection [negative remote hits > neutral remote hits; 
neutral remote hits > negative remote hits]. In order to assess group effects, the 
resulting contrast images were then taken forward to 4 second-level, one 
sample t-tests. 
 
We also sought to examine how neural activity associated with the recollection 
of overall and emotion-specific remote memory was influenced by post-learning 
92 
 
SWS and REM. Accordingly, the contrast images acquired from the 8 
aforementioned first-level analyses [all remote hits > all recent hits; all recent 
hits > all remote hits, positive remote hits > positive recent hits; positive recent 
hits > positive remote hits, negative remote hits > negative recent hits; negative 
recent hits > negative remote hits, neutral remote hits > neutral recent hits; 
neutral recent hits > neutral remote hits]  were carried forward to two sets of 8 
additional second-level, one sample t-tests (16 in total) where SWS (%) was 
included as a covariate in one set, and REM (%) as a covariate in the other set. 
Thus, activation changes were suggestive of brain areas whose involvement in 
overall or emotion-specific remote image recollection was predicted by the 
amount of SWS or REM obtained during the night after learning. Specifically, 
positive responses indicated an increase in brain activity which was predicted 
by SWS or REM. Negative responses however, indicated a SWS- or REM-
related decrease in brain activity.  
 
Analyses were initially conducted at the whole brain level with a threshold of p < 
0.001 (uncorrected) and a minimum cluster extent threshold of k = 10 voxels. 
Relevant contrasts were then further examined with region of interest (ROI) 
analyses (p < 0.05 family-wise error (FWE) corrected, minimum cluster extent 
threshold: k = 5 voxels) conducted at a priori regions of interest: hippocampus 
and parahippocampal gyrus (both bilaterally). These were carried out using the 
Wake-Forest University (WFU) pickatlas software version 3.0 (Maldjian, et al., 
2003) with automated anatomical labelling (aal) templates (Tzourio-Mazoyer, et 
al., 2002). 
 
Functional connectivity 
In addition to examining localised changes in activation, a psychophysiological 
interaction (PPI) was used to assess patterns of hippocampal connectivity that 
increased or decreased with 24 hours of consolidation. The peak voxel 
coordinates (p < 0.001, uncorrected) attained from a prior second-level contrast 
[SWS*negative recent hits > negative remote hits] (see table 9) were used to 
93 
 
create a 6mm radius volume of interest in the right hippocampus (x, y, z, mm: 
27, -10, -17) of each participant, from which the time-series was extracted. The 
deconvolved time series were then multiplied by contrasts for the effect of 
remote recollection for all images [all remote hits > all recent hits], positive 
images [positive remote hits > positive recent hits], negative images [negative 
remote hits > negative recent hits] and neutral images [neutral remote hits > 
neutral recent hits], forming 4 PPIs. For each participant, first-level GLM 
analyses were conducted for each of these PPIs, containing psychological 
(remote > recent recollection factor), physiological (the deconvolved time series) 
and interaction (psychological x physiological) regressors. The model also 
included six movement parameters. Eight linear t-contrasts were calculated at 
the first level to examine increases and decreases in hippocampal connectivity 
associated with the recollection of overall [all remote hits > all recent hits; all 
recent hits > all remote hits] or emotion-specific remote memories [positive 
remote hits > positive recent hits; positive recent hits > positive remote hits, 
negative remote hits > negative recent hits; negative recent hits > negative 
remote hits, neutral remote hits > neutral recent hits; neutral recent hits > 
neutral remote hits]. To examine group effects, the resulting interaction contrast 
maps were taken forward to 8 second-level, one sample t-tests.  
 
Finally, we investigated how consolidation-related changes in hippocampal 
connectivity were modulated by post-learning SWS or REM. To do this, the 
interaction contrast maps from our 8 first-level PPI analyses [all remote hits > all 
recent hits; positive remote hits > positive recent hits; negative remote hits > 
negative recent hits; neutral remote hits > neutral recent hits] were carried 
forward to two additional sets of 8 second-level, one sample t-tests (16 in total). 
The first set examined increases and decreases in hippocampal connectivity 
associated with the recollection of positive [positive remote hits > positive recent 
hits; positive recent hits > positive remote hits], negative [negative remote hits > 
negative recent hits; negative recent hits > negative remote hits], neutral 
[neutral remote hits > neutral recent hits; neutral recent hits > neutral remote 
hits] and overall remote memory [all remote hits > all recent hits; all recent hits > 
all remote hits] with SWS (%) included as a covariate. The second set was 
94 
 
equivalent to the first, but included REM (%) as covariate instead. Thus, 
activation changes were suggestive of brain areas whose connectivity with the 
right hippocampus during overall or emotion-specific remote image recollection 
was predicted by the amount of SWS or REM obtained in the night after 
learning. Specifically, positive responses indicated a SWS- or REM-related 
increase in right hippocampal connectivity, whereas negative responses 
indicated a decrease in connectivity with the right hippocampus, which was also 
predicted by SWS or REM. Analyses were conducted at the whole-brain level 
with a threshold of p < 0.001 (uncorrected) and a minimum cluster extent 
threshold of k = 10 voxels. 
 
Results  
Pre-study sleep data 
The mean number of hours slept on the night preceding the first experimental 
session was 7.84 [S.D. ± 0.85], and the mean hours slept in an average night 
was 7.47 [S.D. ± 0.50]. The difference between these two measures was not 
significant (t(15) = 1.54; p = 0.15), confirming that participants’ pre-study sleep 
did not deviate from their usual practices.  
 
Alertness 
Alertness was measured subjectively with the Stanford Sleepiness Scale. No 
significant difference in alertness score was found between session one (2.25 
[S.D. ± 0.77]) and session two (2.00 [S.D. ± 0.52]) (t(15) = 1.00; p = 0.33). In 
addition, no significant correlation was found between the percentage of SWS 
obtained overnight and RT’s for all remote or recent images, irrespective of 
valence (remote positive: r = -0.13; p = 0.64, negative: r = -0.20; p = 0.46, 
neutral: r = -0.13; p = 0.64, recent positive: r = -0.14; p = 0.62, negative: r = -
0.22; p = 0.41, neutral: r = -0.12; p = 0.66), suggesting no deficit in alertness 
related to homeostatic sleep pressure.  
 
95 
 
Behaviour 
As mentioned earlier, our experimental task was designed to allow for separate 
analyses of recollection (R responses) and familiarity (K responses) in 
recognition memory (Tulving, 1985). However, one sample t-tests showed that, 
while recollection performance (R hits - R false alarms) was above chance for 
remote and recent images, irrespective of valence (all p < 0.0001), familiarity 
performance (K hits – K false alarms) was not (all p > 0.2). Thus, our 
behavioural analyses were focused exclusively upon recollection performance 
(d’) and RT’s for correctly recollected remote and recent images. All relevant 
behavioural data is available in tables 5A and 5B.

0.42; p = 0.66), RT’s for emotionally positive images were significantly faster 
than those for negative or neutral images (F(2,30) = 5.12; p = 0.012). Neither

Sleep analysis 
In order to examine how post-learning SWS and REM impacted upon remote 
memory processing, correlation coefficients were calculated between these 
sleep parameters and a measure of behavioural consolidation [remote memory 
performance (d’) – recent memory performance (d’)] for positive, negative and 
neutral images. Sleep data is available in table 6. 
 
Table 6: Polysomnography data - percentage of total sleep time spent in each sleep stage (mean ± standard error) 
SWS = slow-wave sleep, REM = rapid eye movement sleep. 
 
Interestingly, the behavioural consolidation of negative remote memories was 
significantly predicted by the amount of SWS obtained in the night after learning 
(r = 0.57; p = 0.02), indicating that the offline processing of such memories may 
have been modulated during this sleep stage (see figure 10A). Conversely, the 
behavioural consolidation of positive remote memories was inversely correlated 
with post-learning REM (r = -0.58; p = 0.02), suggesting that mnemonic 
processes occurring during this sleep stage may have inhibited the stabilisation 
of representations with an emotionally positive tone (see figure 10B).

We found no evidence of a predictive relationship between SWS and the 
behavioural consolidation of positive (r = 0.04; p = 0.88) or neutral (r = -0.15; p 
= 0.58) remote memories, or between REM and the behavioural consolidation 
of negative (r = -0.25; p = 0.35) or neutral (r = 0.24; p = 0.37) remote memories. 
Importantly, no significant correlation was revealed between the percentages of 
total sleep time spent in SWS and REM (r = -0.22; p = 0.41).

98 
 
For completeness, correlation coefficients were also calculated between the 
behavioural consolidation of positive, negative and neutral remote memories 
and the percentage of post-learning sleep spent in S1 and S2. As expected, 
none of these correlations were found to be significant (all p > 0.2). In contrast 
to memory performance (d’), differences between RT’s for correctly recollected 
remote and recent images, irrespective of valence, showed no predictive 
relationship with either SWS (all p > 0.5), REM (all p > 0.4), S1 (all p > 0.1), or 
S2 (all p > 0.1). 
  
Functional imaging 
In order to avoid performance confounds, our fMRI analyses were focused on 
successful recollection (correct R responses) alone. We first examined brain 
activity associated with the recollection of emotional or neutral remote image 
memories [positive remote hits <> neutral remote hits; negative remote hits <> 
neutral remote hits]. Positive remote memories, as compared to neutral, were 
associated with a large cluster of parietal activation, which included the right 
precuneus. Negative remote memories however, were associated with stronger 
activity than neutral remote memories in several brain areas, including bilateral 
clusters of occipito-temporal activation. A full account of these results can be 
found in table 7.

We then examined brain responses associated with overall (all images 
combined across valences) or emotion-specific (positive, negative, neutral) 
image recollection, which increased or decreased over 24 hours of 
consolidation [remote hits > recent hits; recent hits > remote hits]. The results of

Of greater interest to the current study, we examined the impact of post-learning 
SWS or REM upon brain activity associated with the recollection of remote 
memories. Thus, our group analyses addressing the effect of overall and 
emotion-specific recollection were repeated first with SWS, and then with REM, 
as covariates. Interestingly, SWS mediated a reduction of activity in the right 
parahippocampal gyrus and several other areas associated with overall remote 
memory (see table 9). Similar but far more pronounced effects were found for 
negative remote recollection, in which a SWS-related reduction of activity in the 
right hippocampus was observed (see figure 11, but see table 9 for other 
emotion-specific responses).

Taken together, both whole brain and ROI analyses provide support for a SWS-
related shift in declarative retrieval dependency away from the hippocampus, 
which is particularly prominent for emotionally aversive memory representations. 
In contrast, REM-related changes in activity were not found in any region of 
interest for overall or emotion-specific remote recollection.  
 
Functional connectivity

centred upon peak right hippocampal coordinates (x, y, z, mm: 27, -10, -17) 
from an earlier comparison [SWS*negative recent hits > negative remote hits], 
were used to examine hippocampal connectivity associated with overall or 
emotion-specific image recollection, which increased or decreased over 24 
hours of consolidation [remote hits > recent hits; recent hits > remote hits] (p < 
0.001 uncorrected, minimum cluster extent threshold: k = 10 voxels). Positive 
remote memories, as compared to recent, were associated with a weaker 
degree of connectivity between the right hippocampus and both superior and 
middle frontal gyri. Neutral remote memories however, were associated with a

Finally, we examined the impact of post-learning SWS or REM upon 
hippocampal connectivity associated with remote recollection. As such, second-
level PPI analyses addressing the effect of overall and emotion-specific remote 
recollection [remote hits > recent hits] were repeated with SWS, and then REM, 
as covariates. Interestingly, for overall and positive remote memory, SWS was 
associated with a decrease in connectivity between the right hippocampus and 
a number of cortical areas, including the right middle frontal gyrus (see figure 
12). REM on the other hand, was associated with an increase in right 
hippocampal connectivity with several cortical regions, including middle and 
superior frontal gyri, for overall and negative remote memory (see figure 13). 
Complete accounts of the SWS- and REM-associated changes in right 
hippocampal connectivity are provided in tables 12 and 13 respectively.

Summary  
Behavioural analyses revealed no difference in memory performance between 
remote and recent images, irrespective of valence. RT’s for emotionally positive 
images however, were faster than those for their negative or neutral 
counterparts. SWS was associated with a greater degree behavioural 
consolidation for negative remote memories, whereas REM predicted a poorer 
degree of behavioural consolidation for positive remote memories. Functional 
imaging analyses showed that SWS was associated with reduced responses in 
the right hippocampus and parahippocampal gyrus for negative and overall 
remote memory, and reduced hippocampal-cortical connectivity for overall and 
positive remote memory. REM however, predicted an increase in hippocampal-
cortical connectivity for overall and negative remote memory.   
 
 
108 
 
Discussion  
While a number of studies have demonstrated that the overnight consolidation 
of emotional memories is accompanied by changes in the neural substrates 
underpinning their retrieval (Lewis, et al., 2011; Payne & Kensinger, 2011; 
Sterpenich, et al., 2007), little is known about the specific properties of sleep 
which play a more critical role in this process. In the current study, the brain 
regions associated with successful recollection of emotionally positive, negative 
and neutral image memories that had undergone 24 hours (remote memory) or 
30 minutes (recent memory) of consolidation were assessed with event-related 
fMRI. Importantly, remote learning was followed by a night of PSG monitored 
sleep, enabling us to examine the role of SWS, REM and other sleep stages in 
the reorganisation of emotional memories.   
 
Our data provide the first evidence that SWS mediates a targeted 
reorganisation, and thus consolidation, of emotionally affective memory 
representations. In addition to predicting the extent of negative remote memory 
consolidation, SWS was associated with reduced responses in the right 
hippocampus during the retrieval of negative remote memories, and a reduction 
in hippocampal-cortical connectivity during the retrieval of overall and positive 
remote memory. Reduced hippocampal responses for overall remote memory 
were also predicted by SWS, but this was a considerably weaker effect. While 
REM appeared to inhibit the consolidation of positive remote memories, 
retrieval-related activity in memory relevant brain regions was unaffected by this 
sleep stage. However, REM was associated with an increase in connectivity 
between the right hippocampus and several cortical regions during the retrieval 
of negative and overall remote memory, including the bilateral superior frontal 
gyrus. Thus, mnemonic reorganisation, particularly for emotionally negative 
representations, appears to be influenced by SWS and REM in qualitatively 
diverse manners. A full discussion of these findings, and the other results of this 
study, is provided below. 
 
109 
 
The role of SWS and REM in neural reorganisation  
Changes in neural activity 
Functional imaging analyses revealed that positive and negative remote image 
memories were associated with considerably different patterns of brain activity 
to neutral remote memories, indicating that a post-learning delay which includes 
nocturnal sleep impacts upon the consolidation of emotional and neutral 
memories in highly distinct manners. Recent accounts of the active systems 
consolidation model have highlighted the importance of mnemonic selectivity, 
whereby the most valuable or salient representations are preferentially 
redistributed into long-term memory during sleep. In view of this, a number of 
studies have indicated that increasing the perceived relevance, and thus 
salience, of a novel memory trace can increase its affinity for sleep-dependent 
consolidation processes (Fischer & Born, 2009; Saletin, et al., 2011; Wilhelm, et 
al., 2011). Since slow oscillations are thought to play a critical role in declarative 
memory processing (Born, et al., 2006; Born & Wilhelm, 2011; Marshall, et al., 
2006; Molle, et al., 2004), these electrophysiological phenomena may also 
support a targeted consolidation of the most salient elements of memory. In line 
with this notion, Wilhelm and colleagues (2011) reported that sleep slow 
oscillation activity was increased after the salience of newly formed declarative 
memories was manipulated, and that the extent of this increase was positively 
correlated with subsequent retrieval performance. Thus, it is reasonable to 
assume that emotionally affective memories, which also carry a high degree of 
salience, may undergo a selective consolidation process during states of 
vigilance where slow oscillations prevail. Accordingly, our data showed that 
SWS predicted a greater extent of behavioural consolidation in remote memory, 
but only for highly salient, emotionally negative images. More importantly 
however, our fMRI data revealed a SWS-related reduction in right hippocampal 
activity associated with negative remote memory. While our ROI analyses 
showed that SWS also predicted a decrease in right hippocampal and 
parahippocampal activation for overall remote memory, these effects were 
considerably weaker.  
110 
 
Building upon previous work (Takashima, et al., 2006), our findings suggest that 
SWS plays an active role in reorganising declarative retrieval dependency away 
from the short-term hippocampal memory store, and that these effects are 
enhanced for emotionally aversive memory representations. Taken together 
with previous findings (Wilhelm, et al., 2011), our data may also suggest that 
the unique biological properties of SWS support a targeted consolidation, and 
perhaps semanticisation, of highly salient memories, irrespective of whether 
they are emotional or neutral.  
 
However, such a proposal should be treated with some caution. According to 
the memory modulation hypothesis (LaBar & Cabeza, 2006; McGaugh, 2004; 
McGaugh, et al., 1996), the amygdala modulates encoding and consolidation 
processes in the medial temporal lobe as a result of an emotionally arousing 
experience, leading to the formation of a highly robust memory representation 
(LaBar & Cabeza, 2006; McGaugh, 2004; McGaugh, et al., 1996). This 
hypothesis has been supported by a wealth of literature (Canli, et al., 2000; 
Dolcos, et al., 2004b; Hatfield & McGaugh, 1999; Kilpatrick & Cahill, 2003; 
Liang, et al., 1990; McGaugh, 2002; Pelletier, et al., 2005; Roozendaal & 
McGaugh, 1996) and implies that processes exclusive to SWS, or any other 
state of vigilance, should not impact upon emotional and neutral memories in 
the same manner, regardless of salience. Nevertheless, manipulating the 
motivational salience attributed to novel information with a neutral tone may 
also have a knock-on effect for subjective levels of arousal either during, or 
shortly after, the learning phase. While speculative, under these conditions, 
neutral and emotional information could undergo a similar form of mnemonic 
processing during SWS. Future research endeavours could examine this 
prospect through a direct comparison of highly salient memories that are neutral 
or emotional.  
 
Owing to the unique neurobiological characteristics and increased amygdala 
activity of REM (Maquet, et al., 1996; Marrosu, et al., 1995), this sleep stage is 
regularly implicated in the consolidation of emotional memory representations 
111 
 
(Hu, et al., 2006; Walker, 2009; Walker & van der Helm, 2009).  In contrast to 
this view, our findings suggested that REM exerted an inhibitory influence upon 
the consolidation of positive remote memories. Such discrepancy may relate to 
the emotional valence of the memory in question. While our REM-related finding 
pertained to positive images, previous studies have only reported a beneficial 
impact of REM for the retention of negative memories (Nishida, et al., 2008; 
Wagner, et al., 2001), indicating that this sleep stage holds a particular affinity 
for emotionally aversive representations. This being the case, we may have 
also expected to observe a predictive relationship between post-learning REM 
and the consolidation of negative remote memories, but this was not so. 
However, a recent study by Baran and colleagues (2012) also failed to find an 
association between overnight REM and negative image retention, suggesting 
that the conditions of the current study may have prevented a REM-related 
mechanism from emerging within our data. Instead, our findings indicate that 
SWS plays a broader role in facilitating the redistribution of highly salient 
representations, which include emotionally aversive memories. 
 
Changes in functional connectivity 
Our PPI analyses also revealed a SWS-related reduction in hippocampal-
cortical connectivity associated with the recollection of overall and positive 
remote memory. These findings provide further support for the active systems 
consolidation model, in that the need for the hippocampus to integrate 
neocortical memory components is decreased over SWS. While these results 
partially compliment the SWS-related reductions in hippocampal activity 
described above, equivalent changes in hippocampal connectivity were not 
revealed for negative remote memory. This suggests that the pattern of neural 
reorganisation underpinning memory consolidation processes may be 
influenced in diverse manners by SWS, depending upon the emotional valence 
of the memory in question.  
 
112 
 
Interestingly, we also observed REM-related increases in hippocampal-cortical 
connectivity associated with negative and overall remote memory. This forms 
an important result as the active systems framework does not account for a 
mnemonic role of REM  (Diekelmann, et al., 2009), a sleep stage which in 
earlier years was regularly implicated in declarative memory processing 
(Empson & Clarke, 1970; Greenberg, et al., 1983; Tilley & Empson, 1978). In 
terms of elucidating a potential contribution of REM to memory consolidation, it 
is important to first acknowledge that beyond the veridical preservation of newly 
acquired information, sleep is also thought to assist an integrative stage of 
memory processing, whereby new memories are assimilated into generalised 
cognitive schemata (Lewis & Durrant, 2011; Tse, et al., 2007). Building upon 
previous sequential models of sleep and memory consolidation (Ambrosini & 
Giuditta, 2001; Giuditta, et al., 1995), recent work has suggested that SWS and 
REM may hold diverse, yet complimentary roles in optimising the potential 
efficacy of recently acquired information (Walker & Stickgold, 2010). Specifically, 
SWS is thought to facilitate the preservation of new memories, whilst keeping 
individual representations separate and detached. REM on the other hand, is 
proposed to support the integration of these and older memories into rich and 
generalised associative networks. In terms of the current study, it is possible 
that emotionally negative memories, which were selectively consolidated during 
SWS, may have been preferentially assimilated into pre-existing networks of 
related information during the ensuing REM period. Importantly, effective 
integration  is thought to require several periods of REM (Walker & Stickgold, 
2010), and presumably manifests within modifications in the associative neural 
trace at retrieval (Lewis & Durrant, 2011). Therefore, while speculative, such a 
process may have been reflected within the REM-related increase in 
hippocampal-cortical connectivity observed in our data, which was exclusive to 
negative and overall remote memory. Although a large body of work has 
suggested that sleep, and REM in particular, may augment such an integrative 
memory process (Cai, et al., 2009; Ellenbogen, et al., 2007; Stickgold, et al., 
1999; Walker, et al., 2002), research supporting a complimentary role of SWS 
and REM for memory consolidation is still in its relative infancy (Ficca & 
Salzarulo, 2004; Stickgold, et al., 2000b). However, this approach does explain 
113 
 
how sleep preserves memories but also allows them to evolve into more 
generalised representations of the world around us (Walker & Stickgold, 2010).  
 
Consolidation and the redistribution of emotional m emory  
The basic principle of the standard consolidation model (Frankland & Bontempi, 
2005; Marr, 1971; McClelland, et al., 1995) is that memories undergo a time-
dependent process of reorganisation, whereby retrieval dependency is shifted 
away from the temporary hippocampal store to the long-term neocortical 
memory networks. In line with this framework, overall remote memory, as 
compared to recent, was associated with stronger responses in the right middle 
temporal gyrus. The retrieval of recently formed memories however, was not 
exclusively associated with stronger responses in the hippocampus or any other 
memory relevant brain region. Using neuroimaging techniques, several studies 
have reported that the retrieval of new memories is heavily reliant upon the 
hippocampal formation, and that this retrieval dependency decreases with time 
(Sterpenich, et al., 2007; Sterpenich, et al., 2009; Takashima, et al., 2009; 
Takashima, et al., 2006), although some work has also reported a time-
dependent increase in hippocampal retrieval dependency (Bosshardt, Degonda, 
et al., 2005; Bosshardt, Schmidt, et al., 2005). Nonetheless, the aforementioned 
studies adopted protocols that were very different to those used here. Thus, 
under the conditions of the current study, changes in the hippocampal retrieval 
response may not have been observable over 24 hours.  
 
While positive remote memories were associated with stronger activity in the 
frontal and temporal cortices than positive recent memories, negative remote 
memories were not exclusively associated with any significant brain response. 
The retrieval of recently formed negative memories however, induced stronger 
responses in the angular gyrus than those that had been consolidated over 24 
hours. Although the angular gyrus has been implicated in both episodic and 
emotional memory retrieval in recent years (Huijbers, et al., 2011; Wagner, et 
al., 2005; Wang, et al., 2009), why this region should be exclusively active for 
114 
 
recently formed affective representations is unclear. Moreover, previous fMRI 
research has suggested that the retrieval of remote memories with an 
emotionally aversive tone is largely dependent upon the amygdala and vmPFC 
(Sterpenich, et al., 2007; Sterpenich, et al., 2009), two areas which, amongst 
others, are often associated with emotional memory processing (Dolcos, et al., 
2004a; Dolcos, et al., 2004b; Pelletier, et al., 2005). However, it is important to 
note that Sterpenich and colleagues (2007; 2009) adopted study paradigms in 
which remote memories were consolidated across 3 days and 6 months 
respectively. Accordingly, our interval of 24 hours may be too short to reveal 
consolidation-related changes in the brain areas known to support emotional 
memory processing.  
 
Our PPI analyses revealed that positive remote memories were associated with 
a weaker degree of hippocampal-cortical connectivity than positive recent 
memories, whereas neutral remote memories elicited a stronger degree of 
hippocampal-cortical connectivity than their recent counterparts. Assuming that 
neutral and positive memories are influenced by sleep in similar ways, these 
results may provide further physiological evidence for the concept of mnemonic 
selectivity in sleep-dependent consolidation (Born & Wilhelm, 2011). Specifically, 
positive memories, which were presumably highly salient, may have undergone 
a targeted consolidation process during sleep. Thus, the need for the 
hippocampus to integrate disparate neocortical memory modules during the 
subsequent retrieval phase may have been substantially reduced, and 
manifested within a lower degree of hippocampal-cortical connectivity. In 
contrast, non-salient neutral memories may have been processed in a typically 
gradual fashion over sleep, meaning that mnemonic integration, and thus 
hippocampal-cortical connectivity, was still critical to remote memory retrieval. 
However, other components of our data present some difficulty for this 
interpretation. If mnemonic salience, and thus a selective consolidation process, 
can account for such functional diversity between positive and neutral remote 
memories, an even stronger reduction in hippocampal-cortical connectivity 
should have been observed for negative remote memories, but this was not the 
case. Although, as mentioned earlier, this approach follows a rather contentious 
115 
 
assumption that emotionally aversive memories undergo similar offline 
consolidation processes to highly salient neutral or positive memories (see 
McGaugh and colleagues, 1996).  
 
Emotional memory and sleep 
As mentioned above, our functional imaging data showed that both positive and 
negative remote memories were associated with a significantly different pattern 
of brain activity to that of neutral remote memories, suggesting that emotional 
representations had undergone a unique form of processing over a delay which 
contained nocturnal sleep. It is therefore relatively surprising that emotional 
remote images were not better remembered than their neutral counterparts, an 
effect which has been consistently shown across short retention delays, 
including 1 hour (LaBar & Phelps, 1998) and 24 hours (Sharot & Phelps, 2004; 
Sharot & Yonelinas, 2008). Nevertheless, it is important to note that, despite 
increased responses in several brain networks, the recollection of emotional 
relative to neutral remote memories was not associated with stronger activity in 
the amygdala, medial prefrontal cortex or any other brain region commonly 
associated with emotional memory retrieval (Buchanan, 2007; Dolcos, et al., 
2004a; Dolcos, et al., 2004b). This being the case, a certain degree of caution 
should be maintained when suggesting that sleep may modulate memory 
consolidation processes in an emotion-specific manner.  
 
Overall memory performance  
While the precise mechanisms of forgetting are unresolved (Wixted, 2004), over 
a century of research has indicated that much of what we forget is a result of 
mental exertion, whereby the acquisition of novel information interferes with 
ongoing consolidation processes retroactively (Fillmore, et al., 2001; Lamberty, 
et al., 1990; Müller & Pilzecker, 1900; Skaggs, 1933). Importantly, previous 
work has suggested that the induction of hippocampal long-term potentiation 
(LTP) during interference learning negates the LTP associated with a previous 
learning episode in a temporally graded fashion, even if the tasks are unrelated 
116 
 
(Brun, et al., 2001; Izquierdo, et al., 1999; Villarreal, et al., 2002; Xu, et al., 
1998). As such, an equivalent memory performance for images that were 
encoded 24 hours or 30 minutes prior to retrieval forms a rather unexpected 
outcome. While it could be argued that remote memories were protected during 
the overnight period, sleep would certainly not have prevented forgetting. 
Moreover, being as the initial encoding phase was followed by a waking interval 
of approximately 8 hours, a substantial degree of interference could have 
occurred even before the onset of sleep. Future research endeavours should 
address both the causes and reliability of such unanticipated findings.  
 
Conclusions 
In the present study, we used fMRI and PSG to investigate how different stages 
of post-learning sleep impact upon the reorganisation of emotionally positive, 
negative and neutral image memories over 24 hours of consolidation. Our sleep 
and functional imaging data suggest that SWS supports an active and targeted 
strengthening of emotionally salient memories, which are integrated within rich 
and generalised associative networks during the ensuing REM episode. In 
accordance with the standard consolidation model (Frankland & Bontempi, 
2005; Marr, 1971; McClelland, et al., 1995) our findings also suggest that the 
recollection of pictographic memories is more dependent upon neocortical brain 
regions following 24 hours of consolidation.

This research was funded by the Engineering and Physical Sciences Research
