Biotechnology and Biological Sciences Research Council (BBSRC) New 
Investigator Award to PAL.   
 
 
117 
 
 
 
CHAPTER 4 
 
 
 Cuing neural replay with sounds during slow-wave sleep 
has dissociative effects upon emotionally                                     
negative and neutral memories 
 
 
Scott A. CAIRNEY, University of Manchester, UK 
Johan HULLEMAN, University of Manchester, UK 
Penelope A. LEWIS, University of Manchester, UK 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
This chapter is based on a manuscript that is being prepared for submission for peer 
review. 
118 
 
Abstract 
Recent work has indicated that experience-dependent patterns of neural replay 
can be augmented during slow-wave sleep (SWS) with auditory cues, leading to 
superior declarative memory performance. However, the precise nature of these 
effects is not well understood. One possibility is that cued replay strengthens 
associative memory representations directly, whilst another more indirect view 
is that auditory cues serve to ‘prime’ associative representations for a targeted 
consolidation process which occurs throughout the ensuing SWS period.  
Moreover, since previous work has focused on the reactivation of neutral 
memories alone, how cued replay should influence emotional representations is 
unclear. Here, thirty (10 male) participants encoded a number of emotionally 
negative and neutral picture-location associations, which were each paired with 
a semantically related sound. Participants then took a 90 minute nap where 
they were re-exposed to half of the learning-associated sounds during SWS. 
Shortly after waking, memory for all previously learned picture locations was 
tested. The impact of cued replay was assessed with memory performance and 
response times (RT’s) for correctly recalled items. A 2 (Replay: cued/not cued) 
by 2 (Valence: negative/neutral) repeated measures ANCOVA (SWS duration 
covariate) allowed us to assess whether the impact of cued replay was 
dependent on time spent in SWS. While no significant effects were found for 
memory performance, a 3-way interaction was revealed for RT’s. Subsequent 
analyses showed that SWS duration predicted faster RT’s for negative cued (vs. 
neutral cued) picture locations, but slower RT’s for neutral cued (vs. neutral 
non-cued) picture locations. These findings not only indicate that the mnemonic 
influences of cued replay are indirect in nature, but also suggest that SWS may 
mediate a targeted enhancement and suppression of respective negative and 
neutral cued memories. Thus, in order to preserve information that is most 
valuable for the future, SWS may exert qualitatively diverse effects upon cued 
memories with varying levels of emotion.  
 
Keywords :  Memory Consolidation, Neural Replay, Emotional Memory, Slow-
Wave Sleep.  
119 
 
Introduction  
The active systems model of sleep-dependent memory consolidation proposes 
that slow oscillations (~0.75Hz) occurring predominantly during slow-wave sleep 
(SWS) actively promote consolidation processes by driving a covert reactivation 
of the brain regions initially involved in encoding information (Born, 2010; Born 
& Wilhelm, 2011). This replay is thought to promote a progressive 
reorganisation of declarative memory, such that retrieval dependency is shifted 
from the short-term hippocampus to the long-term neocortical memory networks.  
 
Several years of animal and human research has demonstrated that 
experience-dependent patterns of regional brain activity can be replayed during 
SWS (Kudrimoti, et al., 1999; Peigneux, et al., 2004; Sutherland & McNaughton, 
2000; Wilson & McNaughton, 1994). While compelling, these studies have been 
often criticised for failing to establish whether neural reactivation represents a 
genuine mechanism of consolidation, or simply reflects a use-dependent by-
product of previous waking activity (Gais & Born, 2004). In view of this issue, 
recent investigations have indicated that SWS-dependent neural replay can be 
manipulated in humans with associative mnemonic cues, providing evidence for 
a causal role of this phenomenon in offline memory processing. Rasch and 
colleagues (2007) for example, reported that re-presenting a learning-
associated odour during SWS had a beneficial impact upon subsequent visuo-
spatial memory performance. Using a similar paradigm, Dieklemann and 
colleagues (2011) suggested that cuing memories with odours during SWS also 
renders them more resistant to retroactive interference. Furthermore, Rudoy 
and colleagues (2009) reported that retrieval performance was better for 
picture-location memories that were cued with learning-associated sounds 
during SWS.  
 
While these studies were the first to suggest a decisive role of neural 
reactivation in declarative memory consolidation, the question of exactly how 
novel representations are strengthened by cued replay remains unanswered. 
120 
 
One possibility is that stimulating replay with sensory cues exerts an immediate 
and profound boost to the consolidation of the memory in question, representing 
a direct impact of cued replay. Another more indirect view is that external cues 
serve to ‘prime’ their associative memory traces for a targeted consolidation 
process, which unfolds continuously throughout the ensuing period of SWS. In 
line with this indirect approach, the extent to which declarative representations 
are strengthened by cued replay should be dependent upon the amount of SWS 
that occurs after learning.  
 
Furthermore, since the aforementioned studies used entirely neutral stimuli 
(Diekelmann, et al., 2011; Rasch, et al., 2007; Rudoy, et al., 2009), it is unclear 
how cued replay would impact upon memories with an emotionally affective 
tone. Previous work has indicated that a mnemonic trade-off occurs during 
sleep, whereby emotional components of memory are fortified at the expense of 
their more neutral or mundane counterparts (Hu, et al., 2006; Nishida, et al., 
2008; Payne, et al., 2008; Wagner, et al., 2001). As such, while re-presenting 
sensory cues during SWS may reactivate all of the memories in question, a 
limited consolidation capacity may result in a selective strengthening of 
emotional memory representations.  
 
Here, we report a study which examined how SWS-dependent auditory cued 
replay impacted upon the consolidation of declarative memories that were 
emotionally negative or neutral. Participants were trained on a picture-location 
task with both negative and neutral images, which were each paired with a 
semantically related sound.  After training, participants took a nap and were re-
presented with half of the sounds during SWS before having their memory and 
response times (RT’s) assessed for all picture locations in a retrieval test. Using 
a 2 (Replay: cued/not cued) by 2 (Valence: negative/neutral) repeated 
measures ANCOVA with SWS duration (mins) as a covariate, we were able to 
investigate whether SWS-dependent cued replay boosted the strength of 
memories directly, or indirectly assisted consolidation processes through a form 
of neural priming. Moreover, we were able to assess whether cued replay 
121 
 
influenced all associative memories in an equivalent fashion, or if these effects 
were more pronounced for emotionally salient representations.  
 
Since previous research has shown that manipulating the perceived relevance 
of recently formed memories can increase their affinity for sleep-dependent 
memory processes (Fischer & Born, 2009; Saletin, et al., 2011; Wilhelm, et al., 
2011), we presumed that auditory cued replay may induce a similar effect offline. 
In line with these findings, and those of other work highlighting a predictive 
relationship between SWS and subsequent declarative memory performance 
(Plihal & Born, 1997, 1999a), we reasoned that cuing replay with sounds during 
SWS would prime memories for a targeted, but yet continuous, consolidation 
process. Therefore, in line with an indirect mechanism of cued replay, we 
expected that the degree of replay-related improvement would be dependent on 
SWS duration. Furthermore, following previous work on sleep and emotional 
memory (Hu, et al., 2006; Wagner, et al., 2001; Wagner, et al., 2006), we 
predicted that cued replay would support a selective strengthening of 
emotionally negative picture-location memories.  
 
Materials and Methods 
Participants 
Thirty (10 male) healthy participants aged 18-28 (mean age 20.37 [S.D. ± 2.63]) 
were recruited on a voluntary basis and took part in exchange for £15 or 
undergraduate psychology course credit. However, 15 participants were 
excluded for a number of reasons including: failure to obtain sufficient SWS (4), 
waking up during sound presentation (10), and poor task performance (1). 
Therefore, the data presented is based upon the remaining 15 participants (3 
male) aged 18-28 (mean age 20.40 [S.D. ± 3.07]). As evaluated with a pre-
study screening questionnaires and telephone interviews, participants had no 
history of sleep, depressive or neurological disorders and reported regular 
sleep-wake patters across the month preceding the study. Participants were 
free from any form of psychologically active medications and agreed to abstain 
122 
 
from alcohol and caffeine from 24 hours prior to the study until its completion. 
Written informed consent was acquired from all participants in line with the 
School of Psychological Sciences Research Ethics Committee, University of 
Manchester. In order to assess potential differences in alertness levels, 
participants completed the Stanford Sleepiness Scale at the beginning of each 
experimental session. To ensure that no deficit in alertness occurred in relation 
to homeostatic sleep pressure, we also calculated correlation coefficients 
between all retrieval response times and the amount of SWS obtained by 
participants. 
 
Experimental task 
We used a modified version of the object location task used by Takashima and 
colleagues (2009), utilising photographic imagery rather than faces. At encoding, 
participants were presented with a number of semantically congruent picture-
sound pairs (picture dimensions H85mm W70mm), which were each associated 
with one of six locations on a computer screen. In a forced choice retrieval task, 
participants were re-presented with the picture-sound pair and had to retrieve 
the associated screen location with a joystick.  
 
Stimuli 
A total of 72 images (36 negative and 36 neutral) were selected from the 
international affective picture system (IAPS)  (Lang, et al., 2005). IAPS pictures 
range from everyday scenes, to images of injury, violence, decay and 
contaminated foods, and are rated on 9-point scales for emotional valence (1 = 
extremely negative, 5 = neutral, 9 = extremely positive) and arousal (1 = very 
low arousal, 9 = very high arousal). The negative and neutral image sets were 
significantly different in terms of both mean valence rating (negative: 2.74 [S.D. 
± 0.62]; neutral: 5.60 [S.D. ± 0.77], t(35) = 16.24; p < 0.0001) and mean arousal 
rating (negative: 5.81 [S.D. ± 0.74]; neutral: 4.00 [S.D. ± 0.85], t(35) = 8.55; p < 
0.0001), but were balanced for human content. Each image was paired with a 
semantically related sound taken from the International Affective Digitized 
123 
 
Sounds (IADS) battery (Bradley & Lang, 2007), to create 36 neutral and 36 
negative picture-sound pairs. Each IADS item is 6000ms in length and rated on 
the same 9-point valence and arousal scales as the IAPS. The sounds used for 
the negative and neutral picture-sound sets were also significantly different in 
terms of both mean valence rating (negative: 3.60 [S.D. ± 1.33]; neutral: 5.32 
[S.D. ± 1.23], t(35) = 7.19; p < 0.0001) and mean arousal rating (negative: 6.17 
[S.D. ± 1.16]; neutral: 5.29 [S.D. ± 1.00], t(35) = 3.16; p = 0.003). See the 
supplementary information (S1) for a complete account of the picture-sound 
pairs.  
 
The 72 sounds were split into two subsets of 36 (18 negative, 18 neutral). One 
of these subsets was re-presented during SWS, whereas the other subset was 
not. The negative and neutral components of each sound sub-set did not differ 
in terms of mean valence rating (set 1 negative: 3.51 [S.D. ± 1.31]; set 2 
negative: 3.69 [S.D. ± 1.38], t(17) = 0.42; p = 0.68, set 1 neutral: 5.38 [S.D. ± 
1.29]; set 2 neutral: 5.27 [S.D. ± 1.20], t(17) = 0.25; p = 0.81) or mean arousal 
rating (set 1 negative: 6.10 [S.D. ± 1.36]; set 2 negative: 6.24 [S.D. ± 0.95], t(17) 
= 0.35; p = 0.73, set 1 neutral: 5.30 [S.D. ± 1.13]; set 2 neutral: 5.28 [S.D. ± 
0.87], t(17) = 0.05; p = 0.96). The sound subset used for cued replay was 
counterbalanced across participants.  
 
Equipment 
Experimental task 
The encoding and retrieval phases of the picture-location task were written and 
implemented with Presentation© version 14.1 on a Toshiba© Satellite Pro laptop 
with a 13” screen. Sounds were heard through a pair of Sennheiser© HD207 
noise-cancelling headphones and participant responses were recorded with a 
Logitech© Attack™ 3 joystick.  
 
 
124 
 
Polysomnographic recording 
Polysomnographic (PSG) monitoring was carried out using an Embla© N7000 
sleep monitoring system with RemLogic© 1.1 software. Silver-silver chloride 
(Ag-AgCl) electrodes were attached using EC2© electrogel after the scalp was 
cleaned using NuPrep© exfoliating agent. Electroencephalography (EEG) scalp 
electrodes were attached according to the international 10-20 system at six 
standardised locations: Central (C3 & C4), frontal (F3 & F4) and occipital (O1 & 
O2), and each was referenced to the contralateral mastoid (A1 or A2). Left and 
right electrooculagram, left, right and upper electromyogram, and a ground 
electrode were also attached. All electrodes were verified to have a connection 
impedance of less than 5kOhms. All signals were digitally sampled at a rate of 
200Hz.  
 
Sound presentation during SWS 
An algorithm for presenting sounds during SWS was created and implemented 
using Presentation© version 14.1 on a Toshiba© Satellite Pro laptop. Using a 
10m extension cable, the laptop was connected to PC speakers placed on a 
table approximately 1m away from the participant in the bedroom. The volume 
of sounds was loud enough that they could be readily distinguished during 
wakefulness, but soft enough to prevent most participants awakening. To 
further prevent participant awakening, sounds were embedded in brown noise, 
which was played throughout the napping period. 
 
Procedure 
Session one (12pm) 
The first experimental session began with the encoding phase of the picture-
location task. Here, participants were asked to direct their attention to a laptop 
screen which initially contained a black background with six small grey circles at 
the top, middle and bottom left and right. In addition, a grey rectangular mask 
with the same dimensions as the picture stimuli could be seen at the centre of 
125 
 
the screen. To direct participants focus during the task, the grey mask also 
contained a small black crosshair in its centre. For each randomised trial, the 
grey mask was shown for 1000ms before one of the 72 (36 negative, 36 neutral) 
picture-sound pairs were presented in its place for 6000ms. One of the 6 grey 
circles surrounding the image then flashed green for 1000ms and the picture 
moved to its location. The picture remained at this location for 2000ms before 
the next trial began. Participants were instructed to memorise the pictures and 
their associated screen locations, and to move the joystick in the direction that 
each picture moved.  
 
Immediately after the encoding phase, participants undertook a retrieval test 
which probed their memory for the screen location associated with each picture. 
For each trial, participants were re-presented with the black screen and six 
circular screen locations, but a small white crosshair had replaced the grey 
rectangular mask present at encoding. After a delay of 1000ms, one of the 
picture-sound pairs was randomly presented, with the picture disappearing 
upon the completion of the sound stimulus (6000ms). Using a joystick, 
participants were then required to move a pink cursor to the circle that they 
believed the picture-sound pair was previously associated with as quickly and 
as accurately as possible. So that participants knew their response had been 
recorded, the circle flashed white for 200ms upon being selected. Participants 
were not given any correct/incorrect feedback for their responses. After making 
their location choice, participants were required to indicate how certain they 
were that their answer was correct by moving the cursor to one of 5 circular 
locations. Each of these circles was a different colour (blue, green, yellow, 
orange and red) and depicted a different level of certainty (for reference: 1 = 
very uncertain, 5 = very certain). After making this response, the next 
randomised trial began. In order to facilitate learning, the entire encoding and 
retrieval process was carried out twice, thus session one took approximately 1 
hour to complete.  
 
 
126 
 
Retention interval & SWS reactivation (2pm) 
Upon the completion of session one, participants were connected to a PSG unit 
(1pm-2pm) and asked to sleep in a bedroom within the sleep research 
laboratory at the University of Manchester for approximately 90 minutes (2pm-
3.30pm). When participants had exhibited at least 2 minutes of sustained online 
SWS, one half of the picture-associated sound cues (18 negative and 18 neutral) 
were re-presented in random order. The sound set was played once, with each 
sound separated by a 3 second interval. The entire set required 324 seconds to 
complete. After waking, participants were disconnected from the PSG unit and 
given a break to wash the electrogel out of their hair and recover from the 
general effects of sleep inertia (3.30pm-4pm). 
 
Session two (4pm) 
After returning from their break, participants undertook a third and final run of 
the picture-location retrieval task. At the end of the session, participants 
confirmed that they were unaware of any sound re-presentation during sleep 
and were asked to guess which 36 sounds they were presented with using a 
questionnaire. The experimental procedures and tasks are illustrated in figure 
14. 
 
Data analysis 
Behaviour 
Since participants were forced to choose one of six locations in the picture-
location task, some proportion of correct responses may have resulted from 
guessing. In order to protect our results from this confound, our behavioural 
analyses only included responses that were accompanied with a high degree of 
confidence (a certainty rating of 4 or 5).  
 
 
127 
 
Figure 14 : The experimental procedures and tasks used in this study  
 
.  
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
A: Session one (12pm-1pm).  At encoding, participants were presented with each of 72 (36 negative, 36 neutral) pictures and semantically related sounds. After each picture/sound presentation, the picture moved to one of 6 screen locations. Here, participants were instructed to move a joystick in the same direction as the picture and memorise its final location. At retrieval, participants were presented with the picture/sound pairs again, but had to select the location that they thought was associated with each picture using the joystick. Each retrieval response was followed by a certainty rating. To facilitate learning, the encoding and retrieval process was carried out twice. B: Participants took a nap and were monitored with polysomnography (2pm-3.30pm). During slow-wave sleep (SWS), half of the sounds (18 negative, 18 neutral) were re-presented to participants. C: Session two (4pm-4.30pm). Participants completed a third and final run of the retrieval task. 
128 
 
In order to examine the mnemonic influence of SWS-dependent cued replay, 
the sensitivity index (d’) was calculated by subtracting the normalised false 
alarm rate (high confidence incorrect location choice / number of high 
confidence trials) from the normalised hit rate (high confidence correct location 
choice / number of high confidence trials) for picture locations in the final (post-
sleep) retrieval phase. As an additional measure of cued replay, our analysis 
was also focused on response times (RT’s) for correctly recalled (high 
confidence) picture-locations in the final retrieval phase.    
 
Thus, a 2x2 repeated measures analysis of covariance (ANCOVA) was adopted 
for this study, with ‘Replay’ (cued/not cued during SWS) and Valence 
(negative/neutral) as factors, and the total amount of SWS obtained by 
participants (mins) as a covariate. Using this approach, a significant relationship 
between the covariate and ‘Replay’ would indicate that the impact of cued 
replay for memory consolidation is dependent upon SWS duration, and thus 
indirect in nature. To prevent the covariate from altering the standard effects of 
this analysis (i.e. those that did not include the covariate itself), SWS values 
were mean-centred (value – mean) (Delaney & Maxwell, 1981). Since previous 
research has implicated rapid eye movement sleep (REM) in emotional memory 
processing (Nishida, et al., 2008; Wagner, et al., 2001), this ANCOVA was also 
conducted with total REM duration (mins) as a mean-centred covariate. All 
behavioural data was analysed with SPSS version 16.0 statistical software with 
a two-tailed p < 0.05 considered as significant. 
 
PSG  
For the purposes of delivering sound cues during SWS, all PSG sleep 
recordings were visually scored online with RemLogic© 1.1 software by an 
experienced sleep researcher (SAC). Online sleep scoring was conducted upon 
the referenced central electrodes (C3-A2 and C4-A1) according to the 
standardised sleep scoring criteria of Rechtschaffen and Kales (1968), with 
sleep stages three and four collectively scored as slow-wave sleep (SWS). To 
129 
 
confirm that sound re-presentation had occurred during a definitive period of 
SWS, offline sleep scoring was also conducted independently by two sleep 
researchers (SAC and SJD) with RemLogic© 1.1 software. For offline scoring, 
sleep data were categorised into 30s epochs and scored in the same manner 
as described above. The data was then partitioned in terms of the duration of 
time (mins) spent in each sleep stage: stage one sleep (S1), stage two sleep 
(S2), SWS and REM. Sleep data are available in table 14.

SWS = slow-wave sleep, REM = rapid eye movement sleep, TST = total sleep time. 
 
Results 
Pre-study sleep data 
The mean hours slept during the night preceding the study, as reported in the 
participant sleep questionnaire, was 7.37 [S.D. ± 1.03]. There was no significant 
difference between this value and subjective estimations of mean hours slept in 
a typical night: 7.60 [S.D. ± 0.91] (t(14) = 1.20; p = 0.25), confirming that 
participants’ pre-study sleep did not deviate from their usual practices. 
 
Alertness 
The Stanford Sleepiness Scale revealed no difference in mean levels of 
alertness between session one and session two, which took place before and 
after sleep respectively (session one: 2.40 [S.D. ± 0.99]; session two: 2.27 [S.D. 
± 0.96], t(14) = 0.56; p = 0.58). In addition, no significant correlation was found 
between the duration of SWS (mins) and all RT’s for negative (r = -0.39; p =

suggesting no deficit in alertness related to homeostatic sleep pressure. Taken 
together, these measures indicate that the results of this study were not 
confounded by deficits in participant alertness. 
 
Behaviour   
Pre-sleep performance 
To optimise picture-location learning, two pre-sleep encoding/retrieval phases 
were included in the study protocol. Pre-sleep retrieval data however, is focused 
on the second retrieval test alone. No significant difference was found between 
memory performance (d’) (t(14) = 0.43; p = 0.68) or RT’s (t(14) = 0.50; p = 0.63) 
for neutral and negative picture locations. All relevant behavioural data relating 
to memory performance and RT’s can be found in tables 15A and 15B 
respectively.

131 
 
Auditory cued replay 
In order to examine the mnemonic impact of re-presenting learning-associated 
sounds during SWS, we conducted a 2x2 repeated measures ANCOVA for 
memory performance (d’) and RT’s with factors ‘Replay’ (cued/not cued during 
SWS) and ‘Valence’ (negative/neutral), and total SWS duration (mins) as a 
mean-centred covariate.  In addition to a significant interaction between SWS 
and Valence F(1,13) = 4.99; p = 0.044), a significant 3-way interaction was 
revealed between SWS, Replay and Valence (F(1,13) = 9.04; p = 0.01) for RT’s. 
However, no interaction between SWS and Replay (F(1,13) = 0.58; p = 0.46) 
was revealed for RT’s, nor was a main effect of SWS (F(1,13) = 0.42; p = 0.53). 
For picture-location memory, no interaction was found between SWS and 
Replay (F(1,13) = 0.57; p = 0.46), between SWS and Valence F(1,13) = 0.04; p 
= 0.85) or between SWS, Replay and Valence (F(1,13) = 1.28; p = 0.28), and 
no main effect was found for SWS (F(1,13) = 0.20; p = 0.66). 
  
Turning to the standard effects of the analysis (i.e. those that did not involve the 
SWS covariate), no main effect of Replay was found for picture-location 
memory (F(1,13) = 0.04; p = 0.84). While RT’s were numerically faster for items 
that were cued during SWS, this difference was not significant (F(1,13) = 1.94; 
p = 0.19). No main effect of valence was found for picture-location memory 
(F(1,13) = 0.25; p = 0.63) or RT’s (F(1,13) = 0.62; p = 0.45), and there was no 
interaction between factors for either measure (memory performance: F(1,13) = 
0.26; p = 0.62, RT’s: F(1,13) = 1.03; p = 0.33). 
 
To elucidate the nature of the SWS-related interactions described above, we 
calculated a number of RT difference measures, which pertained to the 
experimental factors of the ANCOVA: the emotionality of the correctly recalled 
picture location (negative/neutral) and whether or not it had been cued during 
SWS. Correlation coefficients were then calculated between these difference 
measures and the amount of SWS obtained after learning (mins). 
 
132 
 
One such difference measure was calculated by subtracting RT’s for negative 
cued items from that of neutral cued items, thus a positive outcome represented 
faster RT’s for negative cued items. We found that SWS duration was 
correlated with RT’s for negative cued (vs. neutral cued) picture locations (r = 
0.66; p = 0.008), suggesting that the consolidation of reactivated negative 
memories was modulated during the ensuing SWS period (see figure 15A). 
Importantly, no significant correlation was found between SWS duration and the 
difference in RT’s between negative and neutral picture locations that were not 
cued during SWS (r = 0.06; p = 0.83). 
  
Another difference measure was calculated by subtracting RT’s for neutral cued 
items from that of neutral non-cued items, thus a positive outcome represented 
faster RT’s for neutral cued items. Interestingly, RT’s for neutral cued (vs. 
neutral non-cued) picture locations were negatively correlated with SWS (r = -
0.60; p = 0.018), while the equivalent correlation between SWS and RT’s for 
negative cued (vs. negative non-cued) picture locations was in the opposite 
direction but not significant (r = 0.37; p = 0.17) (see figure 15B). Taken together, 
these findings suggest that SWS may have not only promoted the consolidation 
of negative cued memories, but also facilitated an offline suppression of neutral 
cued memories. In order to ensure that these effects were not due to a non-
specific effect of confidence (i.e. correct responses with high certainty rating) we 
repeated our analyses to include all correct responses. As expected, these 
produced a very similar outcome (negative cued (vs. neutral cued) RT’s*SWS: r 
= 0.69; p = 0.004, negative non-cued (vs. neutral non-cued) RT’s*SWS: r = 0.07; 
p = 0.81, neutral cued (vs. neutral non-cued) RT’s*SWS: r = -0.56; p = 0.03, 
negative cued (vs. negative non-cued) RT’s*SWS: r = 0.31; p = 0.27). 
 
Since previous research has implicated REM in emotional memory 
consolidation (Nishida, et al., 2008; Wagner, et al., 2001), we repeated the 
aforementioned ANCOVA with the total duration of REM (mins) as a mean-
centred covariate.  
133

No significant relationship was found between SWS and RT’s for correctly retrieved negative non-cued (vs. neutral non-cued) picture-location memories. B: Negative correlation between SWS and RT’s for correctly retrieved neutral cued (vs. neutral non-cued) picture-location memories. The equivalent correlation between SWS and RT’s for correctly retrieved negative cued (vs. negative non-cued) picture-location memories was in the opposite direction, but not significant. Collectively, these results suggest that SWS may support an active enhancement of emotional cued memories and a concomitant suppression of neutral cued memories.  
134 
 
This analysis revealed no significant effects for either memory performance 
(REM main effect: F(1,13) = 2.82; p = 0.12, REM x Replay: F(1,13) = 0.25; p = 
0.63, REM x Valence: F(1,13) = 0.04; p = 0.84, REM x Replay x Valence: 
F(1,13) = 1.98; p = 0.18) or RT’s (REM main effect: F(1,13) = 0.01; p = 0.92, 
REM x Replay: F(1,13) = 0.14; p = 0.71, REM x Valence: F(1,13) = 3.04; p = 
0.11, REM x Replay x Valence: F(1,13) = 1.34; p = 0.27).  
 
For completeness, we also included total sleep time (TST) and the duration of 
S1 and S2 (mins) as mean-centred covariates in the ANCOVA. As expected, no 
significant interactions were found between these sleep parameters and any of 
the experimental factors for either memory performance or RT’s (S1: all p > 0.1, 
S2: all p > 0.1, TST: all p > 0.2). 
 
Sound awareness 
In addition to confirming that they had no knowledge of sound re-presentation, 
participants performed at chance when asked to guess which of the 36 sounds 
they were presented with during SWS (t(14) = 0.26; p = 0.80). 
 
Discussion 
Behavioural and physiological research has indicated that SWS-dependent 
neural replay can be augmented with external mnemonic cues, subsequently 
strengthening declarative memory representations (Diekelmann, et al., 2011; 
Rasch, et al., 2007; Rudoy, et al., 2009). However, the nature of this cued 
replay effect is not fully understood, and previous research has focused on the 
reactivation of memories with an entirely neutral tone. In the present study, we 
examined how cuing SWS-dependent neural replay with auditory stimuli would 
impact upon the consolidation emotionally negative or neutral picture-location 
memories, and whether such effects were more direct or indirect in nature.   
 
135 
 
In contrast to previous findings (Rudoy, et al., 2009), re-presenting learning 
associated sounds during SWS had no effect upon subsequent retrieval 
performance, irrespective of whether picture-location memories were 
emotionally negative or neutral.  However, when SWS duration was included in 
our analyses, an entirely different pattern of results were obtained. While 
memory performance remained unaffected, SWS duration predicted faster RT’s 
for correctly recalled negative cued (vs. neutral cued) picture-location memories, 
but slower RT’s for correctly recalled neutral cued (vs. neutral non-cued) 
picture-location memories. These findings suggest that cued replay may not 
boost the strength of individual memory representations directly, but rather 
indirectly ‘prime’ memories for a targeted consolidation process, which occurs 
throughout the subsequent SWS period. Thus, after cued replay has occurred, 
time spent in SWS may represent the critical factor for memory consolidation. 
 
Importantly, our data also indicate that the emotional characteristics of a cued 
representation may determine the manner in which it is influenced by SWS-
dependent processes. While cued emotional memories appeared to be 
selectively strengthened during SWS, their neutral counterparts appeared to 
undergo a simultaneous targeted suppression. Such findings are suggestive of 
a cooperative SWS-dependent consolidation network which exerts diverse 
effects upon emotional and neutral memories in order to strengthen the most 
significant representations. A more detailed discussion of the mechanisms that 
are proposed to underpin our results is provided below.  
 
Cued replay and SWS: an indirect process? 
The notion that SWS-dependent neural replay can be augmented with external 
cues, leading to superior memory performance, is not a new one (Rasch, et al., 
2007). However, the exact nature of this effect is relatively unknown. Here, we 
provide preliminary evidence that cued replay exerts an indirect impact upon 
newly formed memories, priming their associative representations for an active 
and targeted consolidation process during SWS.  
136 
 
In light of recent research, such a mechanism could be considered as not 
altogether surprising. A number of studies have corroborated an active sleep-
dependent process which selectively strengthens the most relevant or salient 
components of human memory (Born & Wilhelm, 2011; Fischer & Born, 2009; 
Saletin, et al., 2011). In one such study, Wilhelm and colleagues (2011), 
demonstrated that post-learning sleep, as compared to wakefulness, only 
benefited declarative memory performance if the perceived relevance, and thus 
salience, of learned information had been increased before sleep. Such effects 
are thought to reflect a form of neural tagging, which facilitates the access of 
highly salient representations to SWS-dependent consolidation processes 
(Fischer & Born, 2009; Marshall & Born, 2007). Our findings suggest that the 
selective consolidation that occurs as a result of manipulating mnemonic 
salience prior to SWS may be triggered in a similar yet implicit fashion by cuing 
replay during SWS. In line with this concept, Wilhelm and colleagues (2011) 
also reported that slow oscillation activity, which characterises SWS, was 
increased after mnemonic salience was manipulated, and that the extent of this 
increase was positively correlated with subsequent retrieval performance. 
 
Dissociative influences of SWS 
Our data also indicate that the emotional properties of a cued memory 
representation may determine the precise manner in which it is influenced 
during subsequent SWS. To potentially protect or enhance the most important 
components of memory, SWS-dependent processes appeared to support a 
concomitant enhancement and suppression of respective emotional and neutral 
picture locations that were reactivated with auditory cues. While previous 
research has shown that emotional memories are preferentially enhanced over 
sleep (Hu, et al., 2006; Payne & Kensinger, 2011; Payne, et al., 2008; Wagner, 
et al., 2001), we provide evidence that the preservation of affective information 
is partly mediated by a SWS-dependent suppression of neutral memories.  
 
137 
 
However, it is possible that these effects were driven by the particular nature of 
our study paradigm. Under normal circumstances (i.e. without cued replay), 
sleep would operate in a typically biased manner, strengthening highly salient 
emotional memories whilst avoiding non-salient neutral information encoded at 
the same time (Payne, et al., 2008). In contrast, when neutral memories are 
cued by auditory stimuli during SWS, they may become primed for a targeted 
consolidation process within cognitive space that is usually dominated by 
emotional representations. To ensure a selective strengthening of highly salient 
memories in these circumstances, a refined SWS-dependent consolidation 
network may actively suppress neutral information whilst enhancing emotional 
memory traces concomitantly. In line with this concept, recent work has 
indicated that sleep spindles, which occur during stage two sleep and SWS, 
may support a suppression of irrelevant or unwanted memories (Saletin, et al., 
2011).  
 
Although speculative, this notion may also support recent work attempting to 
reconcile two diverse models of SWS and memory consolidation (Lewis & 
Durrant, 2011). While the active systems consolidation model (Born & Wilhelm, 
2011) proposes that declarative memories are stabilised as their retrieval 
dependency is shifted from the short-term hippocampus to the long-term 
neocortex during SWS, the synaptic homeostasis hypothesis (Tononi & Cirelli, 
2003, 2006) suggests that synapses potentiated as a result of waking learning 
experience are actively downscaled during SWS, leaving behind a more 
efficient memory trace which affords better recall. Importantly, the synaptic 
homeostasis hypothesis also proposes that in order to survive such 
depotentiation, the strength of mnemonic synapses must exceed a pre-
determined threshold. Therefore, while strong and enduring memory traces may 
exist in a more efficient form after downscaling, weak and labile representations 
may be abolished forever. In line with the active systems model of consolidation, 
cuing emotionally salient memories may have stimulated a targeted 
reorganisation of their associative representations during SWS. Conversely, in 
accordance with the synaptic homeostasis hypothesis, reactivating non-salient 
neutral memories with external cues may have evoked an autonomous 
138 
 
downscaling of their associative synaptic connections, thus indirectly supporting 
the formation of memories deemed to be important for the future.  
 
Theoretical issues 
A potential concern within our data relates to the proposal that REM may play a 
critical role in emotional memory processing (Walker, 2009; Walker & van der 
Helm, 2009). While we found no association between REM and subsequent 
emotional memory performance, studies reporting such a relationship did not 
involve cued replay during either REM or SWS (Nishida, et al., 2008; Wagner, 
et al., 2001), which, as described above, may lead to an entirely different 
pattern of offline consolidation. In addition, several participants in this study 
achieved very little, if any REM (n=7), during their nap, meaning that potential 
relationships between REM and emotional memory could not be established. 
Furthermore, although REM may augment the consolidation of emotional 
memories, our data suggest that SWS mediates an enhancement of highly 
salient representations that are cued by external stimuli, which include those 
with an emotional tone.  
 
This study is the first to suggest that cuing neural replay with learning-
associated sounds during SWS exerts distinct effects upon the consolidation of 
emotionally negative and neutral picture-location memories. However, it is 
important to note that previous investigations have reported replay-related 
changes in memory performance (Rasch, et al., 2007; Rudoy, et al., 2009), 
whereas the effects found in this study were specific to RT’s.  
 
Summary 
In the present study, we sought to examine the nature of SWS-dependent cued 
replay effects in emotional and neutral declarative memory. While re-presenting 
sound cues during SWS had no impact upon picture-location memory 
performance, SWS duration predicted faster RT’s for negative cued (vs. neutral 
139 
 
cued) picture locations, but slower RT’s for neutral cued (vs. neutral non-cued) 
picture locations. These findings suggest that, in order to ensure the 
preservation of inherently significant information, SWS may support a 
respective enhancement and suppression of negative and neutral memory 
representations whose replay is manipulated with external sensory cues.

CHAPTER 5 
 
  
 Sleep-dependent consolidation of emotional context 
memory: the diverse influences of stage two sleep and 
sleep spindles. 
 
 
Scott A. CAIRNEY, University of Manchester, UK 
Rebecca JACKSON, University of Manchester, UK 
Penelope A. LEWIS, University of Manchester, UK 
 
 
 
 
 
 
This chapter is based on a manuscript that is being prepared for submission for peer 
review. Due to the formatting requirements of the targeted journal, this chapter is 
arranged such that the detailed Materials and Methods section follows the Discussion. 
As the behavioural data reported on pages 147-150 is published in Neuropsychologia 
(2011) 49: 2619-2629, this paper is focused on the polysomnography data.  
143 
 
Abstract  
Post-learning sleep has been shown to selectively protect emotional memories.  
In this paper, we ask whether sleep also selectively protects the associative 
linkages between neutral memories and emotional context information and 
examine the specific aspects of sleep which may mediate these effects. 
Participants encoded neutral foreground images paired with either emotional or 
neutral backgrounds.  Immediate and delayed tests for the 
foreground/background association were separated by a 4-hour retention 
interval which consisted of either total wakefulness or included a 2-hour nap 
with polysomnography. Behavioural data revealed equivalent protection by 
sleep for both emotional and neutral context memories, however 
electrophysiological data showed opposing effects on negative and neutral 
associations.  Specifically, the number of sleep spindles recorded over frontal 
cortex predicted increased forgetting and slowed response times (RT’s) for 
correct neutral associations, while time spent in stage two sleep (S2) predicted 
attenuated forgetting and speeded RT’s for correct negative contextual 
associations. Interestingly, time spent in slow-wave sleep (SWS) predicted RT 
slowing for negative associations, and thus appeared to counteract the impact 
of S2. Our findings are suggestive of a paradoxical sleep-dependent 
mechanism, which may prevent the preferential strengthening of highly salient, 
emotional information in the contextual domain. While the consolidation of 
negative contexts may be boosted during S2, sleep spindles may also offer 
indirect support to such memories by suppressing their neutral counterparts. 
However, SWS-dependent processes may nullify the former effects, leading to 
an absence of emotion-related memory enhancements after sleep.   
 
Keywords :  Emotional Memory, Context Memory, Memory Consolidation, 
Stage Two Sleep, Slow-Wave Sleep, Sleep Spindles.  
 
 
144 
 
Introduction  
In the domain of memory research, consolidation refers to a neuro-cognitive 
process whereby recently formed, weak or labile memory traces become strong 
and enduring representations over time. Evidence from behavioural and 
physiological investigations has demonstrated that a night of post-learning sleep, 
relative to an equivalent period of wakefulness, facilitates the consolidation of 
declarative memories (Born, 2010; Born, et al., 2006; Born & Wilhelm, 2011; 
Walker, 2008; Walker & Stickgold, 2004). Sleep-dependent memory effects 
have been reported across a variety of learning materials including vocabulary 
(Gais, et al., 2006), word pairs (Plihal & Born, 1997) and object-location 
associations (Rasch, et al., 2007), and have also been shown across diurnal 
naps (Lau, et al., 2010; Tucker, et al., 2006). 
 
Rather than strengthening all recently acquired memory traces equally, sleep 
has been shown to mediate a targeted consolidation of the most relevant 
components of memory (Fischer & Born, 2009). A recent study showed that 
sleep-dependent memory effects only occurred when the experimenters 
manipulated the perceived importance of previously learned items by informing 
participants of an upcoming test (Wilhelm, et al., 2011). Similarly, a number of 
studies have shown that sleep promotes an emotion-based trade-off in 
declarative memory, such that affective representations are strengthened ahead 
of their more neutral or mundane counterparts (Hu, et al., 2006; Nishida, et al., 
2008; Payne, et al., 2008; Wagner, et al., 2001), although a recent study failed 
to show such an effect (Baran, et al., 2012). Taken together these findings 
suggest that sleep may offer a special protection to memories with the highest 
degree of salience.  
 
Declarative memory representations contain two relatively distinct components. 
The first is the central or focal information, which may relate to an object, 
person or event. The second relates to contextual aspects of memory, such as 
the environment where the experience took place or the emotion associated 
145 
 
with the focal memory component itself. Objects are associated with the context 
in which they were encountered, and this may be either emotional or neutral. 
For example, an everyday item such as a kettle could be encoded within a 
memory of making a cup of coffee, which would form a relatively neutral context. 
However, if you were to spill boiling water out of the kettle and scald your hand, 
the same neutral item would be associated with an emotionally negative context. 
While a great deal of research has addressed the beneficial impact of sleep for 
central declarative information (Gais, et al., 2006), including emotionally focal 
memory components (Hu, et al., 2006), research addressing how contextual 
associations are affected by sleep has been somewhat limited (Cairney, et al., 
2011; van der Helm, et al., 2011). In previous work, we showed that post-
learning sleep, relative to equivalent periods of wakefulness, led to a significant 
protection of associations between neutral target images and the context of an 
associated background image (Lewis, et al., 2011). Although this effect was 
shown across both nocturnal sleep and diurnal napping, our data provided no 
evidence for a preferential consolidation of emotionally negative contexts, 
suggesting that affective representations may not be selectively strengthened 
by sleep in the contextual domain.  
 
Importantly, the participants in the daytime nap group of Lewis and colleagues 
(2011) were monitored with polysomnography (PSG) whilst they slept, but 
because the behavioural data from this group was used to supplement the 
principal findings of the overnight neuroimaging experiment, the PSG data was 
neither analysed nor discussed in the resulting publication.  
 
In the current article, we report a detailed analysis of the PSG data recorded 
from participants who undertook a two hour nap between immediate and 
delayed memory testing for emotional and neutral contexts.  We expand upon 
our previously reported behavioural findings by examining the sleep-specific 
mechanisms underpinning the consolidation of contextual associations, with a 
particular focus on sleep stages and sleep spindle activity. For completeness, 
146 
 
the behavioural data from the nap group of Lewis and colleagues (2011) is also 
reported in the results section.  
 
Results  
Pre-study sleep data 
Participant sleep questionnaires revealed that there was no significant 
difference between the wake and nap groups in terms of the mean hours slept 
during the night preceding the study (wake group hours: 7.89 [S.D. ± 1.06], nap 
group mean hours: 7.45 [S.D. ± 1.05], t(36) = 1.30; p = 0.20) or mean hours 
slept in a typical night (wake group hours: 7.74 [S.D. ± 0.93], nap group mean 
hours: 7.53 [S.D. ± 0.70], t(36) = 0.79; p = 0.44). 
 
Alertness 
Subjective levels of alertness, as measured by the Stanford Sleepiness Scale, 
showed no differences between the wake and nap groups at the immediate test 
(wake group: 2.63 [S.D. ± 0.76], nap group: 2.53 [S.D. ± 0.61], t(36) = 0.47; p = 
0.64) or delayed test (wake group: 2.79 [S.D. ± 1.13], nap group: 2.53 [S.D. ± 
0.77], t(36) = 0.84; p = 0.41). Neither the wake group nor the nap group showed 
significant differences in alertness levels at immediate and delayed testing 
(wake group: t(18) = 0.59; p = 0.56, nap group: t(18) = 0.00; p = 1.00). In an 
additional test of alertness related to homeostatic sleep pressure, no significant 
correlation was found between the amount of slow-wave sleep (SWS) obtained 
by the nap group and all delayed response times (RT’s) for either neutral (r = 
0.15; p = 0.53) or negative (r = 0.12; p = 0.64) contexts. Taken together, these 
measures suggest that the subsequent results were not due to any deficits in 
participant alertness.  
 
 
 
147 
 
Behaviour   
Immediate retrieval 
We first examined the immediate retrieval test to ensure that there were no 
differences between groups in terms of baseline performance. A 2x2 mixed 
ANOVA with between subject factor ‘Group’ (wake/nap) and within subjects 
factor ‘Context Valence’ (negative/neutral) was conducted on both retrieval 
scores and RT’s for correctly recalled contexts. This showed no significant 
difference between groups in terms of contextual memory performance (F(1,36) 
= 0.48; p = 0.50) or RT’s (F(1,36) = 0.16; p = 0.69). However, there were main 
effects of context valence, with superior memory (F(1,36) = 11.69; p = 0.002) 
but slower RT’s (F(1,36) = 22.00; p < 0.0001) for negative relative to neutral 
contexts. No interaction was found between factors for either context memory 
(F(1,36) = 0.78; p = 0.38) or RT’s (F(1,36) = 0.90; p = 0.35). All behavioural 
data relating to memory performance and RT’s can be found in tables 16 and 
17 respectively.  
 
Delayed retrieval 
The same analysis at delayed testing showed a numerical, but non-significant 
main effect of Group for context memory (F(1,36) = 2.80; p = 0.1), with 
participants in the nap group remembering more contexts than those in the 
wake group. No such trend was found for RT’s (F(1,36) = 1.19; p = 0.28). There 
were again main effects of context valence, with better memory (F(1,36) = 8.82; 
p = 0.005) and slower RT’s (F(1,36) = 15.05; p < 0.0001) for negative relative to 
neutral contexts. There was no interaction between factors for context memory 
(F(1,36) = 0.85; p = 0.36) or RT’s (F(1,36) = 1.57; p = 0.22). 
 
Memory consolidation: nap vs. wake 
The impact of retention interval upon the consolidation of context memory was 
quantified using a measure of forgetting and RT speeding for correct responses 
(calculated for each participant as immediate retrieval - delayed retrieval).

A 2x2 mixed ANOVA with between subject factor ‘Group’ (wake/nap) and within 
subjects factor ‘Context Valence’ (negative/neutral) was performed upon scores 
of forgetting and RT change. As shown in figures 16A and 16B respectively, 
participants who napped during the retention interval forgot fewer contexts 
(F(1,36) = 5.51; p = 0.024) and showed a greater improvement (speeding) in 
RT’s (F(1,36) = 4.35; p = 0.044), relative to those who remained awake. There 
was however, no main effect of context valence for either memory (F(1,36) = 
0.09; p = 0.77) or RT’s (F(1,36) = 0.43; p = 0.52), and neither measure showed 
an interaction between factors (context memory: F(1,36) = 0.02; p = 0.90, RT’s: 
F(1,36) = 0.17; p = 0.68).

These results suggest that a two hour nap, relative to an equivalent period of 
wakefulness, had a beneficial impact upon the consolidation of context memory, 
as shown through superior memory and faster RT’s for both negative and 
neutral contexts. However, the absence of an interaction between these factors 
for measures of both forgetting and RT change demonstrates that there was no 
preferential consolidation of emotionally negative contexts across post-learning 
sleep. 
 
PSG data 
Correlation coefficients were calculated between the various sleep parameters 
acquired from our PSG data analyses and both the degree of forgetting and 
speeding of RT’s (correctly recalled items) for negative and neutral contexts 
memories. 
 
Sleep stage analysis 
Sleep data were partitioned in terms of the duration of retention time (mins) 
spent in each sleep stage: stage one sleep (S1), stage two sleep (S2), SWS, 
rapid eye movement sleep (REM) and total sleep time (TST). Sleep stage data 
can be found in table 18.

The duration of S2 was found to negatively correlate with forgetting for 
emotional contexts (r = -0.46; p = 0.049) (see figure 17A), and positively 
correlate with improvements in negative context RT’s (r = 0.55; p = 0.016) (see

protecting memory for negative contexts and in speeding RT’s with respect to 
such memories.

Importantly, these findings were specific to the change in memory performance 
and RT’s for negative contexts. No significant relationship was found between 
S2 and negative context memory or RT’s at immediate retrieval (memory: r = -
0.05; p = 0.85; RT’s: r = -0.07; p = 0.79) or delayed retrieval (memory: r = 0.08; 
p = 0.76; RT’s: r = -0.24; p = 0.32). 
 
Correlations between negative context forgetting and the duration of other sleep 
stages were non-significant (S1: r = -0.14; p = 0.56, SWS: r = 0.22; p = 0.37, 
REM: r = -0.12; p = 0.64, TST: r = -0.29; p = 0.23). Interestingly however, while 
improvements in negative context RT’s were not predicted by the duration of 
either S1 (r = -0.17; p = 0.48), REM (r = -0.07; p = 0.78) or TST r = 0.04; p = 
0.89, they were negatively correlated with time spent in SWS (r = -0.52; p = 
0.023). This result is illustrated in figure 17C. 
 
Sleep spindle analysis  
Intriguingly, sleep spindles occurring during S2 and SWS at the right frontal 
channel (F4-A1) predicted the extent to which neutral contexts were forgotten (r 
= 0.63; p = 0.004, see figure 18A) as well as the extent to which RT’s for 
remembered neutral contexts was slowed (r = -0.65; p = 0.002, see figure 18B), 
suggesting that these electrophysiological phenomena may play an active role 
in suppressing memories of this type. While a significant relationship between 
spindles and forgetting was not found at any other EEG channel (C3-A2: r = 
0.28; p = 0.25, C4-A1: r = 0.40; p = 0.09, O1-A2: r = 0.12; p = 0.70, O2-A1: r = 
0.10; p = 0.74, F3-A2: r = 0.45; p = 0.07), a significant negative correlation was 
also found between RT speeding and spindles recorded from the right central 
(C4-A1) channel (r = -0.52; p = 0.024). Spindles recorded at the other channels 
did not significantly correlate with RT improvements (C3-A2: r = -0.40; p = 0.10, 
O1-A2: r = 0.13; p = 0.66, O2-A1: r = 0.01; p = 0.97, F3-A2: r = -0.45; p = 0.07). 
Sleep spindle data is available in table 19.  
 
153 
 
We also assessed the involvement of slow (12 - 13.5 Hz) and fast (13.5 – 15 Hz) 
frequency sleep spindles separately. Despite subtle differences, these analyses 
showed that fast and slow spindles held an equivalent role in the relationships 
described above (see Supplementary Information: S2).
