190 
 
 
CHAPTER 7 
 
General Discussion 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
191 
 
This final chapter will begin with a summary of the main findings within this 
thesis. The theoretical implications of these results will then be discussed in the 
context of the key research questions outlined in the introductory chapter. 
Finally, on the basis of these discussions, potential avenues for future research 
will be suggested.  
 
Summary of findings 
In recent years, a wealth of research has provided a compelling insight into the 
role of time and sleep in emotional memory processing (Baran, et al., 2012; 
Dolcos, et al., 2005; Hu, et al., 2006; Lewis, et al., 2011; Nishida, et al., 2008; 
Payne & Kensinger, 2011; Payne, et al., 2008; Wagner, et al., 2001; Wagner, et 
al., 2006). However, as described in the introduction, the precise nature of 
these effects is relatively unclear. Accordingly, using behavioural 
experimentation, polysomnography (PSG) and functional magnetic resonance 
imaging (fMRI), the research described within this thesis aimed to expand 
contemporary knowledge regarding the mechanisms and specificity of time- and 
sleep-dependent consolidation processes in emotional and declarative memory.  
 
In chapter 2, event-related fMRI was used to compare the neural correlates of 
emotionally positive, negative and neutral image memories that had undergone 
30 minutes (recent memory) or 1 week (remote memory) of consolidation. By 
incorporating a measure of behavioural consolidation (remote hits – recent hits) 
in our functional imaging analyses, we were also able to explore how the extent 
to which remote memories were consolidated over 1 week related to the brain 
regions exclusively associated with their retrieval. The recollection of remote 
images, irrespective of valence, was associated with stronger responses in the 
superior and middle temporal gyri than the recollection of recent images. While 
the retrieval of positive remote memories elicited stronger responses in the right 
superior frontal gyrus than positive recent memories, negative and neutral 
remote memories produced no greater response in any brain area when 
compared to their recent counterparts. Most interestingly, our behavioural 
192 
 
consolidation measure predicted the strength of the neural response in several 
brain regions that were exclusive to remote retrieval. Specifically, the 
recollection of strongly consolidated remote images was associated with 
increased responses in the right precuneus, angular gyrus and supramarginal 
gyrus. In contrast, the retrieval of more weakly consolidated remote images was 
associated with increased responses across several occipital areas, including 
the calcarine sulcus. 
 
Building upon these findings, the research reported in chapter 3 utilised PSG 
and event-related fMRI to investigate the role of slow-wave sleep (SWS), rapid 
eye movement sleep (REM) and other sleep stages in the neural reorganisation 
of emotionally positive, negative and neutral image memories over 24 hours 
(remote memory), as compared to 30 minutes (recent memory). Behaviourally, 
the consolidation of negative remote memories appeared to be facilitated by 
SWS, whereas REM appeared to exert an inhibitory influence upon the 
formation of positive remote memories. Functionally, SWS predicted a decrease 
in right hippocampal activity associated with negative remote memory and, to a 
lesser extent, overall remote memory. Moreover, psychophysiological 
interaction (PPI) analyses revealed that SWS was associated with a reduction 
in hippocampal-cortical connectivity for overall and positive remote memory. 
While REM was not associated with any change in memory-related brain 
activity, PPI data did reveal a REM-dependent increase in hippocampal-cortical 
connectivity for negative and overall remote memory, indicating that this sleep 
stage may offer a complimentary influence to mnemonic processes occurring 
during the preceding SWS period.  
 
Chapter 4 reported an investigation of how cuing neural replay with learning-
associated sounds during SWS impacts upon the consolidation of emotionally 
negative and neutral picture-location memories. SWS was associated with 
faster response times (RT’s) for negative cued items, as compared to neutral 
cued items, but slower RT’s for neutral cued items, relative to neutral non-cued 
items. This data indicates that cued replay may indirectly ‘prime’ negative and 
193 
 
neutral picture-location memories for a targeted consolidation process, whereby 
the former are enhanced and the latter are suppressed throughout the ensuing 
SWS period.  
 
Chapter 5 described a PSG study which examined the role of post-learning 
sleep in the consolidation of emotionally negative and neutral context memories. 
Memory performance, as indexed by a measure of forgetting and speeding of 
RT’s between immediate and delayed testing, was better following a diurnal nap 
than an equivalent period of wakefulness. Unlike previous work addressing 
focal components of emotional memory (Hu, et al., 2006; Wagner, et al., 2001) 
however, sleep did not mediate a preferential consolidation of affective 
contextual associations. In terms of PSG data, stage two sleep (S2) was 
associated with reduced forgetting and RT speeding for negative context 
memories, whereas sleep spindles predicted increased forgetting and RT 
slowing for neutral context memories. SWS on the other hand, was associated 
with RT slowing for negative context memories. This data suggests that specific 
sleep parameters may mediate a trade-off between emotionally negative and 
neutral context memories, such that the former are actively protected by S2-
dependent processes, and the latter are suppressed by sleep spindles. 
However, a potential inhibitory influence of SWS for negative contexts may 
nullify the former effects, preventing such a trade-off from emerging within the 
behavioural data.  
 
Expanding upon these findings, chapter 6 reported a study which investigated 
how the environmental context-dependent memory effect (Smith, 1979) is 
influenced by overnight sleep or an equivalent period of daytime wakefulness. 
While classical context-dependent memory effects were observed after 
wakefulness, sleep appeared to reduce the negative impact of contextual 
incongruence at retrieval, suggesting that sleep promotes an active 
decontextualisation of newly formed memory representations.  
 
194 
 
 Implications for current views of sleep and memory 
consolidation  
In this section, the implications of the findings in this thesis will be discussed in 
the context of the two key questions that have arisen out of recent research into 
sleep and mnemonic processing. These questions, as outlined in the 
introduction, are: 
 
1) What are the neural mechanisms underpinning time- and sleep-
dependent emotional memory processing? 
 
2) Are focal and contextual elements of emotional and neutral memory 
influenced in different manners by post-learning sleep? 
 
 
Elucidating the mechanisms of sleep and emotional m emory processing 
The studies reported chapters 2, 3 and 4 were aimed at investigating different 
aspects of the mechanisms underpinning time- and sleep-dependent 
consolidation processes. Therefore, while cross-referencing will highlight 
investigative commonalities, the implications of each study will be discussed in 
the same order that they appeared in the thesis. 
 
Systems consolidation of emotional memory  
Through the employment of modern neuroimaging techniques, recent research 
has examined how emotional memories are reorganised at the neural level as 
consolidation processes unfold over hours and days (Payne & Kensinger, 2011; 
Sterpenich, et al., 2007) or even months and years (Dolcos, et al., 2005; 
Sterpenich, et al., 2009). How emotional memories are redistributed over a 
more intermediate consolidation period however, forms an unexplored area of 
research. Moreover, how the degree of memory consolidation occurring during 
this period relates to the brain regions supporting retrieval is unknown. To fill 
195 
 
this void, the study reported in chapter 2 investigated firstly, how emotionally 
positive, negative and neutral image memories are reorganised across 1 week 
(remote memory) relative to 30 minutes (recent memory) and secondly, how the 
extent to which remote memories are consolidated over 1 week influences the 
brain regions exclusively associated with their retrieval. 
 
According to the standard consolidation model (Frankland & Bontempi, 2005; 
Marr, 1971; McClelland, et al., 1995), as declarative representations become 
integrated in long-term memory their retrieval dependency shifts from the 
temporary hippocampal store to the long-term neocortical memory networks. 
Such a redistribution of memory is also thought to be accompanied by a 
process of semanticisation, whereby the resultant cortical representations code 
stable decontextualised memories, forming the basis of semantic knowledge 
(McClelland, et al., 1995). In line with this framework, the results of chapter 2 
suggested that remote memories were more dependent upon the superior and 
middle temporal gyri than recent memories. In addition, emotion-specific 
analyses indicated that positive remote memories were more reliant upon the 
right superior frontal gyrus than positive recent memories. Conversely, negative 
remote memories were not associated with any specific change in brain activity 
after 1 week, a finding which, in light of previous research, is somewhat 
unexpected. Sterpenich and colleagues (2009) for example, reported that the 
retrieval of negative image memories was associated with increased activity in 
the ventromedial prefrontal cortex (vmPFC) and amygdala after consolidation, 
two regions that are regularly associated with emotional memory processing 
(Dolcos, et al., 2004a; Dolcos, et al., 2004b; Pelletier, et al., 2005). Unlike the 
current study however, Sterpenich and colleagues (2009), and other studies 
reporting a similar outcome (Lewis, et al., 2011; Payne & Kensinger, 2011; 
Sterpenich, et al., 2007) were focused on how manipulations of post-learning 
sleep affected emotional memory consolidation. Thus, under the protocol 
adopted in chapter 2, a consolidation period of 1 week, relative to one of 30 
minutes, may have been too short to reveal modifications in the brain regions 
supporting emotionally aversive memory representations. Importantly, this 
suggestion is substantiated by the functional imaging data reported in chapter 3, 
196 
 
which revealed similar patterns of brain activity for the recollection of emotion-
specific remote image memories. 
 
The key observation in chapter 2 however, was that the degree to which image 
memories were consolidated over one week, as indexed by our measure of 
behavioural consolidation, predicted the extent of the neural response in several 
brain regions that were exclusive to remote recollection. Although speculative, 
these findings suggest that the relative strength of a remote image memory has 
major implications for the neural processes supporting its retrieval. Specifically, 
weakly consolidated remote image memories may be highly reliant upon  
sensory-specific memory processes (Hofstetter, et al., 2012; Nyberg, et al., 
2000; Wheeler, et al., 2000), as reflected through greater activation of occipital 
visual processing areas, including the primary visual or ‘calcarine’ cortex. In 
contrast, strongly consolidated remote image memories may be more 
dependent upon brain regions which support the retrieval of general and 
contextually rich episodic memories, such as the precuneus (Addis, et al., 2004; 
Gilboa, et al., 2004). Thus, stabilised and enduring remote image memories 
may be recollected in the relative absence of visual processing resources, 
reflecting a sensory-independent retrieval process. 
 
The influence of SWS and REM upon the neural reorganisation of emotional 
memory representations 
In recent years, functional imaging research has provided compelling evidence 
that post-learning sleep promotes an active redistribution of the brain regions 
supporting emotionally affective memories (Lewis, et al., 2011; Payne & 
Kensinger, 2011; Sterpenich, et al., 2007; Sterpenich, et al., 2009). However, 
since these studies did not include PSG sleep monitoring, they were unable to 
delineate the sleep parameters which offer a more profound contribution to this 
process. The primary goal of the research described in chapter 3 therefore, was 
to identify the role of different sleep stages in the reorganisation, and thus 
consolidation, of emotionally positive, negative and neutral image memories. 
197 
 
Since previous research has suggested that both REM and SWS could mediate 
a reorganisation of emotionally salient memory representations (Nishida, et al., 
2008; Takashima, et al., 2006; Wagner, et al., 2001; Wilhelm, et al., 2011), 
particular attention was paid to these parameters of sleep.  
 
Interestingly, SWS was associated with a redistribution of remote memories 
away from the hippocampus, an effect which was particularly prominent for 
negative images. In addition, the extent to which negative remote memories 
were consolidated over 24 hours, as indexed by the behavioural consolidation 
measure, was predicted by SWS. The results of chapter 3 therefore, provide the 
first evidence that SWS supports an active and targeted consolidation of 
emotionally aversive memory representations 
 
Recent accounts of the active systems consolidation framework (Born & 
Wilhelm, 2011) have highlighted the significance of mnemonic selectivity, 
whereby the most important, and thus salient, components of memory are 
preferentially consolidated over post-learning sleep. The salience of a memory 
can be increased by a number of factors other than emotional arousal, such as 
the perceived value or relevance of newly acquired information (Fischer & Born, 
2009; Saletin, et al., 2011). Importantly, recent work has indicated that slow 
oscillation activity, which characterises SWS, supports the consolidation of 
newly formed memories when their perceived relevance is manipulated prior to 
sleep (Wilhelm, et al., 2011). Taken together, the results of chapter 3 may also 
suggest that it is the salience of a novel memory representation, rather than the 
intrinsic emotional properties per se, which increase its affinity for SWS-
dependent consolidation processes.  
 
It is important to note however, that such an approach follows a rather 
contentious assumption that emotional memories are not processed in a unique 
manner. According to the memory modulation hypothesis (LaBar & Cabeza, 
2006; McGaugh, 2004; McGaugh, et al., 1996), the amygdala modulates the 
198 
 
medial temporal lobe in response to emotional arousal, augmenting the 
formation and persistence of memories over time. This hypothesis is supported 
by decades of research (Canli, et al., 2000; Dolcos, et al., 2004b; Hatfield & 
McGaugh, 1999; Kilpatrick & Cahill, 2003; Liang, et al., 1990; McGaugh, 2002; 
Pelletier, et al., 2005; Roozendaal & McGaugh, 1996) and implies that offline 
memory processes should operate on emotional and neutral representations in 
distinct manners, irrespective of salience. While this presents some difficulty for 
salience-specific memory consolidation, it is possible that manipulating the 
perceived relevance of novel information may also have a knock-on effect for 
subject levels of arousal at encoding, or during the subsequent consolidation 
period. While speculative, such an approach may suggest that the unique 
biological properties of SWS support a targeted reorganisation of highly salient 
memories, regardless of their emotional valence.  
 
Importantly, the PPI data of chapter 3 revealed a REM-related increase in 
hippocampal-cortical connectivity associated with overall and negative remote 
image retrieval. Due to its link with vivid dreaming and cognitive processing, 
REM was regularly implicated within declarative memory processing in earlier 
research (Empson & Clarke, 1970; Greenberg, et al., 1983; Tilley & Empson, 
1978), and formed part of preliminary sequential hypotheses of sleep and 
memory consolidation (Ambrosini & Giuditta, 2001; Giuditta, et al., 1995). 
Building on this work, the ‘overnight alchemy’ hypothesis set out by Walker and 
Stickgold (2010) proposes that SWS facilitates the consolidation of new 
memories, which are then assimilated into rich and generalised associative 
networks during the ensuing REM period. In line with this concept, the results of 
chapter 3 are suggestive of an inherent neural mechanism, whereby SWS and 
REM support a respective strengthening and abstraction of emotionally salient 
memories.   
 
An alternative account of these findings however, relates to a potential role for 
REM in synaptic consolidation processes. As outlined by Diekelmann and Born 
(2010), while the active systems model accounts for a redistribution of newly 
199 
 
formed memories, it does not explain how the synaptic connections 
underpinning these representations are strengthened or stabilised during post-
learning sleep. Unlike SWS, REM is associated with an upregulation of 
plasticity-related immediate early gene activity, which is dependent upon prior 
waking experience and localised to brain regions involved in learning (Ribeiro, 
et al., 2002; Ulloor & Datta, 2005). As such, REM is proposed to mediate a 
process of synaptic consolidation, which strengthens the memory 
representations that were reorganised during the preceding SWS period 
(Diekelmann & Born, 2010). Expanding upon this view, the connectivity data of 
chapter 3 may reflect a complimentary consolidation process, whereby the 
synaptic connections of emotionally salient memories, preferentially 
redistributed during SWS, were selectively strengthened during REM.  
 
On a tentative note, if either of the mechanisms described above were 
accountable for the results outlined in chapter 3, emotionally negative images 
should have been better remembered than their positive or neutral counterparts, 
but this was not the case. In fact, the behavioural data of chapter 2 showed that 
across 1 week of consolidation, which included multiple nights of sleep, memory 
performance was actually better for neutral than positive or negative remote 
images. Given that several studies have suggested a selective strengthening of 
emotionally affective memories over sleep (Hu, et al., 2006; Payne, et al., 2008; 
Wagner, et al., 2001), this result may be considered as unexpected, although a 
recent study by Baran and colleagues (2012) also failed to reveal such an effect.  
 
A final discussion point relates to the remember/know/new (R/K/N) procedure, 
which was adopted in the first two experimental chapters. Importantly, the R/K 
paradigm is thought to distinguish between two different forms of recognition, 
known as recollection (R) and familiarity (K) (Tulving, 1985), and has been 
adopted in a number of psychological investigations (Diana, et al., 2007; Hu, et 
al., 2006; Yonelinas, et al., 2005). However, while recollection performance was 
significantly greater than chance in both chapters 2 and 3, familiarity 
performance was not, suggesting that participants misinterpreted the R/K 
200 
 
distinction in terms of recognition strength, rather than ability to recall contextual 
details of encoding that were not present at testing. This issue raises important 
questions regarding the interpretation of both the behavioural and functional 
imaging data presented in chapters 2 and 3, as the R/K procedure used in 
these experiments is likely to have contained a very impure measure of 
recollection. Further research is therefore required to assess whether the 
results of these studies, particularly with regard to the emotional memory effects 
of chapter 3, are indeed specific to recollection in its true form.  
 
Despite the aforementioned concerns, even if participants had performed the 
R/K/N task correctly, and the behavioural data represent a genuine process of 
recollection on the majority of trials, another important issue relates to the 
neural correlates of recollection after varying post-encoding delays. Recollection 
is commonly associated with increases in hippocampal activity (Wixted & Squire, 
2010; Yonelinas, et al., 2005), the extent of which should depend on the amount 
of contextual detail retrieved (Davachi, et al., 2003; Davachi & Wagner, 2002). 
As such, the recollection of recent memories would presumably include a 
greater degree of contextual detail than the recollection of remote memories, 
resulting in a stronger hippocampal response. Therefore, it is possible that the 
inverse relationship between SWS and recollection-related activity in the 
hippocampus reported in chapter 3 may actually reflect a SWS-dependent 
decrease in contextual detail, rather than an active reorganisation of memory at 
the neural level. While this alternative interpretation concurs with the results of 
chapter 6, which suggest that declarative memories are decontextualised over 
sleep, it does not explain why these effects were enhanced for emotionally 
negative memories. 
 
The effect of SWS-dependent cued replay on emotionally negative and neutral 
memories 
The reorganisation of newly formed memories is thought to be underpinned by 
experience-dependent patterns of neural replay during SWS (Born, et al., 2006; 
201 
 
Born & Wilhelm, 2011; Rasch & Born, 2007). Recent work has indicated that 
neural replay can be manipulated by re-presenting olfactory or auditory cues 
during SWS, leading to an augmented consolidation process (Diekelmann, et al., 
2011; Rasch, et al., 2007; Rudoy, et al., 2009). However, whether cued replay 
exerts a direct boost to the memory trace in question or indirectly primes 
memories for a targeted consolidation process throughout the ensuing SWS 
period is unclear. Moreover, previous work on this topic has considered only 
visuo-spatial memories with a neutral tone, leaving open the question of how 
emotionally affective representations are influenced by cued replay. While the 
findings of the study reported in chapter 4 were in line with an indirect influence 
of cued replay, the precise nature of these effects was dependent upon the 
emotional valence of the memory in question. Specifically, SWS was associated 
with a concomitant enhancement and suppression of respective negative and 
neutral picture location memories that were cued with learning-associated 
sounds. These findings suggest that SWS may support a multilayered process 
of consolidation, whereby emotional and neutral representations are influenced 
in qualitatively distinct manners, ensuring that the most important components 
of newly acquired information are stabilised in memory for the future.  
 
In line with the findings of chapter 3, such a mnemonic trade-off may 
substantiate the notion that salience, rather than emotion per se, is the factor 
which enhances sleep-dependent consolidation processes. Several researchers 
have suggested that increasing the salience of a newly formed memory trace 
may induce a form of neural ‘tagging’ (Fischer & Born, 2009; Marshall & Born, 
2007) enabling such representations to undergo a targeted consolidation 
process during the subsequent sleep period. In accordance with this concept, it 
is possible that cuing mnemonic replay with sounds during SWS may, through a 
form of neural priming, increase the salience of a memory implicitly, resulting in 
a similarly selective form of consolidation.  
 
Nevertheless, if auditory cued replay does bring about a targeted consolidation 
of picture location memories during SWS, why should negative and neutral 
202 
 
items be affected in such diverse manners? Like previous studies of sleep and 
emotional memory consolidation (Hu, et al., 2006; Wagner, et al., 2001), the 
study reported in chapter 4 adopted a paradigm in which negative and neutral 
stimuli were encoded concomitantly. Under normal conditions, sleep would 
operate in a typically biased fashion, strengthening highly salient emotional 
memories whilst evading their non-salient neutral counterparts (Payne, et al., 
2008). However, cuing replay during SWS may affect neutral memories in an 
atypical manner, such that they become primed for an augmented consolidation 
process within the same cognitive space as highly salient emotional memory 
representations. In order to maintain mnemonic selectivity under these 
circumstances, a refined SWS-dependent mechanism may mediate an active 
enhancement and suppression of emotional and neutral memories respectively. 
This concept is corroborated by findings from other research, including that 
reported in another chapter of this thesis. An analysis reported in chapter 5 
indicated that sleep spindles, which occur during S2 and SWS, supported the 
consolidation of emotional memories indirectly, by suppressing neutral 
information encoded at the same time. Moreover, a recent study by Saletin and 
colleagues (2011) suggested that spindles may mediate a suppression of 
irrelevant or unwanted memories, providing further evidence that sleep-
dependent processes impact upon the consolidation of newly formed memories 
in qualitatively diverse manners.  
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
203 
 
The impact of sleep on contextual memory processing  
Chapters 5 and 6 were focused on how sleep influences the processing of 
contextual associations pertaining to emotional valence and the external 
environment. As before, although cross referencing will occur, the implications 
of each study will be discussed in the same order that they appeared in this 
thesis.  
 
Sleep and the consolidation of emotional context memory 
Within any declarative representation, there exists a focal and contextual 
memory component. Focal aspects of memory relate to the information that is 
central to an experience, such as a person or an object. Contextual memory 
components however, relate to a number of factors, including the specific 
emotion associated with the focal information itself. For example, while an 
experience such as riding a bike may be initially associated with a rather 
pleasant context, if a car were to get too close and knock the rider off the same 
experience would be suddenly associated with a negative context instead. 
Sleep-dependent processes influence focal aspects of memory in a highly 
discriminative fashion, such that emotionally affective information is 
strengthened ahead of more neutral or mundane information. This effect has 
been demonstrated with emotional texts (Wagner, et al., 2001; Wagner, et al., 
2006) and images (Hu, et al., 2006; Nishida, et al., 2008), although a recent 
study suggested that this is not always true for the latter (Baran, et al., 2012). 
Studies examining how sleep impacts upon memory components pertaining to 
the emotional context of a learning experience however, are rather limited 
(Lewis, et al., 2011). Moreover, whether the parameters of sleep which play a 
role in contextual memory processing are similar to those already implicated in 
the consolidation of focal information presents a novel research endeavour. 
Accordingly, the results of the study described in chapter 5 suggest that, unlike 
focal aspects of memory, contextual associations with an aversive tone do not 
appear to be preferentially strengthened over post-learning sleep. Interestingly, 
sleep data analyses indicated that this effect may relate to a paradoxical sleep-
dependent process, which prevents emotion-based trade-offs from manifesting 
204 
 
within the contextual domain. Specifically, these results suggest that S2 and 
sleep spindles support a selective strengthening of emotional context memories, 
but in fundamentally distinct manners. While S2 may boost the consolidation of 
highly salient, emotional contexts directly, sleep spindles appear to assist this 
process indirectly, by suppressing contextual information with a neutral tone. 
However, a concomitant inhibitory influence of SWS upon negative context 
memories may nullify the mnemonic influences of S2 and spindle activity, 
preventing a targeted consolidation of emotionally affective contextual 
associations. While speculative, this proposal allows for mnemonic selectivity in 
contextual memory processing and explains why the retrieval of negative, as 
compared to neutral contexts, was not better after sleep.  
 
In line with the findings described in chapter 4, the results of this study indicate 
that sleep-dependent processes mediate a trade-off between emotional and 
neutral representations, thus preserving the most important components of 
memory for the future. Building on this point, a collective consideration of the 
data reported in chapters 4 and 5 suggests that such a targeted consolidation 
process may be supported by different stages of sleep, depending on whether 
the newly acquired information is contextual or focal in nature. Specifically, the 
results of chapter 4 indicate that, under certain conditions2, SWS-dependent 
processes may support an active enhancement and suppression of respective 
emotional and neutral information that is central to the memory trace in question. 
Contrastingly, the data in chapter 5 suggest that S2 may mediate an 
enhancement of contextual memory elements with an affective tone, whilst a 
complimentary spindle-dependent process suppresses contextually neutral 
information. However, unlike central elements of memory, contextual 
representations appear to be prone to a conflicting SWS-dependent mechanism, 
which prevents a mnemonic trade-off from appearing within behavioural 
performance.  
 
                                                          2 i.e. when cued replay is used to prime negative and neutral memories for a targeted consolidation process during SWS. 
205 
 
While S2 and sleep spindles have been respectively implicated in the 
consolidation and suppression of newly formed memories (Andrade, et al., 2011; 
Saletin, et al., 2011; van der Helm, et al., 2011), it is unclear why SWS should 
exert such profoundly diverse effects upon focal and contextual elements of 
emotional memory. However, these effects may be taken to indicate that SWS-
dependent memory processes are more selective than currently envisaged. 
Although emotional context memories carry a high degree of salience, their 
focal counterparts may be deemed as intrinsically more important. Thus, to 
ensure that only the most significant information is preserved within a limited 
cognitive framework, SWS may actively strengthen central and highly salient 
memory information, whilst weakening emotionally affective contextual 
representations. Such a process is analogous to what is known as the weapon 
focus effect, whereby an individual remembers an assailant’s weapon at the 
expense of other equally salient peripheral information (Stanny & Johnson, 
2000). In support of this view, the results of chapter 6 suggest that memories 
become decontextualised as SWS-dependent processes mediate a shift in 
retrieval dependency away from the hippocampal store.  
 
Environmental context effects in memory: the influence of sleep 
Typically, declarative memory performance is better when the retrieval context 
is environmentally congruent to that of the learning phase, an effect 
demonstrated across visual, auditory and olfactory modalities (Godden & 
Baddeley, 1975; Parker, et al., 2007; Parker, et al., 2001; Schab, 1990; Smith, 
1979, 1985). While sleep-dependent memory effects have been regularly 
demonstrated in focal aspects of declarative memory (Gais, et al., 2006; Plihal 
& Born, 1997, 1999a), our knowledge of how contextual associations pertaining 
to the external environment are affected by post-learning sleep is relatively 
limited (van der Helm, et al., 2011). The data reported in chapter 6 suggest that 
sleep may promote a decay of contextual information in declarative memory, 
leading to a reduction in the extent to which environmental cues impact upon 
retrieval. In other words, these results indicate that newly formed memories may 
206 
 
be actively decontextualised during a sleep-dependent integration within long-
term memory.  
 
The results presented in chapter 6 can be interpreted in relation to a number of 
models, each of which offer a mechanism by which contextual information may 
be extracted from declarative memory. The first of these, which is most 
appropriate within the context of this thesis, relates to the active systems 
consolidation model (Born, 2010; Born & Wilhelm, 2011; Diekelmann & Born, 
2010). The fundamental premise of this model is that SWS-dependent 
processes mediate a redistribution of declarative retrieval dependency away 
from the temporary hippocampal store towards the long-term neocortical 
memory networks. Importantly, previous research has demonstrated that 
contextual information in both spatial and temporal modalities is highly reliant 
upon the hippocampus (Davachi, et al., 2003; Davachi & Wagner, 2002). 
Therefore, if contextual elements of declarative memory remain exclusively 
hippocampal, it is possible that this information may be lost as an active 
reorganisation of memory ensues during SWS. This notion is supported by the 
fMRI data reported in chapter 3, which is suggestive of a SWS-related reduction 
in hippocampal retrieval dependency for remote image memory.  
 
In order to establish a potential mechanism of mnemonic decontextualisation 
over sleep, we may also turn to a relatively new model of memory consolidation 
known as the transformation hypothesis (Winocur & Moscovitch, 2011; Winocur, 
et al., 2010). Building on the multiple trace theory (Moscovitch & Nadel, 1998; 
Nadel & Moscovitch, 1997), this model suggests that memories undergo a 
qualitative transformation as they are consolidated within the long-term store. 
Specifically, newly formed memories are assumed to be context-dependent and 
reliant upon the hippocampus for as long as it is available. Over time, this 
hippocampal memory is thought to be transformed into a more schematic 
version in the neocortex, which retains the gist of the original representation but 
very few of its contextual details. In support of this view, Winocur and 
colleagues (2007) reported that healthy rats displayed context-dependent 
207 
 
memory impairments over short but not long retention delays. Rats with 
hippocampal lesions however, showed no such contextual impairment, 
irrespective of delay. In terms of the current study, it is possible that post-
learning sleep may have accentuated the transformation process, leading to a 
reduction in the extent to which contextual cues impacted upon retrieval 
performance.   
 
The data reported in chapter 6 may also be considered in line with the synaptic 
homeostasis hypothesis (Tononi & Cirelli, 2003, 2006). According to this model, 
the role of sleep slow-wave activity is to proportionally downscale synaptic 
strength to baseline levels. This is proposed to eradicate weak and inefficient 
synapses pertaining to irrelevant information, leaving behind a more efficient 
memory trace. Under this framework, contextual memory information pertaining 
to the surrounding environment would form a relatively weak synaptic 
representation, unable to survive the downscaling of sleep. As such, contextual 
associations would be lost overnight, eliminating the effectiveness of 
environmental cues at subsequent retrieval.  
 
The concept of contextual memory 
Although chapters 5 and 6 were both focused on how contextual components of 
memory are influenced by post-learning sleep or wakefulness, it is important to 
consider a note of caution when discussing the results of these studies 
collectively. Contextual memory forms a very broad concept, relating to 
numerous aspects of a representation that are associated with the central 
memory information in an explicit or implicit manner. Since chapter 5 
investigated how a diurnal nap impacted upon the explicit retrieval of 
associative emotional contexts, whereas chapter 6 examined how implicit, 
environmental context reinstatement effects were influenced by nocturnal sleep, 
the results of these studies relate to entirely different components of declarative 
memory. Such distinction between explicit and implicit forms of contextual 
memory may also explain why sleep appeared to benefit the consolidation of 
emotional contexts in chapter 5, but weaken environmental cue dependency in 
208 
 
chapter 6. In line with this view, a recent study by van der Helm and colleagues 
(2011) examined how a post-learning nap impacted upon the consolidation of 
contextual associations for the environment. However, unlike the study reported 
chapter 6, participants were required to explicitly recall the visual learning 
context, which in this case was a detailed wall poster.  In keeping with the 
results of chapter 5, learning contexts were better remembered after a nap 
relative to an equivalent period of wakefulness.  
 
Directions for further research 
The research in this thesis has provided some key insights regarding both the 
mechanisms and specificity of sleep-dependent consolidation processes in 
emotional and declarative memory. On the basis of the presented findings, this 
final section will form a brief overview of prospective research endeavours, 
which may build upon the work reported in this thesis. 
 
One idea emerging from the research presented in this thesis, particularly 
chapters 3, 4 and 5, is that a targeted consolidation of affective memories over 
sleep may not specifically pertain to the emotionality of these representations 
per se, but rather their high degree of salience. Accordingly, while a number of  
studies have demonstrated that emotionally aversive memories are 
preferentially consolidated over sleep (Hu, et al., 2006; Nishida, et al., 2008; 
Wagner, et al., 2001), other work has  shown that sleep supports a selective 
strengthening of neutral memories with a higher degree of salience (Fischer & 
Born, 2009; Saletin, et al., 2011), an effect which appears to be dependent 
upon slow oscillation activity (Wilhelm, et al., 2011). To test this possibility, 
future studies could use behavioural paradigms to directly compare the effects 
of post-learning sleep upon the consolidation of emotionally aversive memories 
and neutral memories that also carry a high degree of salience. If this 
hypothesis is correct, then no behavioural difference should occur between 
emotional and neutral memories over sleep. In accordance with the selectivity 
principle of active systems model (Born & Wilhelm, 2011), one would also 
209 
 
expect that the degree of salience attributed to an emotional or neutral memory 
would predict its relative stability after SWS-dependent consolidation processes 
had ensued. Further research could also utilise PSG to compare to parameters 
of sleep which support the consolidation of emotional and highly salient neutral 
information that is focal or contextual in nature. In line with previous research, 
and that described in chapter 3, it may be expected that SWS would exert an 
equivalent strengthening upon focal memory information that is emotional 
affective or neutrally salient. Highly salient contextual information however, may 
be influenced in a different manner by SWS, as indicated by the results 
described in chapter 5. Furthermore, fMRI techniques could be utilised to 
compare the neural correlates of highly salient neutral and emotional memories 
following overnight consolidation. Building on the findings of chapter 3, one may 
expect that SWS would modulate a redistribution of salient memory 
representations, irrespective of emotional valence, away from the temporary 
hippocampal store. In relation to the data presented in chapter 4, future work 
could also examine how SWS-dependent auditory cued replay impacts upon 
the consolidation of emotional and neutral picture-location memories that have 
an equivalent level of salience. Under the aforementioned hypothesis, neutral 
representations would not be actively suppressed following cued replay, but 
would undergo a targeted enhancement in the same manner as their emotional 
counterparts. Due to inherent cognitive limitations however, the extent of 
mnemonic enhancement would depend primarily upon the degree of salience 
attributed to the neutral or emotional memory in question. As such, salient 
memories may still be suppressed during SWS if they are deemed to be 
intrinsically less important than other representations that exist within the same 
congested memory system.

Moral Foundations Theory: An S-Tier Behavioral Designer's Guide
Yu-kai Chou Creator of the Octalysis Framework · cited in 3,700+ academic papers
April 30, 2026 Published
October 8, 2026 Updated
31 min Read time
Moral Foundations Theory proposes six universal moral dimensions — Care, Fairness, Loyalty, Authority, Sanctity, and Liberty — that political tribes and cultures weight differently. The map that determines whether your CD1 narrative reads as righteous or repulsive.
Core Drives covered 1Epic Meaning & Calling 5Social Influence & Relatedness
Short answer: Moral Foundations Theory says moral judgment runs on six innate but culturally tuned dimensions: Care, Fairness, Loyalty, Authority, Sanctity, and Liberty.
Jonathan Haidt and Craig Joseph proposed the framework in 2004, and Haidt's 2012 book The Righteous Mind made it famous.
Graham, Haidt, and Nosek found in 2009 that U.S. liberals weight Care and Fairness far above the rest while U.S. conservatives weight all five original foundations roughly equally, an asymmetry that replicates in U.S. samples and weakens outside them.
Two people read the same campaign and have opposite reactions. One calls it inspiring; the other calls it manipulative. Both are reading the same words, looking at the same images, hearing the same pitch. They are not reading from different facts. They are reading from different moral foundations. Moral Foundations Theory is the only working map I have found of why the same CD1 (Epic Meaning & Calling) narrative can hit one audience as righteous and another as repulsive.
Jonathan Haidt and Craig Joseph proposed the framework in 2004; Haidt and Jesse Graham extended it in 2007 in Social Justice Research. Haidt's 2012 book The Righteous Mind made the framework public-facing. The empirical claim, summarized: humans evaluate moral situations through six innate but culturally-tuned dimensions — Care, Fairness, Loyalty, Authority, Sanctity, and Liberty. Different people, different cultures, and different political tribes weight these foundations differently. The same act can be morally righteous on one set of weights and morally repulsive on another.
This guide is what I wish more brand strategists, charity-campaign designers, and game writers had read before they wrote a single mission statement. The real Haidt-Graham-Joseph framework, the legitimate methodological pushback (factor-structure debates, WEIRD-bias critiques, the “theory vs taxonomy” question), and the design moves that actually use the map without manipulating audiences across foundations they did not consent to.
⚡ Speed Run Notes
The thesis: humans evaluate moral situations through innate but culturally-tuned dimensions. The current six foundations: Care/Harm, Fairness/Cheating, Loyalty/Betrayal, Authority/Subversion, Sanctity/Degradation, Liberty/Oppression. Different audiences weight them differently.
The political-tribe finding: liberals weight Care and Fairness heavily and the others lightly; conservatives weight all six relatively equally. This asymmetry, replicated across many samples, is one of MFT's most-cited results.
Where it falls apart: the factor structure has not held up cleanly cross-culturally. Iurino & Saucier (2020) found that the canonical 5-factor model fails to fit data in many non-WEIRD samples. The “theory” status is contested — critics argue MFT is a taxonomy, not a causal theory.
Why it matters for design: Octalysis Core Drive 1 (Epic Meaning & Calling) narratives implicitly invoke specific moral foundations. A campaign tuned to a Care/Fairness audience will alienate a Loyalty/Authority audience and vice versa — the lever every cross-tribe communicator is implicitly pulling.
The most under-used implication: moral reframing — re-presenting an argument in the foundations the audience cares about — measurably changes persuasion outcomes (Feinberg & Willer 2013). The technique works in either direction politically and is one of the cleanest applications of MFT to applied behavioral design.

Why this guide on Moral Foundations Theory specifically. Octalysis Core Drive 1 (Epic Meaning & Calling) is where the deepest engagement lives, and CD1 narratives almost always invoke moral weight — what is right, what is good, what is worth dedicating effort to. The same CD1 narrative lands the opposite way across moral-foundation profiles, and most teams writing mission statements, founder narratives, or movement-style campaigns are blind to the variance. The most expensive mistakes I have seen in advisory work are CD1 narratives that work brilliantly inside the team's moral-foundation profile and fail catastrophically with audiences whose profile differs. MFT is the diagnostic tool that makes this variance visible. This guide is the operating manual that came out of those engagements.
What is Moral Foundations Theory
Moral Foundations Theory (MFT) is a social-psychology framework proposing that human moral evaluation operates through a set of innate but culturally-tuned dimensions. Jonathan Haidt and Craig Joseph published the foundational paper in 2004; Haidt and Jesse Graham extended it in 2007 in Social Justice Research; Haidt's 2012 book The Righteous Mind: Why Good People Are Divided by Politics and Religion made the framework widely known.
The current six-foundation version proposes that moral evaluation runs along these dimensions:
Care / Harm. Concern for the suffering of others, with virtues like kindness and protection. The foundation triggers when actions cause or prevent suffering, particularly to vulnerable beings.
Fairness / Cheating. Concern for justice, reciprocity, and proportionality. The foundation triggers when reciprocity norms are violated or upheld, when outcomes seem unfairly distributed, or when free-riders are detected.
Loyalty / Betrayal. Concern for solidarity with one's group, family, or nation. The foundation triggers when group members defect, betray, or, conversely, demonstrate sacrifice for the collective.
Authority / Subversion. Respect for legitimate authority and tradition. The foundation triggers when hierarchies are upheld or undermined, particularly when subversion threatens valued institutions.
Sanctity / Degradation. Concern for purity and the sacred, both physical and symbolic. The foundation triggers around contamination, defilement, and conversely around acts that elevate the spirit. Religious traditions activate this foundation heavily, but secular versions exist (the body as sacred, nature as sacred).
Liberty / Oppression. Resistance to domination and concern for autonomy. Added to the original five in Haidt's 2012 work, partly in response to libertarian critiques that the original five did not capture libertarian moral intuition. 
The six moral foundations, each pairing a virtue with the violation that triggers it. Adapted from Haidt, Graham & Joseph.
Three theoretical commitments distinguish MFT from earlier moral-psychology frameworks:
Innateness with cultural tuning. The foundations are claimed to be evolved, present in some form across cultures, but with the specific weights and triggers shaped by upbringing, ideology, and cultural context. This is a “first draft” claim — humans are born with the moral architecture; experience writes the specific moral content onto it.
Intuitionism. Moral judgment is fast, automatic, and emotion-driven. Reasoning typically follows the intuition, justifying it post-hoc rather than producing it. This commitment connects MFT to Haidt's earlier “social intuitionist model” (2001) and to the broader dual-process literature in psychology.
Pluralism. No single foundation is “the right one.” Different moral profiles weight the foundations differently, and these differences are descriptive facts about populations, not normative errors to be corrected. This pluralism is one of the most politically uncomfortable aspects of the theory and one of the reasons it has generated so much critique.
For behavioral design, the load-bearing claim is that any narrative carrying moral weight — mission statements, brand purposes, charity appeals, political messaging, game-story arcs — implicitly invokes specific foundations. The narrative's effectiveness depends on whether the audience's foundation weights match what the narrative is doing. Audiences whose weights differ from the narrative's targeting will either disengage or, worse, react with revulsion — and the revulsion will look unprovoked from inside the team's frame.
The Core Findings
The MFT literature is large and politically contested. A few results carry the most weight in current reviews.
The political-tribe asymmetry
Graham, Haidt, and Nosek (2009), in Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, ran the foundational empirical demonstration. Across multiple U.S. samples (over 11,000 participants total), liberals weighted Care and Fairness much more heavily than the other foundations, while conservatives weighted all five (the original count) relatively equally. The asymmetry — liberals “two-foundation,” conservatives “five-foundation” — became one of MFT's most-cited findings and the empirical basis for Haidt's argument that liberals systematically underestimate the moral seriousness of Loyalty, Authority, and Sanctity concerns.
The most-cited MFT result: liberal endorsement drops sharply after Care and Fairness; conservative endorsement stays level. Schematic of the pattern in Graham, Haidt & Nosek (2009).
Subsequent work has largely replicated the asymmetric pattern in U.S. samples while complicating the interpretation. Kim, Kang, and Kim (2012) found different patterns in South Korean samples; Davis et al. (2016) showed within-population variation that the simple liberal-conservative dichotomy obscured. The asymmetry is robust in U.S. politics; its generalizability to other political systems is more contested.
Moral reframing
Feinberg and Willer (2013, 2015) ran a series of studies showing that political arguments framed in the moral foundations the target audience cares about are substantially more persuasive than the same arguments framed in foundations the audience does not weight heavily. Conservatives shifted on environmental policy when arguments invoked Sanctity (preserving the natural world's purity) rather than the standard Care framing. Liberals shifted on military spending when arguments invoked Fairness (equal protection for all citizens) rather than the standard Authority/Loyalty framing.
The moral-reframing finding is one of MFT's cleanest applied applications. The technique works in both political directions, requires no compromise on the substantive position, and produces measurable persuasion gains. It is also the single most-replicated MFT result in the applied-behavior-change literature.
Cross-cultural validity
Haidt, Koller, and Dias (1993, predating MFT but feeding into it) showed that participants in Brazilian and Philadelphian samples differed substantially in how they morally evaluated harm-free taboo-violation scenarios (eating one's pet dog after it died of natural causes; cleaning a toilet with a national flag). Brazilian participants invoked sanctity-and-disgust framings; Philadelphian participants tended toward harm-and-fairness framings. The cross-cultural data suggested that the harm-and-fairness “modern” moral profile is one of several possible profiles, not the universal default.
Disgust sensitivity and moral judgment
A substantial sub-literature documents the connection between physical disgust sensitivity and the Sanctity foundation. Inbar, Pizarro, and Bloom (2009) found that conservatives report higher disgust sensitivity than liberals; subsequent work showed that experimentally-induced disgust shifts moral judgments on related issues toward more conservative positions. The connection is one of MFT's most viscerally interesting findings and one of the more replicable links between physiological state and moral evaluation.
The Moral Foundations Questionnaire
Graham, Haidt, and colleagues developed the Moral Foundations Questionnaire (MFQ), a self-report instrument used in hundreds of subsequent studies. The MFQ has been translated into dozens of languages and remains the field's standard measurement tool. It is also the focal point of much methodological critique — the factor structure of the MFQ has not held up cleanly across cultures, and several alternative measurement instruments have been proposed.
What Haidt, Graham, and Joseph Got Right
Three contributions hold up across the methodological pushback that has accumulated.
They named pluralism in moral psychology
Pre-MFT, moral psychology was dominated by Kohlberg's stage theory and by Care-and-Fairness frameworks (Gilligan's ethics of care, Rawlsian justice frameworks). The “moral mind” was implicitly assumed to be the U.S. liberal moral profile, and other moral profiles were treated as developmental immaturity or cultural backwardness. MFT made an explicit case that this default was a parochial empirical assumption, not a philosophical truth, and that other moral profiles deserved serious empirical study.
Whatever the methodological problems with the specific MFT instruments, the field-level move — taking pluralism seriously, investigating moral profiles outside the WEIRD-liberal default — has been a genuine contribution. The literature on moral psychology since 2007 is substantively richer because of MFT, even where specific MFT claims have been contested.
They produced moral reframing as a working applied technique
The Feinberg-Willer reframing paradigm is one of the cleanest applied behavioral-science findings of the 2010s. It works, replicates across studies, and provides a concrete prescription for cross-tribe communication that does not require either side to abandon their substantive positions. Charities, advocacy organizations, brand strategists, and political communicators have adopted the framework explicitly. The cumulative practical impact of moral reframing alone justifies the framework's prominence.
They wrote a public-facing book that translated the science honestly
The Righteous Mind (2012) is one of the rare social-science books that translates a research program for general readers without flattening its uncertainties or overselling its conclusions. Haidt was explicit about the framework's contested status, the methodological limitations, and the political reading the work invited. The book's commercial success — bestseller, widely assigned in classes — extended MFT's influence beyond academia, and the framework has become part of the lingua franca of cross-tribe communication. Whatever one thinks of MFT as science, the public-facing translation set a standard most academic frameworks fail to meet.
Where Moral Foundations Theory Falls Apart
The framework has been heavily critiqued from multiple directions. Three serious challenges deserve attention.
1. The factor structure has not held up cleanly cross-culturally
Iurino and Saucier (2020), in a 27-country dataset ( n ≈ 8,000), tested the canonical 5-factor MFQ structure and found it failed to replicate in most samples. The factor solutions varied widely across countries, and several samples produced 3- or 4-factor solutions that did not match the MFT taxonomy. Davis, Hook, et al. (2016) reported similar issues in U.S. samples when subgroups were analyzed separately — the 5-factor structure aggregates over substantial within-population heterogeneity.
Defenders of MFT have pointed to potential measurement problems with the MFQ specifically rather than the underlying foundations. Newer instruments (Moral Foundations Vignettes; Moral Foundations Sacredness Scale) produce somewhat better factor structures in some samples. But the basic empirical claim — that the same five (or six) foundations show up cleanly across cultures — is not as well supported as the framework's public-facing presentation implies.
For applied work, the implication is that you cannot assume the foundations have the same psychological reality across audiences. The framework remains useful as a heuristic for thinking about moral pluralism, but specific predictions about how a given audience will respond to a given foundation's framing should be tested locally, not extrapolated from U.S. data.
2. The “theory” status is contested
A persistent methodological critique, articulated forcefully by Suhler and Churchland (2011) in Journal of Cognitive Neuroscience: MFT is described as a theory but functions empirically as a taxonomy. A theory makes specific causal predictions; a taxonomy classifies. MFT, the critics argue, generates few specific causal predictions that distinguish it from competitors and has been refined repeatedly to accommodate inconvenient findings rather than being decisively tested against them.
The most damning version of this critique: when the original five foundations did not adequately capture libertarian moral intuition, a sixth (Liberty/Oppression) was added. This kind of post-hoc accommodation is a well-known sign of a framework that is descriptive rather than predictive. A genuinely predictive theory would have predicted libertarian intuition from the existing foundations, not been forced to add a new one.
Defenders argue that MFT is at an early-theory-development stage and that taxonomic refinement is a normal scientific process. The middle position — held by many working researchers in moral psychology — is that MFT is a useful empirical taxonomy with theoretical aspirations, more rigorously tested than its critics allow but less predictively powerful than its proponents claim.
3. The political-tribe interpretation has been overgeneralized
The U.S.-specific finding that liberals weight Care and Fairness heavily while conservatives weight all foundations relatively equally has been packaged as a universal claim about political psychology. The empirical record is more mixed. Smith, Hibbing, et al. (2017) showed that the liberal-conservative asymmetry is much weaker outside the U.S., that the pattern reverses in some non-Western political systems, and that the operationalization of “liberal” and “conservative” in MFT studies often relies on U.S.-specific issue positions that do not translate.
This is not a refutation of MFT generally; it is a refutation of the strong universalist read of the political-tribe finding. The U.S.-political application is supported by U.S. data; cross-culture extension requires its own data, not assumption.
For designers operating in cross-cultural contexts, the practical move is to do local moral-foundation surveys before assuming any specific foundation profile applies. Generalizing from U.S. liberal/conservative patterns to other political-cultural contexts has produced predictable backfire effects in advocacy and brand work.
The Brain on Moral Foundations
The neuroscience of moral judgment has converged on a rough picture that is consistent with MFT's intuitionist claim, though the specific mapping to foundations is more contested. The dorsomedial prefrontal cortex, ventromedial prefrontal cortex, and anterior insula are the most consistently implicated regions. Greene et al. (2001), in the influential “trolley problem” fMRI work, showed that personal-harm moral dilemmas activate emotional-processing regions more than impersonal-harm dilemmas, consistent with intuitionist views.
For specific foundations, the mapping is rougher. Care-related judgments engage emotional-processing regions associated with empathy (anterior insula, amygdala). Fairness-related judgments engage reward-processing regions (ventral striatum) when reciprocity is upheld and prefrontal-control regions when reciprocity is violated. Sanctity-related judgments overlap with disgust-processing regions (anterior insula, basal ganglia). Loyalty and Authority foundations are less cleanly mapped, partly because the experimental paradigms for inducing these foundation-specific responses are harder to design without confounds.
One striking finding: Schaich Borg, Lieberman, and Kiehl (2008) showed that disgust-eliciting moral scenarios produce activity that overlaps substantially with physical-disgust elicitors — the same neural circuit appears to handle both. This is one of the cleaner pieces of evidence for MFT's claim that Sanctity-foundation moral judgment piggybacks on evolved disgust-processing machinery.
The broader picture from social-affective neuroscience is consistent with MFT's intuitionist commitment: moral judgments are produced rapidly, by emotional-processing systems, with reasoning systems engaged secondarily to justify the rapid intuition. The pluralist commitment — that different foundations engage distinct neural systems — has weaker empirical support; the neural overlap between foundations is substantial enough that the “modular” version of MFT does not survive in its cleanest form.
For designers, the neuroscience says something important: moral reactions to a narrative are produced before conscious deliberation. Audiences who later “explain” why a campaign feels off are usually rationalizing an emotional reaction that was already present. The intervention point is not the explanation; it is the foundation-relevant emotional cue.
Moral Foundations vs Other Theories
MFT vs Kohlberg's Stages of Moral Development
Kohlberg's stage theory describes moral development as progression through universal stages of moral reasoning. MFT challenges the universalism — Kohlberg's stages, MFT argues, describe one moral profile (the U.S. liberal-academic profile) and treat other moral profiles as developmentally lower. The frameworks are now usually presented as complementary at different levels of analysis, with MFT supplying the cross-cultural pluralism Kohlberg lacked.
MFT vs Gilligan's Ethics of Care
Carol Gilligan's ethics-of-care framework emphasizes Care and relationship as foundations of moral reasoning, arguing that justice-oriented moral psychology underweighted these dimensions. MFT preserves this Care emphasis but extends it — Care is one of six foundations, not the master frame. Gilligan and MFT can be read as complementary refinements of the moral-psychology literature.
MFT vs Social Intuitionist Model
Haidt's earlier (2001) Social Intuitionist Model is the meta-theoretical frame within which MFT operates. SIM says moral judgment is intuitive first and reasoned second; MFT specifies what the intuitive system is responding to. The two are usually presented as a single theoretical package.
MFT vs Self-Determination Theory
Self-Determination Theory emphasizes autonomy, competence, and relatedness as innate psychological needs. MFT's Liberty foundation maps roughly onto autonomy concerns; Care and Loyalty foundations map roughly onto relatedness concerns. The frameworks operate at different levels — SDT at the level of universal needs, MFT at the level of culturally-tuned moral evaluations.
MFT vs Terror Management Theory
Terror Management Theory describes the anxiety-buffering function of cultural worldviews. MFT supplies a description of what those worldviews contain morally. The two are complementary: TMT explains why moral worldviews matter so much; MFT specifies the dimensions on which moral worldviews vary.
Moral Foundations in the Real World
Political campaign messaging
Major U.S. political campaigns since 2016 have explicitly used MFT-derived analysis. Republican campaigns invoke Loyalty, Authority, and Sanctity foundations heavily. Democratic campaigns lead with Care and Fairness. Cross-tribe persuasion — winning over moderates and persuadable opposition voters — depends on foundation-aware messaging that the campaign's own base sometimes resists. The Feinberg-Willer reframing technique has been operationalized in campaign A/B testing with measurable persuasion gains.
Brand purpose and corporate communication
Brand-purpose statements implicitly invoke specific foundations. Patagonia's environmental advocacy invokes Care (suffering of nature) and increasingly Sanctity (the natural world as sacred). Military-adjacent brands (some watchmakers, some apparel) invoke Loyalty and Authority. Consumer-tech companies struggle with foundation positioning because their core audience spans foundation profiles, and a single foundation lean alienates substantial segments. The brands that succeed in cross-tribe positioning typically use foundation-spanning narratives rather than picking one and staying with it.
Charity appeals
Effective charity messaging is one of the most heavily-tested applied domains for moral reframing. Care-focused appeals to conservative donors underperform Loyalty- or Sanctity-framed appeals for the same cause. Loyalty-focused appeals to liberal donors underperform Care- or Fairness-framed appeals. The substantive cause does not change; the framing does. Charities that do this systematically (some major international aid organizations, some animal-welfare groups) outperform charities that use a single moral framing for all audiences.
Game writing and narrative design
Long-form narrative games invoke moral foundations in their character writing, faction design, and story arcs. The Witcher series consistently writes morally ambiguous scenarios that engage multiple foundations and produce strong audience polarization on character choices. Disco Elysium made foundation-pluralism a central design pillar — the player's “thoughts” map roughly onto moral profiles, and the game's outcomes depend on which thoughts the player cultivates. These are conscious design choices that produce measurably different audience reactions and replay patterns.
The Elephant in the Room
The elephant is that MFT is politically loaded. The framework has been adopted on the conservative right as evidence that progressive moral frameworks are partial; it has been adopted on the progressive left as evidence that conservative moral frameworks are atavistic. Neither read is what Haidt and colleagues argued, and the politicization of the framework has badly distorted both its scientific evaluation and its applied use.
Two design rules I treat as load-bearing:
Rule 1. MFT is descriptive, not normative. The framework describes how moral profiles vary across populations. It does not endorse any specific profile as correct. Designs that use MFT to argue for the moral superiority of one profile over another have left applied behavioral design and entered tribal politics. Use the map for understanding, not for ammunition.
Rule 2. Cross-tribe persuasion via reframing requires consent the audience did not give. Moral reframing works because the audience does not realize their moral foundations are being deliberately invoked. The technique is ethically defensible when the substantive position is honest and the reframing is making the same case in language the audience can hear. The technique is manipulative when the substantive position is false and the reframing is being used to bypass the audience's epistemic defenses. The line is real and easy to cross. Designers should know which side of it they are on.
For Octalysis users specifically: Core Drive 1 (Epic Meaning & Calling) is the home base. Every CD1 narrative implicitly invokes specific moral foundations. The MFT-aware design move is to know which foundations the narrative is invoking, which audiences will receive it well, which will not, and whether the cross-tribe gap can be closed by foundation-aware reframing without compromising the substantive mission. The Octalysis White Hat / Black Hat distinction maps onto the difference between honest reframing and manipulative reframing.
How to Apply Moral Foundations with the Octalysis Framework
The Octalysis Framework identifies eight Core Drives that motivate human behavior. Moral Foundations Theory does not map to one Core Drive — it operates as a meta-layer on top of CD1 (Epic Meaning & Calling) narratives, modulating which audiences perceive the narrative as righteous and which perceive it as repulsive.
The Octalysis Framework — eight Core Drives plus the Game Techniques that activate each.
Primary: Core Drive 1 — Epic Meaning & Calling
Every CD1 narrative invokes specific foundations. “Save the planet” invokes Care (suffering nature) and Sanctity (purity of natural world). “Defend our nation” invokes Loyalty and Authority. “Stand up against tyranny” invokes Liberty and Fairness. The CD1 design move is to know explicitly which foundations the narrative is engaging and to design for the audience whose foundation profile matches.
Supporting: Core Drive 5 — Social Influence & Relatedness
Moral foundations shape what counts as “us” vs “them.” Communities organized around Loyalty/Authority foundations have different in-group dynamics than communities organized around Care/Fairness. CD5 mechanics (guilds, factions, alliances) implicitly carry foundation profiles, and mismatched mixes of foundation profiles within a community produce predictable conflict.
Supporting: Core Drive 8 — Loss & Avoidance
Threat framing invokes specific foundations. “Don't let them violate our sacred values” invokes Sanctity. “Don't let them betray our community” invokes Loyalty. CD8 messaging is one of the most foundation-sensitive design surfaces; mismatched foundation invocation in threat framing is a reliable source of audience backlash.
Supporting: Core Drive 4 — Ownership & Possession
Brand and product positioning around “what we stand for” invokes foundations. Luxury goods often invoke Sanctity and Authority (heritage, tradition, refinement). Tech-adoption narratives often invoke Liberty and Fairness (autonomy, equal access). Foundation-aware positioning is one of the highest-impact moves in brand strategy.
White Hat / Black Hat read
The clearest split: White Hat uses foundation-awareness to make honest substantive positions accessible to audiences whose foundation profile differs from the team's; respects the audience's ability to evaluate the reframed argument on its merits; does not pretend the substantive position is something it is not. Black Hat uses foundation-reframing to bypass audiences' epistemic defenses on positions that would not survive direct evaluation; manufactures moral urgency on issues that do not warrant it; weaponizes Sanctity, Loyalty, or Authority foundations to mobilize audiences against perceived threats that are exaggerated or fabricated. The line is real. Designers using MFT in applied work should know which side they are on.
Practical Steps to Apply Moral Foundations Theory
Step 1: Map your audience's moral profile
Run a Moral Foundations Questionnaire (or one of the better newer instruments) on a representative sample of your target audience. The output is a foundation-weight profile that tells you which foundations the audience cares about and which do not move them. The profile is the diagnostic — without it, you are guessing.
Step 2: Audit your existing narrative for foundation invocation
Take your current mission statement, brand purpose, or campaign messaging and identify which foundations it implicitly invokes. Most narratives lean on one or two foundations heavily and ignore the others. The audit usually reveals a foundation profile much narrower than the team realized.
Step 3: Match narrative foundations to audience profile
If your target audience cares about Loyalty and Sanctity but your narrative invokes only Care and Fairness, the narrative will underperform — not because the cause is wrong but because the language is wrong. The Feinberg-Willer reframing technique works here: keep the substantive position, change the foundation language to match what the audience already cares about.
Step 4: Identify the Black Hat temptation
Foundation-aware messaging is so effective that it shades easily into manipulation. The honest test: would the audience endorse the substantive position if the foundation framing were stripped away and the argument presented in their natural language? If yes, the reframing is making your honest case accessible. If no, the reframing is doing something else — usually bypassing their epistemic defenses on a position they would not otherwise accept. The first is White Hat; the second is Black Hat.
Step 5: Test cross-tribe versions of the narrative
For positions that should be tribally neutral (most product brands, most consumer goods), produce multiple foundation-tuned versions of the messaging and test them on different segments. Cross-tribe brands consistently outperform single-tribe brands in long-run market position; the messaging investment to support cross-tribe positioning is real but pays back.
Step 6: Audit your community for foundation-profile mix
Communities with sharply mismatched foundation profiles inside the user base will produce predictable conflict. The CD5 design upgrade is to either (a) explicitly self-segment by foundation profile (different communities for different audiences), or (b) build the community around foundations that span the user base's profile diversity. Generic Care-only or Loyalty-only communities at scale tend to fragment.
Step 7: Update your moral profile data regularly
Audiences shift over time. Generational change, political realignment, and cultural events all move foundation profiles. The profile data you collected three years ago may not reflect your current audience. Build foundation surveys into your regular research cadence.
Closing Thoughts
Moral Foundations Theory is the framework I most often reach for when a CD1 narrative is failing in a way the team cannot diagnose. Almost always, the diagnosis is foundation-mismatch — the narrative is invoking foundations the audience does not weight heavily, or the narrative invokes foundations the audience finds repulsive. The framework is the diagnostic tool. The reframing technique is the prescription. Together they are one of the cleanest applied behavioral-science tools available in 2026.
The framework's scientific status is contested in ways that matter. The factor structure has not held up cleanly cross-culturally. The “theory” status is challenged. The political-tribe interpretation has been overgeneralized. None of this undermines the central observation, which I treat as a working design principle: moral evaluation is multi-dimensional, the dimensions are weighted differently across audiences, and narratives that match audience weights land while narratives that mismatch them backfire. Use the framework with humility about its specific empirical claims, with seriousness about its descriptive insight, and with care about the ethics of cross-tribe reframing. The audience is not fooled forever. Honest substantive positions translate well across foundations. Dishonest ones do not.
